items.title: NZ election 2026 live results: count on as National and Labour battle it out in knife-edge New Zealand poll
paragraphs: Six weeks of campaigning, politicking and debates is done. New Zealand has voted and over the next few hours we’ll find out the results of what has been cast as one of the tightest elections in recent memory.

For weeks, the polls have shown no clear path to government for any potential coalition, left or right. Seemingly unimpressed by National and Labour, polls have tracked voters turning to the smaller parties, such as the centrist Opportunity party.

Tonight could see Opportunity potentially end up as kingmaker, unless that pre-election support and hype has failed to translate into votes. Stay with us as we learn the answer to that big question and others, as we keep you across the counts and results as they come in. It’s going to be an exciting night!
Seats in the house with 20% of the vote counted
More numbers: this time seats in the house with 20% of the vote counted:
National 42, Act 13, NZ First 12 = 67 seats
Labour 35, Greens, 16, Te Pāti Māori 5 = 56 seats
Currently, it is projected there would be 130 seats in the house. For an explanation on this, refer to our overhang post from earlier.

Some of the Labour party candidates are locked in neck and neck races, with tensions high for those at the Labour party event watching the candidates in Hutt South. With more than 20% of the vote counted, Labour’s Ginny Anderson has edged just ahead of the incumbent, National MP Chris Bishop, by just a handful of ballots.
Green MP Julie-Anne Genter is just holding off Labour challenger Craig Renney in Wellington North, while Labour’s Kieran McAnulty is winning against National’s Mike Butterick in Wairarapa.

Elsewhere in Wellington, Labour party MP Ayesha Verrall was hoping to win Wellington North off the incumbent Green MP Tamatha Paul, but early votes suggest this won’t be the case. Paul is leading comfortably, at almost twice Verrall’s count in an electorate where Green is also leading the party vote.
Couple of pics here from Jamie Tahana down at Backbenchers. Bound to be a few of you who know the inside of this place.
Another key feature of this election has been the possibility of an overhang - where a party wins more electorates than its share of the party vote.
If that occurs, more seats will be added to parliament to make up the difference and could dictate which coalition can form a government.

Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) has been calling on supporters to engineer an overhang for its party - by voting for its candidates in the Māori seats, and not giving them a party vote. This could benefit the left bloc.

Meanwhile, if National holds on to a good portion of its seats but its party vote falls short, that will give the party an edge to form a government but could see some of its most prominent MPs out of parliament.
Some more numbers, with 17% of the vote counted.
National are on 30.5%, Labour 29%, the Greens 13%, Act 11.1%, NZ First 9.8%, Opportunity 5.4% and Te Pāti Māori 0.5%.
We’re going to need to start discussing the prospect of overhang seats, as it is heading towards that scenario. We’ll have a post on this soon.
The race between Act leader David Seymour and National’s Paul Goldsmith in the Epsom seat is narrow – a matter of a few dozen votes.
National supporters chanted “Goldsmith, Goldsmith”, when the results appeared on two giant screens, flanking the podium, at the Viaduct Events Centre.
Elsewhere in the Upper Hutt Cosmopolitan Club, punters were ordering crate bottles of local beer Tui and listening to a band kick up a rendition of Tennessee Whiskey.
For Hutt locals, the Cossie Club is a social hub; karaoke on Thursdays, Bingo on Sundays, and a jug of lager for $14 during happy hour.
While everyone spoken to by The Guardian voted for Hipkins in the Remutaka electorate – “he’s a local boy,” – party votes were otherwise split between Labour, the Opportunity party, and NZ First.

“I’ve always voted Labour, Chris knows that,” said Gladys Cooney, 96. “I haven’t heard anything from them this election, I don’t think anyone has gone deep enough.” The cost of living was appalling, she said. “Everything you touch has gone up.”
Fellow local Paul O’Riley also voted for Hipkins, but party voted NZ First. “I worked for 50 years in this country as a truck driver, Winston [Peters] does the most for us.”

Seven of the seats in New Zealand’s 120-seat parliament are Māori electorates. Voters of Māori descent can choose to vote on the Māori roll – allowing them to vote for these seats – or the general roll. More than half of Māori voters are on the Māori roll.
They still get two votes; one for the electorate, and one for their preferred political party.

Last election, Te Pāti Māori won six of the seven seats. But internal turmoil has plagued the party since. Tonight, eyes will be on Te Tai Tokerau – covering the geographical area from New Zealand’s most northern point in Cape Reinga to West Auckland – where the Green’s candidate Hūhana Lyndon could help the party nab their first Māori seat.
Latest polls put her leading the race, followed by Labour’s Willow-Jean Prime and Te Pāti Māori candidate Aperahama Edwards.

Te Pāti Māori remain ahead in most other electorates, aside from Ikaroa-Rāwhiti and Te Tai Tonga (the biggest electorate, covering the entirety of the South Island and Stewart Island) where Labour candidates lead polling.
In an election night that has come down to Chris vs Chris, it’s important to know the difference.

Christopher Luxon, 56, the incumbent, leader of the National party and PM since 2023, is the former chief executive of the country’s national airline, Air New Zealand, and previously worked a slew of corporate jobs worldwide. He entered parliament in 2020, winning the Auckland electorate of Botany. A father-of-two, he is Christian but doesn’t discuss his faith, and has emphasised his business credentials — in 2023, his party was elected on its economic pledges.

Chris Hipkins, 48, the career politician who leads the center-left Labour party, is having a second crack at being PM tonight. Following the resignation of Jacinda Ardern in January 2023, Hipkins, also a father of two, took the reins for nine months ahead of that election, which his party lost. He’s held the Remutaka electorate in parliament since 2008. Some voters still associate him with Covid-19 and strict lockdown measures, while others connect with his pledges for better healthcare and improved cost of living.
Cheers from a rowdy group of National supporters after early results show Chris Bishop may hold on to his Hutt South electorate.
National party faithful are starting to trickle into its event at the cavernous Viaduct Event Centre on Auckland’s waterfront. The room is awash in blue light.
People are grabbing drinks and milling around. The reaction is flicking between nervousness and excitement as the first numbers show the race is - as predicted - neck and neck.

As the first results of the night flashed up onto the big screen, Labour party volunteer Jasmine, 22, who works in the public service and didn’t want to use her last name, stopped talking mid-sentence.

A hush fell over the room as the first poll results show the main parties neck and neck . “That’s close,” she said, exhaling. “It’s great that Opportunity is over 5%, I’m happy about that. It’s just overwhelming; this is years of work, and that’s real numbers.” She’s been working for the party since she was 16.
Cheers are going up in the room as electorate results begin to come in. About 200 party supporters are expected here tonight.

items.title: Parliament restoration delays 'frustrating', says Commons Speaker
paragraphs: Sir Lindsay also questioned why a fire-suppressing mist system had not yet been introduced throughout the building, even though he has called for it for years.
"The major part and the most historic parts of the building haven't got it, and that's what we need."
Asked about reports that Parliament might be given an opportunity to vote on the way forward before the end of 2026, Sir Lindsay said that was a matter for government business managers.
"Who knows when it's going to come forward? Let's see what the House decides," he said.

Much of the 19th-Century building's network of wires and pipes dates back to the 1940s - and some to the Victorian era - according to a report, external which warned of an "impending crisis" a decade ago. Fire safety issues and high levels of asbestos have also been identified.
The BBC understands government whips have discussed holding a debate and vote by the new year, but no date has been scheduled.
This would decide whether to proceed with up to £3bn of initial works and narrow down four current options, ahead of a final decision by 2030.
One proposed option would see MPs and peers move out of the site for up to 24 years from 2032, costing up to £15.6bn.
Another involves moving only the House of Lords out of the building, costing £39bn and taking 61 years.
The chairman of the body in charge of refurbishing Parliament defended the potential costs earlier this year, telling the BBC: "We're already spending £150m a year trying to keep the thing standing."

items.title: From Wild Horse Nine to Kings of Leon: your complete entertainment guide for the week ahead
paragraphs: Wild Horse Nine Out now John Malkovich looks set to be nominated for an Oscar for his portrayal of an ageing CIA agent with terminal cancer who is sent to Easter Island with his younger colleague (Sam Rockwell) in this dark comedy drama from Martin McDonagh (The Banshees of Inisherin).

La Bola Negra Out now Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi were inspired by Lorca’s unfinished four-page fragment of the same name to create this epic Spanish queer drama spanning three timelines, with an international cast including singer-songwriter Guitarricadelafuente, Penélope Cruz and Glenn Close.

I Play Rocky Out now Back in 1975, a struggling actor by the name of Sylvester Stallone wasn’t getting the parts he wanted – so he gave himself three days to write a juicy role. The result was Rocky and the character was so good he had to fight to play it. Anthony Ippolito stars as Stallone in this feelgood dramatisation of the story behind one of cinema’s most famous roles.

One in a Million Out now Winner of the audience award at the Sundance film festival, this documentary follows a girl across an extraordinary decade in her life: from her childhood in Syria to adult life in Germany. Directed by Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes. Catherine Bray

Simple Things festival Various venues, Bristol, 7 November For the first time in its 12-year history, Bristol’s festival celebrating boundary-pushing music has employed guest curators in the shape of Squid, Shabaka, Jeremy Deller and Cobrah. Alongside their picks are the likes of Hannah Diamond, My New Band Believe and the Avalanches. Michael Cragg

London jazz festival Various venues, 13 to 22 November This ever imaginative 10-day festival’s opening night includes spectaculars such as the star-packed John Coltrane centenary celebration (Barbican Hall) and vocal showcase Jazz Voice (Royal Festival Hall), while small-band gems such as saxophonist Jean Toussaint’s JT5 (also Friday, World Heart Beat Embassy Gardens) will be happening all over town. John Fordham

SBTV20 The O2, London, Wednesday The great and the good of the UK grime scene will appear at this 20th-anniversary celebration of the pioneering music platform SBTV. The event, which features Chip, Ms Banks and Tinie Tempah, will also honour the legacy of SBTV’s founder, Jamal Edwards MBE, who died in 2022. MC

Elgar’s Dream of Gerontius The Glasshouse, Gateshead, 8 November The epic oratorio at the heart of the 2025 film The Choral is a blockbuster even without Ralph Fiennes and co. The Royal Northern Sinfonia, local amateurs and a vast choir perform this choral favourite with top-flight soloists Sarah Connolly, Benjamin Hulett and Roderick Williams. Dinis Sousa conducts. Flora Willson

Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires V&A, London, 7 November to 9 May This big, ambitious exhibition looks at 1,600 years of art, design, antiquities and rarities such as the 11th-century Enkolpion of Constantinos, from a city that acts as a cultural bridge between Europe and Asia, east and west, and Islam and Christianity.

Georg Wilson Gainsborough’s House, Sudbury, 8 November to 18 April Young painter Georg Wilson takes an ecological, folkloric, atmospheric approach to landscape painting, which means she should fit in perfectly in the historic surrounds of Thomas Gainsborough’s old gaff.

Ade Adesina City Art Centre, Edinburgh, 7 November to 11 April Aberdeen-based printmaker Ade Adesina uses woodcuts, etchings, linocuts and screenprints to tackle big themes of colonial history and the climate crisis, all with dramatic starkness and intense detail.

Katie Shannon Goldsmith’s Centre for Contemporary Art, London, to 13 December The latest artist to take over GCCA’s experimental Episodes series, where they give a platform to young creatives, is Katie Shannon, with a new body of work looking at lost musical histories and “feminist rereadings of time and space”. Eddy Frankel

The Adam and Joe Show Royal Albert Hall, London, 11 November; Beacon Hall, Bristol, 5 December It has been 30 years since Buxton and Cornish’s cult comedy series was first broadcast. To celebrate, the duo revisit its highlights – toy movies; BaaadDad et al. Rachel Aroesti

Cloud 9 National Theatre: Lyttelton, London, to 13 January Dominic Cooke revives Caryl Churchill’s typically inventive, time-bending, mind-boggling play. It begins in Victorian colonial Africa then jumps to 70s London, with the cast performing theatrical gymnastics along the way. Miriam Gillinson

Owain & Henry Wales Millennium Centre: Donald Gordon theatre, Cardiff, to 28 November Michael Sheen stars as Owain Glyndŵr, a Welsh lord who rebelled against Henry IV after being declared an outlaw. Written by Olivier winner Gary Owen with a cast including Sophie Melville, Linus Roache and Rakie Ayola. MG

Humanhood: Vortex Sadler’s Wells East, London, 10 to 14 November Hypnotic movement from the Birmingham-Barcelona-based duo Humanhood and their company. Artistic directors Julia Robert and Rudi Cole have developed a method that’s somewhere between dance and a spiritual practice. Lyndsey Winship

12 12 12 Apple TV, 13 November A heist: 12 months to plan, 12 hours to execute and 12 days to see whether you’ve got away with it. That’s according to this neat, numbersy cat-and-mouse thriller starring Jamie Dornan as the criminal mastermind behind a Zurich bank vault robbery and Anthony Mackie as the FBI agent on his tail.

Hunting Alice Bell Channel 4, 11 November, 9pm The Guardian’s film critic Peter Bradshaw and his schoolmate David Baddiel once co-starred in a sitcom; now they’ve reunited to create this internet vigilante thriller about a group of women who are all rumoured to be the accomplice of an infamous serial killer (Simon Pegg) living under a new identity.

The Good Daughter Sky Atlantic & Now, 12 November, 9pm Rose Byrne lends her exceptional acting chops to Karin Slaughter’s own adaptation of her characteristically disturbing 2017 novel about the secret truths behind a horrific attack that continues to haunt two sisters. Brendan Gleeson and The White Lotus’s Meghann Fahy also star.

Cunk on Cinema BBC Two & iPlayer, 12 November, 10pm It has been 13 years since “computer typist” Philomena Cunk first appeared as a talking head on Charlie Brooker’s Weekly Wipe; since then Diane Morgan’s alter ego has found fame as a very confused documentarian. Her latest series sees her grill doyens of the film industry in bewildering style. RA

The Devil’s Due PC; out 10 November It’s a classic story: you’ve lost a card game with the devil, and now you must make your way out of hell by defeating all of his minions at poker. Inventive cheating and a characterful collage-esque look make this a trip to hell worth considering.

Shrek 2: Remastered All platforms; out 10 November I’m not sure anyone expected this rerelease of the 2004 movie tie-in, which was surprise-announced just a few weeks ago, but it’s here to capitalise on the run of Shrek nostalgia that has already resulted in an immersive experience, a musical and several Shrek-themed raves. Keza MacDonald

Kings of Leon – O My Beloved Out now On their 10th album, the Followills get reflective. Self-produced, rustic and rooted in nostalgia, O My Beloved looks back at their career, their family life and the moments that shaped them, with the sweet, country-tinged My Whole World a painting of domestic bliss.

Shygirl – Swallow! Out now The artist born Blane Muise channels the likes of the Prodigy, William Orbit-era Madonna and the more interesting aspects of indie on this second album. Songs such as lead single Alyse also bolt on plush string arrangements, creating a sound that feels both decadent and dirty.

Skepta – The Fork and Knife Out now Seven years after his last album, the rapper and producer returns with a record rooted in the sounds of modern Britain. Absorbing everything from grime to house to jungle, its lyrics explore identity and strength via tracks such as the dark-hued Pandora’s Box, while the Fred Again-produced Victory Lap is pure party.

La Roux – Old Flames Out now Never one to be rushed, 00s electropop survivor Elly Jackson, AKA La Roux, follows up 2020’s occasionally brittle Supervision with this warmer album. The minimalist throb of Babyline stands out on a record focused on fresh starts. MC

Talking Common Podcast This engaging new series from author Josh Connolly departs from the usual self-help format and looks for answers to personal problems in community solutions. Guests include the musician Sonny Green on breaking the generational cycle of addiction issues.

International Intrigue Online This daily newsletter briefing from former diplomats is one of the most concise and thorough rundowns of complex geopolitical issues available. Recent topics feature the race for a new UN chief and the EU’s Arctic Strategy.

The Life Scientific BBC World Service, Monday, 8.32pm Associate professor of chemistry Asel Sartbaeva reveals how her research into silica materials has the potential to free lifesaving vaccines from needing to be constantly refrigerated and therefore reducing their risk of becoming spoiled in transit. Ammar Kalia

items.title: This week Kengo Kuma unveiled a pyramidal brick bathhouse
paragraphs: This week on Dezeen Japanese designer Kengo Kuma’s Kai Water Culture House, which features pyramidal towers, was revealed nearing completion in Copenhagen.

The 5,800-square-metre aquatic centre on the city’s harbour will contain 10 indoor and outdoor pools and is opening next month. Kuma designed the project alongside Danish firms Cornelius Vöge, Søren Jensen and Vilhelm Lauritzen Architects.

In Sydney, museum Powerhouse Parramatta opens today. Designed by architecture studios Moreau Kusunoki and Genton, it is described as the largest cultural project in Australia since the Sydney Opera House.
Powerhouse Parramatta is located on the banks of the Parramatta River in western Sydney and wrapped by a steel-lattice exoskeleton.

Annual design week Designart Tokyo is currently taking place in venues across the Japanese capital. Among six standout projects featured by Dezeen from this year’s event, was an exhibition that explores people’s perspectives on forests and a lamp that unfolds like an accordion.
Also on show in the city was the emerging design exhibition Alter, which featured work including an AI-powered tea ceremony and washi paper furniture.
Also this week, automotive brand Fiat launched its Multiplay concept car, which can transform from an SUV into a pickup, with movable seats and an interior designed to be flexible.

Cars were also on the agenda in London, where British car brand Jaguar redesigned its flagship store in Knightsbridge. It is the only place in the world where people can see the recently unveiled Type 01 electric car.
French studio Lacaton & Vassal Architectes, which is led by architects Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal, was named the recipient of the Le Prix Charlotte Perriand 2027.

The studio is known for its social housing designs and was recognised by the Créateurs Design Association & Awards for contributing to contemporary architecture through its work in transforming and improving existing buildings.
Popular projects on Dezeen this week include an arched London apartment building by Alison Brooks, a former workshop converted into a Japanese home and a “quiet yet present” garden studio.
Our podcast this week looked at architects’ salaries in the UK and discussed why architects don’t get paid much.
This week on Dezeen is our regular roundup of the week’s top news stories. Subscribe to our newsletters to be sure you don’t miss anything.

items.title: The Papers: 'Meghan's father charged' and 'Brand investigation widens'
paragraphs: Several of the front pages feature Thomas Markle, with the Daily Mirror describing his charge of possessing child sexual abuse material as a "court bombshell".

The Sun, external features an image of Markle Sr in handcuffs, and reports a "dozen armed agents swooped on his care home" after FBI officers searched "Hollywood lock-ups" he had rented for years. The Duchess of Sussex's father has previously denied wrongdoing.

The Times, external leads on the prime minister's response to Brand's rape and sexual assault conviction. The paper quotes Andy Burnham as saying there is a constant need to "look at the way rape trials are conducted" to ensure victims do not feel "on trial".

The Guardian, external says the "disgraced star" is "suspected of attacks on at least 10 more women", according to its sources. And Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley tells the Daily Mail, external that Brand's conviction could be a "tipping point" which prompts people to come forward with claims about other celebrities.

Burnham will be told to spend up to £6bn getting people back into work, according to The Daily Telegraph, external. The paper understands the recommendation will form part of Alan Milburn's report on youth unemployment - which it says will argue for an "invest to save" strategy.
A spokesperson for the Department for Work and Pensions said they would not pre-empt the review's findings.

The i Paper, external suggests Burnham will be under pressure from within his party to get it right: it quotes the Labour MP Rachael Maskell as saying she wants to see "detail and evidence" that proposals for welfare reform will help people on benefits - not punish them.

The Financial Times , externalreports early success for the pedestrianisation of London's Oxford Street. The paper says spending across the West End increased by 13% in the six days after cars were banned from a stretch of the shopping hub.
And several papers picture Monty Don, who's bid farewell to the BBC's Gardeners' World after more than 20 years. But, as the Daily Star, external quips, "he'll still remain an expert in the field".

items.title: Relief, tears and sadness: Married at First Sight UK cast react to show being axed
paragraphs: Married at First Sight UK cancelled after rape allegations
"I'm delighted and so relieved no-one else will have to go through the same again."
That's what one woman - who alleged she was raped on Married at First Sight UK - texted to me, as the news broke that the show was being cancelled.

Another woman, who also says her on-screen husband raped her, was in tears at the news. She told us she felt "great, consuming relief", but added she was "astounded" it had taken an external review for Channel 4 to finally pull the plug on the show.

Commenting on the review, she said: "Suggesting the programme could reasonably continue with the implementation of a 'safe word', 'panic button' or 'lockable bathroom with an extra bolt inside' is absolute insanity to me."

The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis in May this year, after the BBC's Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - alleged a non-consensual sex act.
The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.

As the news emerged on Thursday morning that Married at First Sight UK - better known as MAFS UK - was being axed, my colleagues and I reached out to the three women who had contributed to our investigation.
None of them had been informed in advance of the decision to cancel the show, they said, although two had contributed to the review.
Shona Manderson appeared on the 2023 series of Married at First Sight UK
Shona Manderson told me by telephone her main feeling was relief that their voices had been heard.
"Speaking out wasn't easy, but knowing that our voices have helped bring about change makes it all worthwhile," she said.
Over the day, more MAFS UK cast members were in touch with us.
Several were pleased by the decision to scrap the series, but others said it did not go far enough and called for more accountability.
One cast member, who asked to remain anonymous, said people watching at home do not always appreciate this "isn't simply a television show" for those taking part.
April Banbury took part in the 2023 series of MAFS UK
Others we spoke to felt the show should have been taken off-air sooner.

They include April Banbury, who took part in the 2022 series and whose on-screen husband was subsequently arrested on suspicion of controlling and coercive behaviour. The police investigation against him was later dropped, and her partner called the allegations against him "false".
"I'm glad MAFS has been cancelled. It should have happened years ago," Banbury told us.

"Cancelling the show does not make what happened go away," added another cast member, who asked to remain anonymous. "We want answers, we want those responsible to be held accountable, and we want to know how this was allowed to happen in the first place."
Others writing on social media said their experiences had been more positive, and that they were sad to see it go.

Jay Howard, from the 2023 series, external, said the show had brought her friendships and opportunities, while Marilyse Corrigan, a 2021 bride, external, said it was a chapter of her life she looked back on "with fond memories".
A number of cast members we spoke to also expressed concern for staff who had been working on the show, as well as sorrow for fans.

Lara Eyre, who appeared on the 2022 series, told me she felt we were now "on the edge of a curb on how we treat reality TV stars and safeguarding", adding it was a "real shame" for those who filmed this year's series, which will never be aired, as well as a shame for fans of the show.

"I know a lot of people loved it, I loved it," she said. "Yes, I know it was traumatic, for sure, and there was a lot of bad things that went with the good. But it was a big part of a lot of people's lives, so it's sad it's not going to be on any more, but I also think this could've been avoided."
As the dust settles, there are still many questions.
Only "a summary of findings" from Channel 4’s review has been released, rather than the full report.
We still do not know what the broadcaster did when it was first warned about the serious allegations by the production company.
Why did it take them so long to investigate? And why did they only do so once BBC Panorama raised the alarm?
We put some of these questions to Channel 4's boss Priya Dogra on Thursday. She said the broadcaster's handling of incidents as they arose was appropriate, and that the review had borne that out.

In a statement to BBC News on Friday, Channel 4 said its review “did not seek to adjudicate on the serious allegations of wrongdoing against a small number of past contributors highlighted by Panorama, as those allegations remain a matter for the relevant authorities”.
Panorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm.
It said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom’s broadcasting code.
Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee on 17 November, so we may hear more then.
Either way, this is not the end of the story. There is an ongoing Ofcom investigation into the show - and in June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.
The decision to scrap MAFS UK will also inevitably raise questions about what happens with the wider Married at First Sight format.
If one broadcaster says the show has “run its course” - then those global versions may also come under the spotlight.
Channel 4 has already said it will not be showing international editions like MAFS Australia again.
And for the TV industry more broadly, questions will once again be asked about reality TV - and whether shows like this can ever keep their contributors safe.
If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

items.title: What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?
paragraphs: It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.

Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.”
“They have decided that there is no appetite for negotiation, with the US out of Paris,” said another developing country diplomat. “Countries won’t engage.”

The summit ended with a deal, although few loved it. But, as the faultlines from the Brazilian decision deepen going into this year’s summit, it is clear that the Paris agreement, and climate action around the world, has reached an impasse.
And it is not just Cop insiders who are worried. For many outside the vast white air-conditioned conference halls, the question, as this year’s summit begins, will be: what is the point?

Those same governments have pledged year after year since the Paris agreement was signed in 2015 – and entered into force a year later – to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Yet temperatures for two years have exceeded that threshold, and the UN revealed a few weeks ago that its most optimistic estimate was now for about 1.7 to 1.8C of heating.
There could be no clearer evidence that the Paris agreement, on the face of it, has failed. It is impossible not to wonder whether the Cop process itself is just not fit for purpose.

The charge sheet against Paris is long, with the central issue being the failure to achieve its goal. Beyond that immediate failure, the negotiation processes are endlessly convoluted and cause their own problems. It took more than five years just to negotiate the Paris “rulebook” under which the treaty is interpreted and put into effect.

The convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given bad actors free rein. Donald Trump’s allies – in Saudi Arabia, Russia, Venezuela and some other petrostates – frequently veto measures and obstruct progress.

It took more than 30 years of negotiation since the UN framework convention on climate change was signed in 1992 for fossil fuels even to be addressed directly. This was at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away from fossil fuels” but failed to set a timeframe or any policies to back up the resolution.
The US, the world’s biggest economy and responsible for about one in every eight tonnes of carbon dioxide emitted today, has withdrawn from Paris under President Trump.

Even parts of the developed world which support the process have mostly failed to come up with convincing plans: Australia, co-host of Cop31, has set no end to fossil fuel exports; its fellow co-host Turkey plans to increase its carbon output. The UK is opening a gasfield and mulling a new oilfield, Germany has dropped its electric vehicle sales targets and scrapped a renewable heating law. Meanwhile, most rich countries are reducing their contributions to climate finance for the poor.
Most of all, the slow pace of the Paris timetable might have seemed fine in 2015, when temperatures were rising at 0.2C a decade. Today, the rate of rise is 0.4C a decade and still accelerating.

“The structures of Cops and Paris are labyrinthine, bureaucratic, and ultimately dispiriting,” said Paul Bledsoe, a former Clinton White House climate adviser, now with the American University. “It may be time to streamline them to focus more deliberately on national emissions reduction goals.”

As ordinary people watch these failures outside and inside the process, some are losing faith. The Paris agreement was a sensation, celebrated around the world. In the years since, the aura of Cop has faded, as meetings seem to disintegrate into arguments over wording and compromise.

“A lot of the commitments, the promises that were made, just turned out to be a bunch of hot air,” said Juan Carlos Monterrey, former climate envoy for Panama, now chief executive of the Vanglabs consultancy. “Under that measure, we have failed.”

Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said: “The fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast, that Earth’s resilience is showing worrying signs of decline, and that we still allow ourselves to follow a global path that will take us to a catastrophic 2.6C-3C, and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”

But, like most involved in international climate efforts, both refuse to concede that Paris is done for. “On the other hand,” said Rockström, “Paris is all we have. And we know that the global climate crisis can only, in the end, be solved if all countries in the world simultaneously move away from planet-damaging heat injection.”

Monterrey agrees. The most important fact about the Paris agreement, and the Cop process, he says, is that they exist. “Paris is our moral compass. It has told us where we should go. The speed of travel is not what it needs to be, but Paris has set the direction.”

This year’s Cop is the first to have a split presidency and host. Being held in Turkey but presided over by Australia, Cop31 is a messy compromise between two countries whose other chief point of commonality is an admiration for coal.

Unexpectedly, however, the skies are a little brighter over this year’s meeting than anyone might have expected. Brazil has decisively re-elected Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva who has already overseen the biggest reductions in deforestation for decades.

The US midterms delivered a drubbing for the right, while in Serbia and Hungary this year democracy has won out over authoritarianism. Though the far right is still on the march across much of Europe, and autocrats still rule in most of the countries with the biggest fossil fuel industries and highest emissions, the replacement or weakening of anti-climate authoritarians by pro-climate parties is a positive sign. Globally, a large majority of people support climate action.

Action beyond the framework of Cop is marching on. After the failure of last year’s Cop30 in Brazil to provide a strong statement on phasing out fossil fuels, a group of nearly 60 countries held an alternative meeting in Colombia in April and agreed to draw up their own national roadmaps for the “transition away from fossil fuels”.

Three major countries have so far done so: France, Germany and the Netherlands. Bledsoe wants to use this model for more side agreements on the “super pollutants” such as methane, refrigerant chemicals called HFCs, ground-level ozone, nitrous oxide and black carbon, or soot.
Cutting methane by 40% could alone hold down temperatures by about 0.3C in the next decade, and deeper cuts beyond that could yield a 0.5C decrease by 2100.

“Paris was never intended to do all the hard work itself,” Bledsoe said. “We need to use the G7, the G20 and other forums too, and we need to elevate the climate to the level of national security concern, and see it as an economic threat.”
While the failures of Paris might seem obvious, its “moral compass” has also translated into greater success in the real world than many people realise.

“The solar panels on my roof and the BYD Dolphin [electric car] my neighbour drives are exhibit one and exhibit two of Paris’s success,” said Claudio Angelo, of the Observatório do Clima thinktank. “Will Paris prevent overshoot of 1.5C? No way. Will it prevent 2C of warming? Unlikely. But the transformation it has triggered can’t be exaggerated.”
Perhaps the clinching argument lies in China, the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and second-largest economy.

“China is taking multilateral climate efforts more seriously than many other countries, and certainly more seriously than it did a few years ago,” said Li Shuo, director of the China climate hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. “The reason is simple: its economic stakes have grown enormously. If the world abandons decarbonisation, where will China sell its solar panels and electric vehicles?”

And, stung by high fossil fuel prices, many developing-country consumers are grasping clean technology without waiting for assistance. In Pakistan, plagued by blackouts and grid supply issues, rooftop solar panels have taken off, now making up about a quarter of electricity use in the country. Similarly, drivers in Vietnam are increasingly opting for cheap electric vehicles from China, which now make up more than 40% of its car sales.

Meanwhile, the conference hosts themselves, from unpromising beginnings, have brought forward one of the biggest new ideas in the last decade for putting the world on track to lower emissions – changing fuel sources for cars and heating to electricity. The electricity should be from clean sources where possible – but its efficiency means that even if the energy source is fossil-based, it still uses less power.

Jan Rosenow, professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University, estimates that the superior efficiency of electricity over fossil fuels will mean that the world’s total final energy use can be halved by switching to electric for everything – meaning we need to generate a lot less, too.

If countries can agree a target at Cop31 of deriving 35% of final energy use from electricity by 2035, up from 23% today, that would be a major boost to decarbonisation efforts. Adair Turner, former chair of the UK’s climate change committee and now co-chair of the Energy Transitions Commission thinktank, said: “Electrification is the single most important thing you have to do [to reach net zero emissions].”

Cops provide a place where countries can come together to share experiences, to seek advice, to find support and fellowship. “That’s very valuable,” said Ilana Seid, ambassador of Palau and chair of the Pacific Small Island Developing States. And in a world in which the bulk of current and future emissions, and fossil fuel production, comes from non-democracies or authoritarian states, Cops also provides one of the few forums where they can be held to account.
That “societal pressure” is crucial, said Seid. “We small islands and vulnerable nations are on the frontline. For us, this is existential. We are all very committed to Paris.”

After all, despite all the doubts, the power of a decision at Cop should not be underestimated. While “coalitions of the willing” are a “good thing” according to Nick Stern, the economist, the universality of the Paris agreement and Cops give them a unique authority.

Sue Biniaz, a former US climate negotiator, said: “Any time you have a consensus decision, it sends a signal to investors, to people who finance things, and to countries. I think that’s true these days with the geopolitics of the world – if something can be agreed by the whole world, it’s impactful.”

Cop31 may bring progress on electrification, on climate finance and on the transition that countries, rich and poor, need to make to a low-carbon world. But we already know that whatever the summit produces, it will not be enough.

However flawed yet substantive they are, Cops last only a fortnight, while efforts to tackle the climate crisis will require such wholesale transformation of our economies and societies that they should top governments’ agendas all year.

“Imagine you have lost your loved one without having their bodies to bring back home. Lost livelihood where you spent your whole life to accumulate those assets. We faced a horrific situation,” said Sujeeta Mathema, executive director of ActionAid Nepal, who was quickly on the scene to help people after the catastrophic glacier collapse there.
“It feels like living with grief, fear and uncertainty about the future. The devastation is not just physical; it is deeply emotional and psychological.”
People are traumatised, she says, and deeply feel the injustice of how the climate crisis is created by the rich while hurting the most vulnerable. But Cop can still be a place of hope, Mathema adds.
“Cop is an important space for us to raise our voice, clearly putting our agenda. Cop can help prevent such disasters if the commitments come off paper and are put into action.”

items.title: Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE
paragraphs: The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.

The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid.
"I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."
There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.

Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates.
"For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said.

Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.
Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order.
He also called on Congress to change federal immigration rules, saying "ICE needs better training. They need body cameras. They need to be trained in de-escalation."
He added, "But this can only be done in Washington. I can only control what I can control."

In response, a spokesperson for the DHS told Houston's NBC affiliate, KPRC 2, in a statement: "We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities."
"Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country," the spokesperson added.
Another Texas city, Austin, has also begun implementing a similar policy change.
Democrats won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.

Texas, a long-time Republican stronghold, was the site of one of the most stunning upsets in the vote, with the state electing its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa, as the first Democrat governor since 1995. It also elected its first Democratic senator since 1988.
Whitmire has previously faced criticism for abiding by immigration enforcement policies under the Trump administration.
He had resisted previous calls to implement similar changes over concerns that the White House could send a surge of immigration officials in response. , external
Abbott has also threatened to take pull millions in funds from cities like Houston, Dallas and Austin unless they allow police to cooperate fully with federal immigration officials.
The BBC has contacted Abbott's office for comment.
Whitmire's announcement comes a week after an ICE officer was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after he allegedly hit a man with a vehicle in Texas.
Earlier this year, large protests broke out in Houston after an ICE officer fatally shot a man driving to work.
The deceased, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national who lived in the US as an undocumented immigrant for decades, was not the indented target, officials said after the incident.

items.title: Paraguay's president impeached after collapse of bank
paragraphs: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after the collapse of a digital bank with links to his private business interests.

Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office due to a widening crisis triggered by the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this week.

He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The demise of the digital bank has left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions prompting widespread protests particularly in the capital, Asunción.

The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
Peña is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.
Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Paraguay's Vice-President Pedro Alliana was then sworn in as interim President.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as President until 2028.

items.title: One of the year's most prolific meteor showers to light up the night sky this weekend
paragraphs: The Leonid meteor shower is set to dazzle sky gazers across the UK throughout November.
The celestial spectacle takes place from now until 30 November with the peak taking place on the night of 17 November.
There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.
The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.
These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second - meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.
Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.
The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.
However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark - perhaps 20 or 30 minutes - will give you the best chance of spotting them.
A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.

Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant - the point from which they seem to appear - will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze.
As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.
This weekend's forecast will not necessarily be great news for those hoping to catch the start of the shower.
While the weather will often be dry, large amounts of cloud are expected to fill the sky in many areas with the chance of a few spots of rain or drizzle.

At the moment the best opportunities for clear skies appear to be in southern and western areas of England and Wales on Friday and Saturday nights, with more cloud in northern England, Northern Ireland and Scotland.
By Sunday night it is likely that more parts of the UK will be clear.
However, fog could be an additional issue, forming in any areas where skies remain clear for any length of time, obscuring the view.

Overnight temperatures will drop into single figures with the chance of a touch of frost in a few locations so if you are looking at the night sky for any length of time you will want to wrap up warmly.
You can always check the hour-by-hour cloud, fog and temperature forecast for your area by checking BBC Weather online or the app.

And if you miss them this weekend then take heart that viewing conditions look particularly good around their peak in the middle of November. This is because the Moon will be below the horizon around midnight, meaning its reflected light will be less likely to spoil the view.

items.title: Skepta: 'I'm what it looks like if you give an immigrant child a chance'
paragraphs: One of the biggest names in grime is back - and he's picked his moment.
"Finally," Skepta promises BBC Newsbeat, "some good rap music, some good UK grime sounds."

The Fork and Knife has been a long time in the making. Seven years on from his last album, Ignorance Is Bliss, and more than two years since it was first teased, the rapper knows how to keep fans waiting.
But, as he's keen to point out, "you can't rush greatness".
And with a Mercury Prize, a Brit and two Ivor Novello Awards under his belt, greatness is no less than what fans expect from this titan of the rap scene.
It's taken so long in part because Skepta's got big issues in his sights, with the new album taking on everything from immigration and racism, to Brexit and culture wars.
"Every time I write a lyric, it's important for me," he says.
"It doesn't matter whose song, what feature, what track, I'm always taking time in writing my music because I want my lyrics to be able to stand the test of time."
Regarded as one of the pioneers of British grime music, he has gone on to draw enormous crowds at festivals like Glastonbury and Reading and Leeds - not to mention his millions of monthly listeners.
His 2009 track Reflecting, which charts his journey from a difficult childhood to becoming a successful musician, was a major turning point for him and grime, he says.
"I feel that was the first grime tune that was introspective and wasn't just about getting hype...
"That was the first time I thought, 'OK, cool, this is a talent of mine'.
"I'm able to speak my true emotion with no filter, no chorus.
"I could just spit my emotions on a track that I made and people will feel it for years to come."
Born and raised in Tottenham, north London, to Nigerian immigrant parents fleeing the country's civil war, Skepta, real name Joseph Olaitan Adenuga Jr, has long drawn on his early life in his music.
Dipping into multiple genres for his sixth album, he's set out to explore what it means to exist between cultures and how it's shaped him as an artist.

In Innocent Smile, his new track featuring Chase and Status and Madness frontman Suggs, he raps: "Ain't no love for an immigrant child / The writing's on the wall, has anyone else noticed? / Was it Brexit? Was it Covid? / They point fingers, I feel hopeless."
"I think grime is a product of immigration," he says, with some of the genre's biggest names and pioneers - like Wiley, Stormzy and Dizzee Rascal - all coming from similar backgrounds.
"That was important for me to represent what it looks like if you give an immigrant child a chance.
"I'm British and I thought before I even get into a campaign, I wanted to let my stance be known that I'm for multiculturalism."
And while Skepta's been focused on the message, he has also been deliberate about how he's delivering it.
"It took six years to make this because it's important to make sure we're not tone deaf," he says.
He learned the value of that when, in 2024, he had to take down artwork for his single Gas Me Up (Diligent), following allegations that it referenced the Holocaust.
The image showed a group of men with shaved heads, one featuring a tattoo reading "Gas Me Up".
It had been a reference to skinhead culture, but Skepta acknowledged how without that context people could find it offensive and promised to be more mindful going forward.
Determined not to miss the mark this time around, he says: "I feel like we've delivered a classic."

Early reviews are mixed as to whether critics agree, however. While Complex said The Fork and Knife was "top-tier" and worth the wait, external, The Observer said it was well-intentioned but questioned whether it was "over-egged", external.
At a time when he thinks standards have been slipping though, striving for a classic is more important than ever.
"I don't think there's been a good grime album for a long time," Skepta says.
In September, Digga D called out the viral 'UK Poo' trend, which saw a wave of tracks blowing up on TikTok defined by what he described as "foolishness".
"I can't sit on here and be like 'I'm happy with how the UK scene is right now'," the rapper told 1Xtra's DJ Target. "Because I'm not."
Drawing on his idols, and even featuring some of them like Suggs, he says he is "here to make rap sophisticated again".
As BBC Radio 1Xtra launches the first UK rap chart show, he's hopeful more grime artists will be inspired to sharpen their pen game.
"Rap is a sport and it's very hard for visibility when we're being compared to people who have major machines behind them," he says.
"So this rap chart is going to give all the newcomers and a lot of people who are producing in their bedroom a chance to be seen and heard."

items.title: Ousted Paraguay president under house arrest after banking crisis leaves 60% of country unable to access accounts
paragraphs: Paraguay’s rightwing president has been placed under house arrest minutes after he was impeached by Congress, amid a severe crisis that left more than half the country’s population unable to access their bank accounts.

Santiago Peña is being investigated about allegations he used his political influence to favour a bank that expanded exponentially under his government and was suspended this week after irregularities.

The move froze the accounts of 2.9 million people, about 60% of the country’s adult population, who were customers of the bank – Ueno - and who overnight could no longer use their own money even for basic purchases such as bread and water.
Protests spread across the country, some involving violent clashes with police. Impeachment proceedings began on Wednesday before being concluded on Friday, minutes before Peña’s arrest was ordered.

His vice-president, Pedro Alliana, was being sworn in as the country’s new leader while a public prosecutor, accompanied by police outside Peña’s home, told local media the former president had been placed under house arrest.
“It has been established that he is indeed inside his home. He voluntarily allowed officers to enter and made himself available for all procedural purposes,” said prosecutor Elena Fiore Franco.
The public prosecutor’s office had opened an investigation into Peña on Thursday on suspicion of illicit enrichment, money laundering and influence peddling.

Peña, who was one of US president Donald Trump’s main allies in the region, had tried to resign on Thursday in an attempt to retain the special jurisdiction afforded to former presidents – who become senators for life in Paraguay – but lawmakers did not accept his resignation, leaving him subject to the ordinary courts.

Amid rumours he had fled to Argentina, the 47-year-old economist was expected to appear before Congress to present his defence during the impeachment proceedings, but left that to his lawyers and instead continued posting on social media.

Before the impeachment was concluded or the arrest warrant issued, he posted: “I say goodbye with gratitude, while fully recognising the anguish of those who are now waiting for answers,” referring to former Ueno customers who are unable to access their own money.

Soon after taking office, Peña appointed Carlos Carvallo Spalding, a former CEO of Ueno, head of the country’s central bank. Three months later, Spalding – who was by now regulating the company he used to run – allowed Ueno to become a digital bank, which put it on the path to becoming one of Paraguay’s largest banks by deposits in just a few years.
The arrest warrant for Peña also includes Spalding.

Peña himself had about US$1m in shares he bought in 2019 in a company that would become Ueno Holding in 2022, the parent company of the conglomerate that controlled Ueno Bank. Even after becoming president, he only disposed of the shares in April 2025. He said he had bought them purely as an “investor”.

As the bank aggressively expanded through an easy account-opening system and by promising returns far above those offered by the rest of the market, it also managed to bring public pension funds controlled by Peña’s administration into its portfolio.

“Because Ueno had the blessing of the presidency, most of the pension funds close to the government went to deposit their money in the bank,” said political analyst Hugo Duarte. An estimated $800m to $860m in state and pension funds were invested in Ueno.
As pressure mounted and retail sales fell by as much as 80% because much of the population could not access their own money, Peña lost the support of his own party.

During the impeachment session, opposition senator Rafael Filizzola said Paraguay was facing “one of the biggest corruption scandals since the return of democracy” and the “biggest fraud carried out from political power in the democratic era”.

items.title: 'My mortgage is going up £200': How rising interest rates are hitting people's pockets
paragraphs: The BBC spoke to three people about how they could be affected by rising interest rates
ByDaniel Thomas and Raphael SheridanBBC News
On Thursday, the Bank of England increased interest rates for the first time in over three years as it tries to get a grip on rising inflation linked to the Iran war.
Experts say there could be more hikes over the next 18 months, as the conflict continues to push up food, fuel and energy prices across the UK and worldwide.
Higher interest rates affect borrowing costs, however, which means mortgages, credit cards and personal loans could get more expensive for millions, even as savings rates improve.
For some, it could mean extra financial pressure at a time when they are already struggling with the cost of living. The BBC spoke to three people about how they could be affected.
Peter Gill says his family's costs are rising
Peter Gill, 48, is one of the around 1.3 million Britons on a variable rate mortgage.
These loans track the Bank of England base rate, with a margin on top determined by the lender, so any rise in interest rates can push up repayments.

Peter, who runs a small tiling business in Halifax, says his monthly repayments will go up by roughly £45 following Thursday's quarter-percentage point increase and he's worried they could climb higher.
But he still thinks it'd be more expensive to move onto a fixed-rate deal - which is when you pay a set amount of monthly interest for a period - and is prepared to stay put for now.
Watch: What does the raise in interest rates mean?
His higher mortgage costs come as the "cost of everything is going up", he says.

The father of two, who has a combined household income of £45,000 with his wife Faye, is having to pay his staff more because of increases in the national minimum wage. Raw material costs have also risen due to the war in Iran.
At home, the family's food, gas and electricity bills have gone up and he says he's working "about six and a half days a week" to shield them from the worst of it.
"From my point of view, inflation goes up which costs you, then interest rates go up and you have even less money."
Dawn Fazackerley-King is struggling but says there's "no more fat to trim"
Most UK mortgage holders are on fixed-rate deals, but that doesn't necessarily protect them when the Bank of England puts up rates.
David Hollingworth, from brokers L&C Mortgages, says many people will be shocked at how much higher fixed-rate deals are than they were five years ago following recent increases.
"Fixed rates have already risen due to market anticipation that interest rates would need to rise to combat higher inflation," he says.
Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living.

She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother of two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month.
"I don't know where that money is going to come from, it's something we are going to have to figure out as a family. It's stressful."
She and her husband, who have a joint income of about £70,000, have already gone through their direct debits and there's "no more obvious fat to trim".
There is also no scope for them to take on additional work, as they both work full time.
"We're still living in the same property, our household costs are remaining the same," Dawn says. "It's an additional cost of several hundred pounds but we're not getting anything extra for that."
Higher interest rates are "another cost to deal with", says Ben
When the Bank of England increases its base rate, credit card borrowing costs also tend to increase, although the impact is not always immediate.
It may affect people with outstanding debts, as providers can increase the interest rates they charge with 30 days' notice.
Ben Thomas, 41, from Shropshire, ditched his career as a chartered accountant during the Covid pandemic after a mental health crisis and retrained as a paramedic.
But the drop in income left him reliant on credit cards and personal loans for everyday living expenses and he is now £52,000 in debt.
Ben says he's reached an agreement to pause the interest on most of it, but he is still incurring charges on around £2,000 of credit card debt and is worried about his repayments going up.
"With all that's going on, rising interest rates is another cost to deal with," he tells the BBC.
As well as overall debt repayments of around £300 a month, he and his wife pay £760 on their mortgage. They have also struggled with higher food and energy bills.

Simon Trevethick is head of communications at StepChange, which has been helping Ben manage his debt. He says the debt charity has seen a 20% increase in people asking for support this year and warned of tougher times ahead.
"If higher borrowing costs feed through into household budgets over the coming months, we could see further pressure on people seeking support."

items.title: Gladiator II stuntman sues over injuries from on-set explosion
paragraphs: A British stuntman and actor is suing one of the companies behind Gladiator II, saying he suffered "excruciating" burns and permanent scarring in an accident while filming a scene on a burning ship.

Edward Sarsfield was playing a dead soldier in the movie in 2023 when a gas line used for special effects exploded on the vessel, causing 20ft flames that made his costume catch fire, his legal claim said.
He "panicked and ran" before colleagues threw bottles of water over his burns, which covered about 15% of his body, including his face, his arms and hands, he said.
Sarsfield is suing August Street Films, whose defence said it admits liability for the accident, but has not made an admission about the alleged injuries or agreed to the requested £200,000 damages.
Gladiator II, released in 2024, was the long-awaited sequel to the hit 2000 drama starring Russell Crowe. The follow-up was directed by Sir Ridley Scott and starred Paul Mescal and Denzel Washington.
Sarsfield, 47, from Liverpool, said he was working as an extra in a scene in Morocco in which a coastal castle was under siege from an approaching ship.

"The Claimant, playing a dead soldier, was lying on the port side of a ship which had been lit up by gas powered flame bars to simulate it being on fire," according to documents he filed at London's High Court.
"He was positioned only a few feet away from the gas line. Without warning, there was a gas explosion that caught the Claimant and blew him forwards.
"He saw 20 foot tall flames and felt immense heat. His costume caught fire. He was immediately aware that strips of skin had peeled from his arms.
"He panicked and ran, falling over a few times before escaping the flames. Bottles of water were thrown on him by colleagues, he was undressed and clingfilm was applied to his burns."
The legal claim said he suffered "flash burns" to 15% of his body, plus injuries to both knees and his right wrist, and was flown by helicopter to hospital in Marrakesh.
"He remained in excruciating pain. Treatment there was limited," Sarsfield's claim said. He was repatriated to the UK four days later, where his wounds were "treated appropriately" in hospital.

"Formerly a man of considerable physical prowess, the Claimant suffered considerable physical de-conditioning," with limitations to his mobility, and also suffered psychological symptoms, his claim said.
It added: "He has sustained significant scarring that is permanent and which is hypersensitive. He needs to keep out of the sun."
August Street Films' legal defence said "no admissions are made as to the alleged injuries sustained by the Claimant".
The company is a subsidiary of film studio Paramount, which said several people were hurt in the accident.

A Paramount spokesperson said in 2023: "While filming a planned stunt sequence on the set of the Gladiator sequel, an accident occurred during which several crew members experienced non-life-threatening injuries.

"The safety and full medical services teams on-site were able to act quickly so that those who were impacted immediately received necessary care. They are all in stable condition and continue to receive treatment.

"The well-being of the cast and crew is of the utmost importance to us, and we have strict health and safety procedures in place on all our productions. We will continue monitoring the situation and taking all necessary precautions as we resume production."
Sarsfield, August Street Films and Paramount declined to comment further.

items.title: This man refused life-saving treatment because of his religion - days later the rules changed
paragraphs: In August this year, 26-year-old Isaac Valdez had an epileptic seizure while browsing in his local library, causing him to convulse and strike his head against the ground.
He lost consciousness. Later, in hospital, it transpired Isaac had hit his head with such force it had led to a brain haemorrhage.

Treatment was seriously complicated by the fact that, as a Jehovah's Witness, Isaac carried a "No Blood" card, an indication that he would not accept treatment involving any form of blood transfusion because of his religious beliefs.
As a result, a procedure to drain fluid from Isaac's brain did not take place.
But his family, from Waxahachie, Texas, were encouraged by the fact that he regained consciousness and even started to talk again. He was able to confirm that he stood by his "no blood" beliefs.
The family's relief at his apparent improvement was short-lived. Isaac slipped into a coma and his condition worsened rapidly.
A neurosurgeon told Isaac's family the only way to save his life was an emergency operation, but that it was one that required blood transfusion.
His family took the decision to abide by Issac's wishes as a lifelong Witness not to accept such a procedure.
Isaac - who his twin brother Jacob Valdez describes as an intelligent man who loved volunteering and helping the elderly - died on 26 August 2026 when doctors turned off his life support.

Just 23 days later, the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body announced a seismic change in teaching that would, in effect, have given Isaac the religious green light to have the life-saving treatment he had refused.

The change suddenly means the vast majority of medical procedures using donated blood are no longer prohibited to followers. Now, decisions on whether to accept such treatments are to be left to individuals.

Jacob, already dealing with the death of his twin, was angered at the Jehovah's Witnesses' leadership for not coming to their conclusion sooner. He told BBC News he believes Isaac could well still be alive if they had.

The original rule on blood transfusions dates back to 1945, towards the very end of a war during which the use of blood transfusions had been increasingly widespread. The leaders of Jehovah's Witnesses announced that their believers were not permitted to accept transfusions.

This was based on their interpretation of Bible verses from both the Old and New Testaments prohibiting the consumption of blood, including one from the Book of Acts that instructs believers to abstain from blood, from food offered to idols, and from things that had been strangled.
So, why has the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body, based in New York state, now decided to change the rules, 81 years after introducing them?
It comes after years of pressure from both within and outside the faith, but that is not how leaders of the faith describe the decision.

"The change is basically the application of Bible principles to modern medicine and its methods," says the Jehovah's Witnesses international spokesperson, Paul Gillies, who described it as both a fresh look at scripture and at medical advances.

We meet Gillies at the Jehovah's Witnesses UK headquarters set in 85 acres of Essex countryside. It is a vast modern complex where hundreds of volunteer followers of the faith live and work without pay.

He insists the basic teaching has not changed and that the transfusion of whole blood is still prohibited. However, for decades, most transfusions have not used whole blood, instead using the specific components of blood that are needed by the patient.
The change is being justified by permitting the use of blood components, like plasma and red blood cells and platelets, in the huge numbers of medical procedures that were previously banned.
Gillies says the Bible references "abstaining from blood" but not "various components that could be extracted from blood".
He says the Governing Body felt it their duty to avoid scriptural "overreach" and only apply what was specifically described in the Bible.

But that explanation has stunned many and led them to ask if it was not a huge overreach 81 years ago to ban blood transfusions in the first place, when transfusions are not specifically mentioned in the bible.
Others are then also asking why it has taken so long to come to this landmark decision, given that transfusions that do not use whole blood have been the norm for decades.
These are questions Jacob asked as soon as the ban was lifted, just days after a memorial service for Isaac.

Jacob, who had already left the Jehovah's Witness faith he was brought up in, texted prominent figures from Isaac's congregation in Texas after Isaac's death. The messages are full of angst, and painful to read.
He asked them to consider "the part you played in encouraging so many people to sacrifice their life for something that was never God's will".
Most did not reply, but one "elder" responded saying he could not understand why Jacob was so angry and fixated on the policy shift.
This all further infuriated Jacob, who particularly wants the faith's decision-makers to be accountable for all the lives lost.
"I want to ask them if they could apologise directly, I would like not to have a deflected answer, just straightforward apology," he says.

It is extremely difficult to say how many Jehovah's Witnesses, among the estimated nine million followers of the faith worldwide, died each year having refused treatment involving blood transfusions. But research in one medical journal in 2016, The Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey, put the figure at around 1,100.
"We're sympathetic to their feelings, and if individuals have lost family members and are concerned about some of these questions, they deserve to be heard compassionately," says Gillies.
But there was little clarity about why the change did not come earlier.
"Why has it taken this time? Well, I guess because it takes time, it doesn't necessarily mean that there is some magic change that's taken place," says Gillies.

And when asked, Gillies deflects calls for the leadership to apologise, saying that many lives had, in fact, been saved because faithful Jehovah's Witnesses had not been exposed to blood contamination scandals.

He also insists that even after the new edict, some Jehovah's Witnesses could still decide they did not want to accept a transfusion, and that may have been the case even if the edict had come years ago.

Indeed, the BBC spoke with Alex Ball, 58, a Jehovah's Witness from West Sussex, who says in 2012 a doctor told him he would not survive the chemotherapy he needed to treat his blood cancer unless he also had a transfusion.
"I wanted to adhere as closely to the scriptures as possible when I was sick, and I think I did that well."

With help from what is called "a Jehovah's Witness Hospital Liaison Committee", Alex found an American consultant who could perform a treatment to boost Alex's blood cells without the need for any products from someone else. His UK consultant agreed to treat him using the new method and it worked.
More than a decade later, Alex says he would make the same decision again, despite the change in blood policy that would have permitted the transfusions he had been told he needed.
It is not just receiving blood which has been an issue.
Elisha Cummings, 50, a Jehovah's Witness from Trinidad and Tobago, was unable to donate blood to her aunt, who died, because of the rules.

They also cost her her marriage too, with her husband of 10 years leaving the faith and divorcing her after it came to light that he had had a blood transfusion as a child, something that was looked down upon in her Witness community.
"Since the blood policy change, I have not been myself," she says. "It left me in a sort of depressed mode."
"How many houses did I go to trying to convince people about the blood doctrine? And you're coming now and it's something totally different," Elisha says.
Elisha says her beliefs as a whole have been shaken, yet she feels reluctant to leave the faith, partly because it is what provides her with her community and she fears isolation.
In the past, those who disagreed with "blood doctrine" were ostracised or felt like they needed to leave the faith. Will they now be able to come back?
"Any individual that wants to come back to the faith is warmly welcomed," says Gillies, speaking of those who had left the faith because they had accepted a transfusion for themselves or a relative.
"If they would like to become one of Jehovah's Witnesses again and would like to speak to the elders, then they're very welcome to do so."

items.title: Ben Roberts-Smith collaborates with gym business run by influencer that sold ‘war crimes’ pre-workout supplement
paragraphs: Ben Roberts-Smith has collaborated with a gym supplements company run by a rightwing influencer which recently sold a pre-workout product called “war crimes”.

Roberts-Smith, one of Australia’s most decorated living soldiers who is currently awaiting trial on war crimes charges, has recently launched an apparel brand, Epic 1 Two, producing T-shirts and gym wear.

In October, he also appeared in a social media video collaboration between his brand and Zero Limits supplements, co-owned by the rightwing podcaster and fitness coach Chris Katelaris, also known as “Big Chocky”.

Roberts-Smith, Katelaris and others were filmed during a gym workout, with on-screen graphics reading “Zero Limits Supplements x Epic 1 Two”. Both brands were labelled “collaborators” on the video, which is also published on the Instagram grids of both brands.

Months earlier, Zero Limits had repeatedly posted online about a product titled “war crimes”, an energy supplement in the flavour “kill or capture cola”. Its label depicted a hooded captive on a chair in a room with an Australian flag on the wall, and a tall figure wearing a balaclava and military-style clothing.
In a video on 26 July, Katelaris promoted the product while holding a tub at the gym.
“You wanna drink out of a prosthetic leg? You wanna re-enact a Sparta kick? You wanna execute your workout?” he said.
“War crimes, it’s the pre-workout for you.”

Zero Limits, which says it is “veteran owned and operated”, does not currently list the “war crimes” product on its website, and Roberts-Smith is not shown endorsing, referencing or using that particular product.

The former soldier has praised another product from Zero Limits, posting an Instagram story – since shared by the brand – from Epic 1 Two’s Instagram page of himself drinking a separate pre-workout drink.

Roberts-Smith gave the brand a “massive shout out” and told followers to “get on their website and take a look”, sharing a link to its website. Roberts-Smith also last week appeared on the Zero Limits podcast, hosted by another founder of the supplements company of the same name.
Roberts-Smith was in April arrested and charged with five counts of war crime – murder, in relation to three incidents stemming from his service in Afghanistan in 2009 and 2012.

He has denied the charges, saying in a statement after his arrest: “As I’ve always maintained: I categorically deny all of these allegations … I will be taking this opportunity to finally clear my name. I’m proud of my service in Afghanistan.”
