The three incidents allegedly involved Afghan nationals being shot dead by Roberts-Smith, or a subordinate under his command, while he was present, the AFP commissioner, Krissy Barrett, said in April.

Roberts-Smith was previously found in a defamation suit – using the civil standard of the balance of probabilities – to have murdered unarmed civilians while serving in the Australian Special Air Service Regiment (SAS) in Afghanistan.

The federal court found to the lower civil standard that Roberts-Smith kicked Afghan man Ali Jan in the chest, sending him falling backwards over a cliff before he landed on the ground. The court found that Roberts-Smith then ordered another soldier to shoot him dead.
Roberts-Smith was also accused in media reporting of shooting an unarmed prisoner who had a prosthetic leg. The leg was later used as a drinking vessel by soldiers.
Zero Limits, Katelaris and Roberts-Smith were contacted for comment.
In a statement via a lawyer, Zero Limits did not respond to specific questions, only answering: “The products are great, make sure you check them out.”
In a statement via the same lawyer, Katelaris also did not respond to specific questions, but said: “If you thought this was wild, wait until next week’s campaign drops.”

Katelaris lists himself as a “co-owner” of the supplements brand in his Instagram bio. He also promotes a range of merchandise under his own name in support of Roberts-Smith, including “I stand with BRS” T-shirts, hats, hoodies and stubby coolers.

items.title: What happens if all the lights go out? This is the plan for a 'Black Sky' event
paragraphs: It was a Saturday night in early December when Roger Kemp realised something was very wrong.

"I was halfway through a Scandi crime drama when everything went off," the professor at Lancaster University told the BBC. "Streetlights were off. The sodium glow that we can see over the horizon from Morecambe was off."
"[It was] almost like a zombie movie," he said. "People trying to find phone reception, wondering where things were, and there was a huge queue at the one working telephone box."
At 22:45 on 5 December 2015, the River Lune - which flows directly through Lancaster - had flooded, and the electricity supply to 61,500 people in the city went.

Households lost light and heat, some water supplies also began to fail because they relied on electric pumps. The railway station closed. So too petrol stations and shops. Most cash machines didn't work. Traffic lights failed.

The two communication systems that survived were copper wire landline telephones and FM radio. The local commercial radio station The Bay had an emergency generator and one landline and a reporter was sent outside the affected area to ring in with information.
Three months later, Kemp, a professor of engineering with a specialism in safety and electrical systems, gathered people together to look at everything that had gone wrong.

"It is perhaps ironic that, in a society with huge commitment to digital infrastructure, the most reliable source of news was a commercial station using technology that would have been familiar to the engineers on the 1960s Radio Caroline pirate radio ship," the subsequent report concluded.

For Kemp and others in the field of civil contingency, Lancaster was a warning. When a town loses power for several days, our connected world falls apart. This kind of disruption has been given a name: a Black Sky event.
At a recent summit on UK resilience, the conversation focused on the need for the UK to be able to withstand a Black Sky event for a minimum of 72 hours.

"We are nine meals from anarchy" is a phrase often heard in the civil contingency world. A brutal reminder of the fear that three days without food would be enough to turn a crisis into chaos. If a Black Sky event takes out electricity, water, shops and communications, there is a good reason the government wants us to have our own supplies.

The much talked about "Be Prepared" campaign is designed to help ready us for all sorts of possible crises, but the government says there is no specific threat to the grid. Regardless, a Black Sky event is definitely at the backs of people's minds.
In a major emergency, we are being told to hunker down and turn on an FM radio, as thousands did in Lancaster. This is why the BBC has its own Black Sky plan.
Only a small number of staff know the full details, but from what I have gleaned, about 100 people in the BBC will run a special emergency radio studio.
It will have secure lines of communication not dependent on the internet, and fuel, water and food to ensure it can operate without resupply for at least three days.
This emergency service will broadcast pre-arranged government messaging. The scripts have already been published online., external
They include instructions on how much people should be drinking each day and how to dispose of toilet waste without flushing the toilet.
Other information will be broadcast via satellite vehicles from a select number of journalists at emergency centres around the UK, which will carry on as long as the diesel lasts.

The BBC's broadcasts will be sent via radio transmission towers, isolated from the internet and equipped with tanks of between five and 40,000 litres (8,800 gallons) of diesel to keep their generators going for three days - FM radio is power hungry. The teams will be using satellite phones to keep in touch and if these stop working there are pre-agreed protocols and meet-up points.
Why FM? Because it works almost everywhere, even in a blackout or a crippling cyber-attack.

"It was originally thought we should plan for five to seven days," I was told quietly by one BBC insider. "The latest advice from Neso [National Energy System Operator] is that they will probably be able to get the power back on in two to three days."

Of course, fears of a grid failure are not new, but recent events such as the mass blackout in Spain, Portugal and south-western France in April 2025 have pushed it up the agenda. And the more it happens, the more it reveals the problems it can create in our networked world.

People need to know power cuts are about more than just the lights going out, says Lord Harris, chair of the UK's National Preparedness Commission. ''It's likely to stop the water supply because unless you happen to be located neatly downstream of a reservoir, that requires electricity," he told me.

More importantly, sewage tends to solidify unless water can move through it, he adds, "and that then causes blockages, the whole thing backs up, you get sewage flowing out, flowing back up the system".
It's common for governments in Europe to regularly advise households to stock up on supplies in case of a national emergency - but the UK is behind in its warnings to the population.

However, work has begun on some backup systems, such as High Altitude Pseudo-Satellites (HAPS). The government is spending £70m developing planes that can circle over the UK and provide at least a week of emergency mobile phone and internet connectivity at times of crisis.

"When ground networks fail, there are limits to what satellites can provide as a fallback," said Rico Chandra, programme director for Enduring Atmospheric Platforms, the company developing HAPS plans.
We live in a complex, electrically powered world - but the more connected everything becomes the more catastrophic it is when that fails.
In the drive towards efficiency over the last five decades, we've lost backup systems, says Lord Harris.

An example of this is the new communication system being adopted by the emergency services, which will replace radio comms with mobile phone network technology, says Lord Harris, "so if the mobile phone goes down it will also impact on emergency services communications".
However, the government insists "moving emergency services onto modern 4G and 5G technologies" is "resilient and reliable".

Government enthusiasm for resilience is nothing new. Oliver Dowden, the then deputy prime minister, launched the last Conservative government's disaster planning initiative in May 2024. The launch was somewhat overshadowed by Sunak announcing an election on the same day but, two years on, calls for at least three days of resilience have only grown stronger.

At the beginning of researching this article I spoke to an engineer about the UK's TV and radio transmission masts, their lonely isolation from the rest of the digital landscape sounded like a failing. It now feels like an argument in their favour.

The current urgency for disaster planning is coming at an interesting moment for technology we used to rely on. The UK's copper wire landline system - which would work even in a power cut - will be switched off on 31 January 2027. The future of FM radio is also under government review.
The response from the government was that while copper landlines had been a useful fallback during power cuts, they were now unreliable and difficult to repair.
As I ended my call with Kemp, I asked him if his report had helped improve our readiness for a Black Sky. He paused.

"If anything, we've gone backwards," he said. "Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you've no longer got power."
While writing this piece last Saturday I had to break off for an hour because my street was suddenly plunged into darkness. We had a power cut.
I found my emergency torch, but the batteries had leaked. My candles had been pushed to the back of a cupboard and I had no idea where I had put my wind-up radio with its emergency torch.

items.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
paragraphs: is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion.

Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects.

OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”
Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

items.title: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
paragraphs: In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.
On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.
Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.

"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.

One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests.
"Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."
Watch: Trump says he appointed Stephen Miller ‘to make a change’

Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.

He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.

He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.
Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.

He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.

Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.

The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.
What has Stephen Miller’s role been in Trump’s second term?
While Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.
It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats – and some Republicans.

"Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X. "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."
Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".
The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.

Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.

On Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-president JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement- by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance".
That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.

Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".
Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises.

"Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.

At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

items.title: Whole Australia team knew of sandpaper use, Khawaja says
paragraphs: Usman Khawaja has claimed the entire Australia team knew about the use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball in the final Test of their 2018 series with South Africa.

In extracts of his autobiography - Sabr - published in the Sydney Morning Herald,, external the former opening batter said Australia had also used the ball-tampering tactic in the Test before the infamous match in Cape Town.
The incident - nicknamed 'sandpapergate' - was widely condemned and led to bans for captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and fellow batter Cameron Bancroft.
"It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," Khawaja, 39, told the Sydney Morning Herald.
The four Australia bowlers who played in that match, including current Test captain Pat Cummins, have consistently denied they had any prior knowledge of the plan.
In 2021, Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon issued a joint statement saying they "did not know a foreign substance was taken on to the field".
Khawaja, who scored 6,229 runs in 88 Tests, said that discussions about tampering with the ball began during the second Test of the series against South Africa.

That match, played at Port Elizabeth - now Gqeberha - led to what Khawaja said was the "discovery of sandpaper as an effective agent" after "open" discussions held in the dressing room at St George's Park.
"At this point Smith essentially threw his hands in the air and said he didn't want to know," Khawaja wrote.
Australia were rumbled in the third Test when television cameras clearly showed Bancroft using sandpaper on the ball to help generate reverse swing.
Khawaja was also shocked not to be asked to provide any evidence during Cricket Australia's investigation.
"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth," he said.
"The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now."
While Smith, Warner and Bancroft - all batters - were punished, there was never an explanation of how bowlers Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon did not notice a change in the state of the ball.
In a 2021 interview with the Guardian, Bancroft was asked if the bowlers knew and replied: "It's pretty probably self-explanatory."
Days after Bancroft's interview was published, the quartet released their statement which said: "We feel compelled to put the key facts on the record again.
"We did not know a foreign substance was taken on to the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.

"And to those who, despite the absence of evidence, insist that 'we must have known' about the use of a foreign substance simply because we are bowlers, we say this: The umpires during that Test match, Nigel Llong and Richard Illingworth, both very respected and experienced umpires, inspected the ball after the images surfaced on the TV coverage and did not change it because there was no sign of damage.
"We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."
Before Australia's recent Test series in South Africa - which the Proteas won 2-1 - Cummins said he had spoken to Khawaja about the publication of the book.
The 33-year-old said he has no concerns about potential sandpapergate revelations and felt it was "all dealt with then" and the team had "moved on".
"He didn't go into too much detail, just basically gave me the heads-up that he is doing a book and, as always, no worries," Cummins said on 8 October.
"Tell your story. It's fine. It's obviously a long time ago and all the investigations, everything was done back then and we answered every question a million times."
Khawaja also said he had consistently argued that the team should take responsibility together, including in the dressing room after the Cape Town Test.
He wrote: "I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'.
"Obviously, it didn't work that way, and those three guys got crucified."
In his memoir, named after an Arabic term for resilience and endurance, Khawaja dedicated the chapter on Cape Town to Smith, Warner and Bancroft.
The left-handed batter said he thought the trio "deserve" the "justice" of collective blame from the team as a whole.
He added: "None of those three want to be the first to say anything. And rightly so, it will just be hearsay and 'their word' if they do. They needed someone else to say something.
"But I'm not doing this for any other reason than I think it's the right thing to do."

items.title: When a single vowel stands in the path to victory, the stakes could not be higher for these spelling bee champions
paragraphs: Competing in a spelling bee is not for the faint of heart. Sometimes, the difference between victory and loss is one incorrect vowel and you’re undone, months of training reduced to nought.
At a small theatre hall in Sydney’s west on Friday afternoon, 34 primary school students sit stony-faced on a brightly lit stage, knowing this pressure only too well.

All have made it past about 200,000 students who competed in spelling bees across 1,070 public schools in New South Wales. The finalists earned their place at this year’s state competition after winning online regional finals in August. They represent the top 0.03%. And they’re not here to mess around.

Five are competing for a third time, having progressed to the last stage in the junior competition. Among them are year 5 student Wafiq Ayyash from the Hunter region, who won the junior state title in 2024, and year 6 student Bobby Ivaneza from the inner west, who was runner-up the same year.

Ewan Mattick from the state’s central west, Caleb Borg from the Riverina, and Alesha Kahfandi from the Hunter have also qualified for the state finals on three occasions. This isn’t their first rodeo.

The format is relatively simple. Contestants begin with “seen” words that they’ve been able to practise at home, before facing “unseen” words testing their broader skills and composure. Each round is sudden death.
To kick off, they’re introduced to the crowd by the host, ABC presenter Rae Johnston, with colourful details.

Archie Griffith likes the Parramatta Eels and his dachshund puppy. He doesn’t like his dad’s jokes. Ivaneza, who is wearing a bright red sweatband, admires Nicola Tesla, a Serbian-American engineer who died in 1943, for his genius. Ivaneza’s favourite food is camembert.
The students are as diverse as the schools they come from. Some 23 speak a language other than English at home, and 18 have travelled from outside Sydney.
Seven go down in the first round, stumbling over obscure words like “tourmaline” and “malapropism”. Another seven are out in round two – but you try spelling “lepidopterist” at home.
In the next four rounds, 13 students fall. Mattick nails “centurion” and gives a thumbs up to his family. Come round seven, Kahfandi begins to pray.
“Pernicious” and “sagacious” bring two more students down. And then there are five: Afeef Ahmed, Ivaneza, Kahfandi, Caroline Wang, and Maximilian Lumley, all in year 6. Two are returning finalists.

In round eight, they all spell their words correctly, though Ivaneza, usually breezing through with confidence, restarts on “whimsical”. Then, in round nine, he’s asked to spell “unserviceable” and omits the second “e”.

Ivaneza, visibly devastated, slumps into his seat and places his head in his hands. The remaining students spell their words correctly, and Ivaneza tearily returns to his family in the crowd and the comforting embrace of his father. The heartbreak is palpable.

Then, in an instant, after Ahmed correctly spells “immemorial”, the remaining three competitors fall. Kahfandi misses “antepenultimate”, Wang gets tied up by “parmigiana” and Lumley is one letter off getting “genealogy”. Ahmed has won.

“We are in an interesting situation,” Johnston says. “We need to play for a runner up.” Wang goes out straight away after being dealt the word “grandiloquent”. But Kahfandi and Lumley appear to be in lockstep. For the next five rounds, they’re either both correct or both wrong.
“We’re just going to keep on going,” Johnston declares. It begins to feel that the audience will grow old in this theatre, steadily working its way through the entire Macquarie Dictionary.
But then, Kahfandi misses the word “vociferous”. Lumley approaches the microphone and awaits his fate. His word is “apocalypse” and, after a deep breath, he nails it.

The crowd bursts into cheers, and Lumley returns to his seat and stares reflectively at the ground, looking like he has endured a war. His grandmother, Sue, is bursting with pride. “It was so stressful,” she says, “and he looked so calm.”
“He’s worked so hard. Some of those words, I didn’t even know what they were. We’re very proud.”

Kahfandi is proud of herself, too. “It was very tense in the room, there was a lot of pressure on everyone,” she says. “I feel a bit disappointed I didn’t get second and I was a bit tired after all those rounds, but getting third place is also really good.”
Ahmed is surprised he’s won, but his mother isn’t. She’s been helping him train for months – half an hour every night before bed.
“He reads a lot,” she says. “I knew he would win; he was three-time champion at school.”
Asked how he felt when he found out he’d won Ahmed says, at first, he “didn’t realise”.
“But then when they said we had a winner, I felt happy,” he says. “The runners-up words were harder than the ones I got.”

items.title: From young offender to junior doctor: 'I wrote a plan and stuck to it'
paragraphs: Steven Beattie was a gang member and is soon to graduate as a doctor
Steven Beattie spent his teenage years in and out of Polmont young offenders' institution, once described by a former governor as "the most violent prison in Scotland", external.
He was sent there at 16 after drunkenly crashing a stolen car, and returned repeatedly over the next four years as his involvement with gangs and violence grew.
For Steven, the turning point came when he was punished for his part in a fight by being locked up for 23 hours a day and having his TV removed.
"I never really had time to sit down and think where my life was going," he told the BBC's Scotcast podcast.
"When they took my telly, I finally had that opportunity."
He asked himself - if he kept doing what he was doing, where would he be in five years' time?
"If I don't like that destination, I'll have to change it," he says.
Steven admits it wasn't easy for a young offender to start a new life but, after years of effort, he's about to graduate as a junior doctor.
Steven will graduate from University of Dundee Medical School in June
Steven, who is now 37, grew up in the Hillington area of south-west Glasgow.
His father had the degenerative disease Parkinson's, and his mother was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia as well as cancer, from which she later died.
"I was under a lot of stress at home," says Steven, who was a carer for both his parents.
He left school at 15, and thinks few of his teachers understood how much stress he had been under because he had been "embarrassed" to tell them.
Looking back, he gives himself "a degree of sympathy" that he didn't do so well in school because of what he was dealing with at home.
"A lot of the time I couldn't make school because I was up to three in the morning looking after my parents," he says.
The Polmont prison riot and life as a young offender

Martin Geissler and David Cowan, Scotland home affairs correspondent, speak to Steven Beattie (pictured) about his time in a young offender institute, problems facing the prison system and his rehabilitation.
Steven says avoiding gangs was "impossible" where he grew up in the 1990s and early 2000s, as "gang violence was rife".
The threat of a spell in Polmont kept him out of trouble for a while, but once experienced, its deterrent effect disappeared.
He made close friends while inside and, at first, life there wasn't as bad as he had feared. But he struggled to cope with the relentless noise, especially when he was trying to sleep.
"You've got people kicking your doors and constantly shouting and screaming, and people are in there for months and sometimes years," he says.
"You can imagine the effect it has on a developing brain, being in that environment for years at a time."
Steven says his early life put him under a lot of stress at home
Eventually, Steven made a decision to change his life and wrote down three things he had to do - leave Glasgow, quit drinking, and stop hanging around people who got into trouble.

When he left Polmont, he thought most employers would find it difficult to trust him, so he started his own personal training business. He is also an award-winning MMA fighter known as 'Doctor Beatdown'.
Working for himself gave him the ability to save up and move out of Glasgow. But his long-term goal was to become a doctor.
He had been inspired by his dad's neurologist, who had noticed how much Steven was able to understand about his father's Parkinson's.
His school grades were not enough to get him into medical school, so he attended an access course at Glasgow Kelvin college to study physiology at the University of Glasgow.
That then got him into medical school, and in June, he'll graduate as a junior doctor. He hopes to specialise in either surgery, neurology or emergency medicine.
Steven was in and out of Polmont over a number of years
Polmont was back in the news last week when it emerged it had recently experienced the worst prison rioting in decades.
Prison officers from four other jails were called in to restore control during the incident, which involved about 30 inmates.
Linda Pollock, chief executive of the Scottish Prison Service (SPS), said it was an example of "bubbling tension" caused by increasing overcrowding.
Steven says overcrowding can add to pressure inside prison.
"Especially in terms of rehabilitation," he says.
"The staff just no longer have the capacity to give attention to individual prisoners."
He says a lack of attention can make inmates feel they're being left behind and unsupported.
Without support they are unlikely to move on with life after prison, he says.
Steven says his teenage experiences have made him more determined to enjoy the chances he has now.
"I think I've got an appreciation for life that a lot of people don't have because I know how bad it can get," he says.

items.title: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says.

Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new.

The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

items.title: Man, 41, and boy, 16, arrested after car damaged by gunshots
paragraphs: Two people have been arrested after armed police responded to an incident in which a car was hit by gunshots.
South Wales Police said a vehicle on the A48 in Morriston, Swansea, sustained damage "consistent with a firearms discharge" on Friday.

A 41-year-old man from Llansamlet, Swansea, had been arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm with intent to endanger life, while a 16-year-old boy, also from Llansamlet, had been arrested on suspicion of affray.
The force said officers were still investigating and that it had been declared a critical incident.
Residents have been told to avoid the area and events, including a local firework display, have been cancelled.
Video circulating online shows police officers next to a stationary car that appears to have been struck by a shotgun blast on Clase Road near an Asda superstore.
A National Police Air Service helicopter was circling the area but has since returned to base.
South Wales Police said the incident was ongoing, with road closures in place.
Ch Supt Stephen Jones said: "A policing presence will be visible in the area whilst this investigation is ongoing."
"It is important that people avoid the area so we can effectively deal with this incident and return the area to normality."
The local football club, Morriston Town AFC, cancelled a planned firework display on Friday.
"Unfortunately, the police have advised due to an issue ongoing, the event has to be cancelled. With immediate effect," it said in a social media post, advising people to stay at home.

items.title: Starlink Mobile: All the news on SpaceX’s major mobile carrier ambitions
paragraphs: SpaceX has declared that it’s going to make Starlink Mobile a “major” mobile carrier. The Elon Musk-owned company has already deployed thousands of direct-to-cell satellites, but its next big challenge is building out its 5G network here on Earth.

As part of its plans to rival AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, SpaceX has inked a deal with Qualcomm, which will deploy its cellular technology across tens of thousands of 5G cell sites starting in 2027. SpaceX is also reportedly in talks to buy Boost Mobile, potentially allowing it to launch Starlink Mobile through the service. Another report suggests SpaceX may tap into 80,000 cell sites across the US to build out its network.

SpaceX’s big plans have garnered some reactions in the telecom industry. Tim Höttges, the CEO of T-Mobile’s parent company Deutsche Telekom, said he takes SpaceX’s plans “super serious” but that it could cost Musk more than $200 billion to pull off.
Follow along for the latest updates on Starlink’s major mobile carrier ambitions.
Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier.

Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.”
What will it take for SpaceX to launch its “major” mobile network?
Bloomberg has a breakdown of how Starlink Mobile will operate — and what SpaceX still needs to do to get its hybrid 5G network up and running.
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images

SpaceX has discussed a deal with Boost Mobile to launch its own service through the budget-friendly carrier, according to a report from The Washington Post. The deal, which comes as SpaceX aims to make Starlink a “major” mobile carrier, reportedly involves the Elon Musk-owned company acquiring Boost Mobile or accessing its network.

Musk discussed the potential agreement with Charlie Ergen, chairman of Boost Mobile parent company EchoStar, last month, as reported by The Washington Post. Boost Mobile’s network is currently powered by T-Mobile and AT&T, meaning SpaceX may need permission from the two carriers to launch its service.
Photo: George Frey / AFP via Getty Images

SpaceX plans to access at least 80,000 cell sites as part of efforts to compete directly with Verizon, T-Mobile, and AT&T, according to a report from Bloomberg. Sources tell the publication that SpaceX is in talks with Crown Castle Inc., one of the nation’s largest cell tower owners.

The move would give SpaceX access to half of the 158,500 cell towers currently operational in the US, according to Reuters. When asked about a potential partnership with SpaceX, Amazon, or other satellite services during an earnings call on Wednesday, Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant said, “I don’t think I want to get into customer-specific detail, but you can assume that we’re talking to all parties.” SpaceX plans to pair a network of cell towers with its constellation of direct-to-cell satellites.
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images

SpaceX has acquired a portfolio of low-band spectrum licenses — a move the company says “will pave the way” for its Starlink Mobile service to become a “major” US carrier. When the Federal Communications Commission signs off on the deal, SpaceX says it will deploy its new architecture that combines its satellite-to-mobile constellation with a terrestrial mobile network, directly competing with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon.

The licenses include up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band, which SpaceX says will allow Starlink Mobile’s signal to penetrate through walls and buildings. SpaceX previously acquired 2GHz spectrum from EchoStar as part of efforts to bolster its direct-to-device service.
Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images

SpaceX is preparing to build a terrestrial mobile network to “acquire quite a few” of the customers now subscribed to T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon. The message to compete head-to-head with the US carriers was delivered by SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and CEO Elon Musk during the Q&A section of the company’s first earnings call.

“The spectrum that we purchased from EchoStar does have terrestrial components, so we definitely intend to build out the terrestrial component,” said Shotwell. “You will have not only the capacity from the satellites themselves, but you will have a buildout of the terrestrial, basically the hardware and systems necessary to make a true mobile service exactly what you want it to be.”

items.title: North Korea’s Binance hack raises global financial security concerns
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

Cybersecurity experts tell VOA that the recent North Korean hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange is particularly concerning because of the speed of both the attack, and how quickly the hackers moved the assets through financial networks.

Michael Barnhart, lead nation-state threat researcher at California-based cybersecurity company DTEX, told VOA that “one of the most significant aspects of the Binance incident was the speed at which the stolen funds were transferred."
"Rather than holding onto the cryptocurrency, the attackers moved it to Chinese money launderers within minutes," he said.

More than $6.3 billion worth of virtual assets were stolen from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, and “about $2.8 billion was frozen before it could be fully laundered or integrated into North Korean control,” Barnhart said. Some $3.5 billion of the stolen cryptocurrency remains in circulation, and efforts to trace and freeze the funds are continuing.

Nick Carlsen is a senior Investigator at TRM Labs who spent 12 years as an intelligence analyst at the FBI initiating major U.S. investigations into North Korea's illicit financial networks. He told VOA in a recent interview the speed and scale of the response to the hack “were unprecedented." He said stablecoin issuers and industry partners moved quickly to freeze substantial assets, but recovering the remaining funds will be difficult because laundering methods have become increasingly complex.

"The stolen funds appeared to have been divided into tens of thousands of transactions, many of them seemingly automated, making them harder to trace," Carlsen said, noting that he expects a substantial portion of the proceeds will ultimately reach the North Korean government, “although the final amount that can be recovered remains uncertain."

Large cryptocurrency exchanges face security challenges because of their size and global reach. Carlsen said exchanges “with thousands of employees have numerous potential entry points for hackers." He said companies handling large amounts of financial assets therefore need multiple layers of security, so that a single compromised account or system cannot expose their holdings.

Analysts also point to the financial objectives behind North Korea’s cyber operations. While Russia and China have often focused on espionage, including the theft of sensitive information and industrial technology, North Korea has increasingly used cyber operations to generate revenue.

“Cybercrime and cryptocurrency theft have become the North Korean government’s largest single source of foreign currency," he said. "The proceeds can be used for a range of government activities, including potentially supporting the country’s nuclear and missile programs."
Barnhart said North Korea has little reason to stop targeting cryptocurrency exchanges.

Previous attacks on platforms including Axie Infinity and Bybit, followed by the Binance breach, show that the sector remains an attractive target. The financial returns remain substantial, while the risks to the North Korean government are comparatively limited.
Both experts said stronger corporate cybersecurity measures are necessary but insufficient to address the threat.
Barnhart argued that “companies can do only so much to defend themselves against repeated attacks without a policy response."
"Governments, particularly the United States and South Korea, must take a more active role in responding to North Korea’s cyber theft operations," added Carlsen.

The Binance breach is part of a series of major cryptocurrency thefts attributed to North Korea. While exchanges continue to strengthen their defenses, the experts say a broader response from governments will be needed to disrupt the networks that move and launder stolen funds.

items.title: Taliban destroys 650 musical Instruments citing music ban
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

The Taliban in Afghanistan's eastern Khost province have destroyed 650 musical instruments and music-related items confiscated during a months-long crackdown on musical instruments, highlighting the continued enforcement of the group's nationwide ban on music.

According to a statement posted on X by Mustaghfir Gurbaz, who identifies himself as a Taliban spokesperson in Khost, officials from the Department for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice burned the items that were seized during operations across the province.

Since returning to power in August 2021, the Taliban have prohibited most forms of music, allowing only certain types of religious vocal chanting. The ban is enforced by the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice.

"Music is forbidden in Islam," ministry spokesman Saif ul Islam Khyber told the Associated Press, arguing that it promotes immoral behavior and distracts people from religious obligations, though many Islamic scholars disagree.

The restrictions have dramatically altered Afghanistan's cultural landscape. Once vibrant music districts, including Kabul's historic Kucha-e-Kharabat neighborhood, have seen music shops replaced by grocery stores, clothing vendors, and household goods businesses.
Many musicians fled Afghanistan following the Taliban takeover, while others hid or smuggled instruments abroad to prevent them from being confiscated or destroyed.

The destruction is Khost is not the first large-scale Taliban campaign against music. In 2024, the group's morality authorities reported seizing and destroying more than 21,000 musical instruments nationwide, an action widely condemned by cultural organizations and musicians as a major blow to Afghanistan's artistic and cultural heritage.
In 2024, Dr. Ahmad Sarmast, founder and director of the Afghanistan National Institute of Music (ANIM), described the campaign as an attack on the country's cultural identity.

"The Taliban's actions are not only an attack on musical instruments, but an assault on the spirit of freedom, creativity, and the vibrant cultural legacy of Afghanistan,” Sarmast said in a statement two years ago. “They have tried to silence the voice of a nation, but music cannot be erased from the hearts and minds of the Afghan people."
ANIM, which relocated from Kabul to Lisbon after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021, continues to support displaced Afghan musicians and preserve the country's musical traditions.
Despite the ban, some Afghan musicians continue to practice their craft secretly.
In a recent Associated Press report, one rubab player speaking anonymously said he continues to play in secret.

"As long as I am alive, I will continue to play," he said. "Perhaps I will do so in secret, but I will not allow the rubab to be silent." The lute-like instrument is widely regarded as Afghanistan's national instrument.

The musician said the ban has devastated his livelihood. Before the Taliban takeover, he taught music and operated a traditional instrument shop. Today, he works as a day laborer and earns only a fraction of his former income.
He also expressed concern that Afghanistan's centuries-old musical traditions risk disappearing if younger generations are unable to learn and perform.
For many Afghan musicians, music represents more than entertainment. It is a family tradition passed from one generation to the next.
The anonymous rubab player said he learned from his father and intends to teach his eldest son despite the risks, viewing music as an essential part of Afghanistan's cultural identity.

Observers say the destruction of musical instruments by the Taliban highlights the tension between the group's religious policies and efforts by many Afghans to preserve the country's artistic and cultural heritage.

As authorities continue enforcing the music ban, musicians across Afghanistan face a difficult choice: abandon their profession, leave the country, or continue practicing in secret while risking arrest and punishment.

items.title: KPop Demon Hunters on 4K Blu-ray costs less than a month of Netflix Premium
paragraphs: is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Buying the 4K Blu-ray disc version of KPop Demon Hunters was already going to be a wise idea for some people, especially those who primarily keep their $26.99 Netflix Premium subscription just to watch the hit animated flick in 4K. But at just $24.99 from Barnes and Noble and Amazon instead of its original $49.95 price, it’s easier than ever to recommend.

The Criterion Collection version of the film recently launched, and comes with a bunch of extras in a gorgeous set. In addition to the 4K digital master, complete with Dolby Vision HDR and Dolby Atmos sound, you also get two standard 1080p Blu-rays, one containing the film, and the other packed with special features (a full feature-length animatic, a making-of documentary, lyric videos, and more). It includes physical goodies, too, like collectible postcards, as well as an essay by Polygon alum Karen Han.
Kpop Demon Hunters was on my list of physical movies to buy, and this deal just turned it into a must-buy ahead of the holiday season.
