items.title: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist
paragraphs: Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023.
In a Times and Sunday Times podcast on Thursday, Rosamund Urwin said she introduced herself to Ian Winter KC outside court after verdicts were delivered.
She claimed he responded with a "snarl" and said "I hope you're pleased with yourself".
"Apparently I said, but I can't actually remember this but I've read it in reporting, 'I am pleased that justice has been done'", Urwin said.
She said that Winter replied "it wasn't" and suggested she was to blame using a profanity.
In a statement, Winter said the "ways matters have been characterised" in the media meant they should be "subject to proper scrutiny".
On Friday, Winter said he considered his professional duty required him to self-report the allegations to the Bar Standards Board.
The Bar Standards Board regulates barristers in England and Wales in the public interest.

In a statement, Winter said: "Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today's press I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board, so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny. I have made such a report."
Four women variously accused Brand of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint investigation by Channel 4 Dispatches and the Times and Sunday Times in September 2023.
The actor and comedian denied the allegations.
On Friday, Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations against Brand.
Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark praised the "bravery" of the women who reported their allegations to police and gave evidence during the trial.

He said police would "do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful people who are responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life" when sexual assault allegations are made to them.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been asked about Labour's past association with Brand.
Some party figures sought his support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.
At the time, Brand had gained a following for his left-wing political punditry.
Then Labour leader Ed Miliband was interviewed by Brand shortly before the 2015 election, and in 2014 Burnham publicly backed Brand during a row over claims about the comedian's housing arrangements.
At the time he said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".
Speaking on Friday, Burham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."
He described Brand's crimes as "horrific" and said he had been rightly held to account, adding: "I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing."
Brand is being held in custody ahead of his sentencing on Monday.
After the jury returned its verdicts, Mr Justice Bennathan told him to expect a "significant custodial term".

items.title: How climate change worsens heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and floods
paragraphs: In January 2026, wildfires in Chile caused the evacuation of more than 50,000 people
Many extreme weather events are becoming more common and more intense around the world, fuelled by human activities such as the burning of fossil fuels.
Here are four ways that rising temperatures are affecting weather extremes.
Even a small increase in average temperatures makes a big difference to heat extremes.
As the range of daily temperatures shifts to warmer levels, hotter days become more likely and more intense.
Scientists use computer models to simulate how individual extreme weather events unfold in two scenarios:
today's world with about 1.4C, external of human-caused warming
a hypothetical world without human influence on the climate
That way, they can estimate, external how much a particular heatwave, storm or drought was affected by climate change.
The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.
Five widespread heatwaves affected the country, resulting in 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F).
Head of Climate Attribution at the Met Office, Dr Mark McCarthy, described summer 2026 as "remarkable" and warned that extreme heat events would only become more common as the world warms.
Climate change has also intensified multiple heatwaves across the world this year, according to scientists at the World Weather Attribution group (WWA).
Examples include Australia's worst heatwave in six years in January, the 45C that India experienced in April and Europe's deadly June temperatures.
Heatwaves can happen as a result of heat domes, external, which are created when an area of high pressure stays over the same area for days or weeks, trapping hot air underneath.
UK winters were 13% wetter, external in the decade from 2016 to 2025 than between 1961 and 1990, the Met Office says.
However, the large annual variation in rainfall makes it difficult to draw conclusions from a single decade, its scientists warn.
Globally, heavy rainfall events have become more frequent and intense over most land regions due to human activity, according to the UN's climate body, the IPCC, external.
For example, in October 2025, Hurricane Melissa became one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the Caribbean.
WWA researchers found that climate change increased extreme rainfall associated with the storm by 16%.
A drought in Puerto Rico led to water rationing in summer 2026
Linking climate change with specific droughts can be difficult because there are lots of different factors that affect the availability of water.
Natural weather systems like El Niño can play a key role, as was the case with drought in southern Africa in early 2024.
But climate change is shifting global rainfall patterns. While some of the world is getting wetter, other parts are becoming drier, which can make them more prone to drought.
And heatwaves fuelled by climate change can worsen dry conditions when they do occur by increasing evaporation from the soil.
This makes the air above warm up more quickly, leading to more intense heat.
During periods of hot weather, increased demand for water, especially from farmers, puts even more stress on the water supply.
Climate-driven heatwaves worsened drought conditions throughout Europe this summer, according to the EU's Joint Research Centre, external.
Four of Europe's key rivers - the Loire, Po, Rhine and Danube - reached record low levels.
Drought was declared in all of Wales and two-thirds of England, with the highest category - "severe drought" - being used for the first time in parts of southern England.
Elsewhere, the WWA found that climate change intensified a severe drought in Jamaica and Puerto Rico from May 2026.
Global warming made extreme dry conditions 40% more likely, external in Jamaica and 30% more likely in Puerto Rico, the WWA said.
Fires happen naturally in many parts of the world.
It is difficult to know if climate change has caused or worsened a specific wildfire because other factors are also relevant, such as changes to the way land is used.
But climate change is making the weather conditions needed for wildfires to spread more likely, the IPCC says, external.
Extreme, long-lasting heat draws more moisture out of soils and vegetation.
These tinder-dry conditions provide fuel for fires, which can spread at incredible speeds, particularly if winds are strong.
In January 2026, fires in Chile and Argentina resulted in 55,000 evacuations. The area burned was around 36% larger due to climate change, according to a global report on wildfires, external.
More than 5,000 wildfires burned across Canada this summer, resulting in some of the worst air quality levels in the world being recorded in nearby cities.
Climate change made the conditions which enabled the fires to spread twice as likely, according to the WWA, external.
Wildfires produced record air pollution in Canadian cities this summer
Many fires are started deliberately or accidentally by humans. But rising temperatures may also increase the likelihood of lightning in some forests, which can in turn trigger more fires.

The combined effects of shifting land use and climate change mean extreme wildfires are projected to become more frequent and intense globally, according to the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), external.
The number of the most extreme fires may rise by up to 50% by 2100, UNEP suggests.
2026 was the UK's second worst year for wildfires after 2022, according to provisional data, external from the housing department.
In Stourbridge, two fires destroyed 19 homes on the hottest day of the year.

items.title: A really simple guide to climate change
paragraphs: Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events
Human activities are causing world temperatures to rise, posing serious threats to people and nature.
Things are likely to worsen in the coming decades, but scientists argue urgent action can still limit the worst effects of climate change.
Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.
The world has been rapidly warming for around a century, causing weather patterns to change.
Since the 1980s, each decade has been warmer than the previous one, the Met Office says.
2024 was Earth's hottest year on record, with climate change mainly responsible for the high temperatures.
It was also the first calendar year to surpass 1.5C of warming compared to "pre-industrial" levels of the late 1800s, according to the Copernicus climate service, external.
Temperatures remained high in 2025, despite a slight cooling from a natural weather pattern called La Niña.
The opposite El Niño pattern, combined with climate change, makes it likely that 2026 will also rank among the hottest years ever recorded.
The climate has changed naturally throughout the Earth's history.
But natural causes cannot explain the particularly rapid warming seen over the last century, according to the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
This has been without doubt caused by human activities, especially the widespread use of fossil fuels - coal, oil and gas - in homes, factories and transport systems.

When fossil fuels burn, they release greenhouse gases - mostly carbon dioxide (CO2). This CO2 acts like a blanket, trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface. This causes the planet to heat up.
Since the start of the Industrial Revolution - when humans began burning large amounts of fossil fuels - the level of CO2 in the atmosphere has risen by more than 50%.
The CO2 released from burning fossil fuels, external has a distinctive chemical fingerprint. This matches the type of CO2 increasingly found in the atmosphere.
Climate change has already had a huge effect, including:
more frequent and intense extreme weather, such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall
rapid melting of glaciers and ice sheets, contributing to sea-level rises
warmer oceans, which can fuel more intense storms and harm sea life
These changes are already having serious consequences for people and economies around the world.
In August 2026, the partial collapse of a glacier caused an avalanche of ice and rock to descend on Nepal and Tibet
Flash floods in Nepal killed more than 1,400 people in August 2026. Nepal's Finance Minister, Swarnim Wagle, said it could cost up to a tenth of the economy to rebuild.
Climate change increased the chances of the glacier collapse which triggered the flood, World Weather Attribution group scientists said.
The more the world warms, the worse the impacts of climate change become.
Nearly 200 countries pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels in the 2015 Paris agreement.
That target is generally understood to mean an average annual increase of 1.5C over 20 years rather than a one-off rise in a single year.
Long-term warming of 1.5C would bring serious consequences for many populations.
But an increase of 2C or more would bring even greater impacts, the IPCC says.
increased risks to food security in some regions due to more extreme weather
greater chances of some climate-sensitive diseases spreading, such as dengue
more species being threatened with extinction
The call to restrict temperature rise to 1.5C was partly designed to avoid crossing so-called "tipping points".
It is not clear exactly where they sit, but once these thresholds are passed, changes could accelerate and become irreversible.
These could include the collapse of the Greenland Ice Sheet, warm Atlantic Ocean currents or further loss of the Amazon rainforest.
The Earth's poles are especially vulnerable to rising temperatures
About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people are highly vulnerable to climate change, the IPCC says.
People living in poorer countries are expected to suffer most as they have fewer resources to adapt.
This has led to questions about fairness, external, because these places have typically only been responsible for a small percentage of greenhouse gas emissions.
However, knock-on impacts could be felt over wide areas. For example, crop failures linked to extreme weather could raise food prices globally.
Reaching net zero CO2 emissions is essential to limit global warming, the IPCC says.
This means reducing emissions as much as possible and actively removing any remaining emissions from the atmosphere.
Most countries have, or are considering, net zero targets, external.
There has been encouraging progress in some areas, such as renewable energy and electric vehicles.
But humanity's CO2 emissions are still at record highs, causing long-term warming to reach 1.4C in 2025.
The latest UN Emissions Gap Report, external said the 1.5C limit was likely to be breached in the coming years.
A return to 1.5C by 2100 was possible, but it would require "urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions", the report added.
Otherwise, global warming could reach nearly 3C by the end of the century, the UN said.
Major changes need to come from governments and businesses, but individuals can help through actions like:
improving their home's insulation and energy efficiency
switching to electric vehicles or living car-free
replacing gas boilers with electric systems like heat pumps

items.title: What is the Paris Agreement and why does 1.5C matter?
paragraphs: Nepal became the first country approved to receive money from a fund for damages linked to climate change after flash floods in August 2026
ByMark Poynting, Esme Stallard and Alex Brian
In Paris in 2015, almost 200 countries signed a landmark agreement designed to limit global warming to 1.5C and avoid its worst impacts.
But despite some progress in areas like renewable energy, the world has continued to warm at a rapid pace.
A recent UN report said the target was likely to be breached in the next few years and that "urgent and stringent" action would be needed to return the world to 1.5C.
The Paris Agreement is at the heart of the international commitment to tackle rising global temperatures.
It came into force on 4 November 2016 and saw almost all the nations of the world agree to cut the greenhouse gas emissions which cause global warming.
However, the United States - the world's second biggest greenhouse gas emitter - withdrew from the deal in January 2026 under President Donald Trump.
The US also withdrew during Trump's first presidency, but it rejoined in 2021 under his successor President Joe Biden.
The only other UN member states outside the Paris agreement are Iran, Libya and Yemen.
The Paris Agreement lists a series of commitments:
to "pursue efforts" to limit global temperature rises to 1.5C, and to keep them "well below" 2.0C above those recorded in pre-industrial times, generally considered to mean the late 19th Century
to achieve a balance - known as net zero - between the greenhouse gases that humans put into the atmosphere and the gases that they actively remove, in the second half of this century
each country to set its own emission-reduction targets, reviewed every five years to raise ambitions
richer countries to help poorer nations by providing funding, known as climate finance, to adapt to climate change and switch to renewable energy
The 1.5C target is generally accepted to refer to a 20-year average rather than a single year.
So, while 2024 was more than 1.5C warmer than pre-industrial times, it did not mean the Paris Agreement threshold has been breached
Every 0.1C of warming brings with it greater risks for the planet, such as longer heatwaves, more intense storms and wildfires, according to climate scientists.
But a very large body of scientific evidence shows that warming of 2C or more would bring far greater impacts, on top of those felt at 1.5C, UN scientists say.
more people being exposed to extreme heat
higher sea levels as glaciers and ice sheets melt
increased risks to food security in some regions due to more extreme weather
greater chances of some climate-sensitive diseases spreading, such as dengue
more species being threatened with extinction
Some changes could become irreversible if so-called "tipping points" are crossed.
It is not clear exactly where these sit, but once these thresholds are passed, changes could accelerate and become irreversible.
These could include the collapse of the Greenland Ice Sheet, warm Atlantic Ocean currents or further loss of the Amazon rainforest.

The Paris deal restated a 2009 commitment that richer countries should provide $100bn (£73bn) annually by 2020 to help developing nations deal with the effects of climate change and build greener economies.
Although only $83.3bn was raised in 2020, data from the OECD, external shows the goal was reached in each of the three years after 2022.
Almost two-thirds of the money in recent years has gone towards efforts to limit global warming, while around a quarter has been used to help nations adapt to climate change.
In 2023, countries agreed for the first time that a fund should be established exclusively for loss and damage. This is money to help countries recover from the impacts of climate change.
Nepal became the first country approved to receive money from the fund after a flash flood in August 2026 killed more than 1,400 people.
At COP29 in 2024, richer nations committed to providing $300bn (£219bn) a year to developing nations by 2035. Developing countries - which had hoped for more - criticised the "paltry sum".
World leaders meet every year to discuss their climate commitments at international summits known as COPs (Conference of the Parties).
All COPs since 2015 have tracked how countries are building on what they promised in Paris.
At COP28 in 2023, countries agreed for the first time to "contribute" to "transitioning away from fossil fuels", although they were not forced to take any specific action.
Countries also agreed to treble the global capacity of renewables - such as wind and solar - by 2030.

But the final deal at COP30 in 2025 failed to directly mention fossil fuels. Instead, the host of the conference, Brazil, published a voluntary roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels, which will be discussed at COP31.
That COP is taking place from 9 to 20 November 2026 in Antalya, Turkey and is co-hosted by Australia.
A "coalition of the willing" composed of 57 countries has also organised its own conferences separate from the COP process to discuss phasing out fossil fuels.
The first meeting was held in Santa Marta, Colombia in April 2026, and another conference is scheduled for July 2027 in Tuvalu.
The long-term 1.5C global warming target has not yet been breached.
But the latest UN Emissions Gap Report, external said the limit was likely to be exceeded in the next few years after "decades of insufficient climate action".
In the "lowest possible" scenario, warming would still reach 1.7 to 1.8C by the mid-century, the report said.
A return to 1.5C by 2100 is possible, but it will require "urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions", the UN added.
Specifically, emissions would need to be cut by 18% between 2025 and 2030.
The report found that the pledges governments have made so far would only cover half of these cuts.
Without further action, global warming could reach nearly 3C by the end of the century, the research said.

items.title: What is net zero and is the UK on track to achieve it?
paragraphs: Achieving "net zero" is the world's key strategy to fight climate change, which is already having serious consequences for people and nature around the globe.
But the political consensus around the UK's net zero policies has collapsed, with the Conservative and Reform parties now branding them too difficult and expensive.
Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.
Effectively this means no longer adding to the total amount of these gases in the atmosphere to limit climate change.

Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane. Their levels in the atmosphere are increasing rapidly due to human activities, including burning fossil fuels, chopping down forests and farming.
In practice, reducing these emissions means switching from coal, oil and gas to cleaner energy sources like wind and solar power.
It also involves adopting green technologies like electric vehicles and heat pumps to replace petrol or diesel cars and gas boilers.
So remaining emissions must be matched by things like planting trees, restoring peatlands or using machines to remove CO2 from the air.
But there are limits to these "carbon removal" techniques in scale and cost. That is why most of the focus is on drastically reducing emissions in the first place.
The world is warming because of humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, which increase global temperatures by trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface.
This is bringing more heatwaves and extreme weather as well as melting ice sheets and raising sea levels.
In 2026, the UK experienced its hottest summer on record, which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.
Aiming to avoid the worst of these impacts, nearly 200 countries signed the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement. A target was set to reach net zero globally in the second half of the century.
Around 140 countries, external have their own net zero targets, covering roughly three-quarters of global emissions and 80% of the world's population.

It's widely accepted that richer nations will need to get to net zero before poorer ones, which often have fewer resources to switch to cleaner technologies and have contributed less to climate change historically.
Sea-level rises increase the chances of coastal flooding during storms
These policies began to be implemented under Sir Keir Starmer's government and have continued to be pursued by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
However, recent decisions have led some environmentalists to question whether the government can still meet its targets:
Approving the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea
Reducing planned investment in heat pumps and carbon capture, external to pay for defence
Holding a consultation on whether to weaken electric car targets
The chancellor's support for a third runway at Heathrow
In June, the government's independent adviser, the Climate Change Committee (CCC), warned that the UK was "not moving fast enough", external towards net zero.
However, the Chancellor, John Healey, said in his autumn budget speech, external that the government remained "unshakably committed" to the goal.
Heat pump installations are rising but remain below targets
When former Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May signed the UK's 2050 net zero target into law in 2019, it passed through parliament with the support of all major parties.
But that political consensus has since fragmented. The term "net zero" is often used by critics to attack environmental targets, which they claim are being put ahead of economic goals.
Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is "determined" to meet the 2050 deadline, a policy also backed by the Liberal Democrats.
Meanwhile, the Green Party wants net zero "as soon as possible, and more than a decade ahead of 2050".

These parties argue that it's in the UK's economic interest to move away from fossil fuels, which can be volatile in price. Supplies can also be interrupted by international events like the US-Israel war on Iran.
But the Conservatives and Reform UK want to scrap the UK's net zero target, calling the current plans costly and unachievable.
They argue that, in isolation, the UK's efforts make little difference to climate change, not least because UK emissions are much smaller than those of countries like China and the US.
The SNP has targeted net zero by 2045 for Scotland, while Plaid Cymru has introduced a 2040 deadline in Wales.
There is no single path to net zero, which means there is no fixed price.

But the Climate Change Committee says the policy will require tens of billions of pounds a year by the end of the 2020s, most of which it expects to come from the private sector rather than government spending.
By the early 2040s, the CCC calculates that the savings from moving away from fossil fuels to cleaner, more efficient technologies should outweigh the costs, external.

Multiple studies have found that, globally, the economic cost of tackling climate change is much smaller than letting warming continue unchecked, which would result in widespread and increasing climate hazards.

However, as with any transition, the costs and benefits can be unequally felt. For example, while there is huge potential for new clean energy jobs, those employed in the oil and gas industry are likely to be negatively affected.

items.title: Burnham responds to BBC question over Labour's past links to Brand
paragraphs: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous association with the comedian.

Some within the Labour Party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him - and in 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when the comedian was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements.
Asked about the 2014 tweet on Friday, Burnham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."
Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday.
In 2014, Brand was writing regular opinion pieces for newspapers and appearing on political discussion programmes, including the BBC's Question Time.
His anti-establishment and left-wing views had also gained him a following on social media.
The same year, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted on Twitter in support of Brand following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.

It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his 2014 tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.
Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned for.
At the time, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".
Asked about that social media post on Friday, Burnham told the BBC "all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do".
The PM added: "His [Brand's] crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here.
"It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life, but what is important is that where there is wrongdoing it is exposed."
The prime minister added: "Credit to the victims, huge credit, the courage that it's taken, but also the journalists who've exposed this."
Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.
Brand, who had previously dismissed the idea of voting, backed Labour following the interview, saying Miliband had convinced him that "this bloke will listen to us".
Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, has previously said he regrets being interviewed by Brand.
On Friday, a spokesman for Miliband told the BBC: "These are horrific crimes that Russell Brand has been found guilty of and Ed's profound sympathy is with the victims.
"As he said in 2023, 'of course, knowing what I know now - and I was not aware of these allegations at the time about Russell Brand - I wouldn't have done that interview and I regret doing it'."
Brand was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault.
During a four-week trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.
The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to court on Monday for sentencing.

items.title: Struggling to spell ‘male chauvinist pig’? Apple’s grey list means your iPhone won’t help you
paragraphs: “Australia is a very bad place to question your sexuality on MDMA with NSA spies” might be a text you would wish to send to your friends, if you have had an extraordinarily complicated night out in Sydney.
But your iPhone won’t help you spell any of it if you try to swipe-type it – that is, by gliding a finger across a keyboard as opposed to pecking out a word.
New research shows that Apple has a “grey list” of more than 100,000 words and phrases that it has restricted from being completed by its predictive text.
So if a user wishes to type phrases such as “Dictator Trump”, “NSA spies” or, surprisingly, “Australia is a very bad place”, “question your sexuality” or “on MDMA”, they will have to spell them out.

Apple’s predictive text will not suggest these words. And, if a user attempts to swipe-type them, they will often stumble, changing “United Ireland” to “United Iceland”, for example, or “Tibetan independence” to “Tibetan independences”.

The “grey list” was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman, whose other projects include using AI to find errors in scientific papers. After noticing that he had problems typing certain phrases – but not others – on his iPhone, Kauffman was able to unearth a table containing the list, encoded in Apple’s operating system.

The list he found includes some unsurprising words and phrases. Apple’s iPhone will not autocomplete references to drugs, sexual acts and, perhaps in the spirit of corporate protection, “iMessage isn’t working”.

But it also includes possibly politically charged phrases, which Kauffman described to Reuters as a “light-touch form of censorship”. Among these are “Trayvon Martin”, the name of the Black teenager shot in Florida in 2012, “Kashmir dispute”, “Muslim extremist” and “male chauvinist pig”.
In Hebrew, Apple will not autocomplete the phrase “the occupied territories”. In Arabic, it will not autocomplete the phrase “the Hamas movement”.
The list is one more glimpse into the dark bowels of how autocorrect – the chirpy keyboard partner that helps you look more educated to your loved ones – actually works.

The technology has taken many forms. In its earliest version, Unix, an operating system, would look up each word a user typed against a table of words, to determine if this word was spelled correctly.

This evolved into n-grams, a tool which allows an operating system to statistically predict what words might come next, based on the words before it. These form the basis of Apple’s familiar autocorrect, which was known to change expletives into prudish alternatives: “fork” and “ducking”, among other gaffes.

Last year, Apple launched a new autocorrect – a “transformer-based” system that was more akin to an LLM. Reddit sleuths saw this as a possible reason behind a spate of avant-garde spelling suggestions their iPhones made last year.

This hard-coded list illuminates one longstanding mystery behind the world’s spelling coach. Others remain, such as a brief glitch in which users of the dictation feature saw the name “Trump” flash across their screen when they spoke the word “racist” into their iPhones – which Apple quickly remedied.

Apple said that it designed its keyboard to avoid offering inappropriate or offensive predictive suggestions. It said iPhone users could always type out specific words or phrases, and override predictive text suggestions to achieve their desired meaning.

items.title: US tech stock rout: is the AI bubble bursting?
paragraphs: Global financial markets have been thrown into a tailspin as investors bet on an AI slowdown after the US midterm elections.
This is not the first time stock markets have wobbled in recent months due to concerns over a tech bubble. But could this volatility be the start of a huge market meltdown?

Shares on Wall Street plunged on Thursday, in a rout driven by AI and technology stocks that extended to Asia and Europe on Friday. US markets rebounded after trading reopened in New York, but failed to recover all of the lost ground amid lingering concerns of a relapse in selling pressure.

More than $3.2tn (£2.4tn) was wiped from the value of the US stock market on Thursday – bigger than the annual output of the Canadian economy – after the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell by 5.5% and the blue-chip S&P 500 fell by 4.4%.

After months of warnings over the valuations of AI companies – amid fears of tinderbox conditions in the world economy fuelled by the Iran war and concerns that the tech bubble could burst – the trigger for the sell-off has been attributed to the Democrats’ sweeping US midterm election victory.

Investors are predicting that a Democrat-controlled Congress could lead to tighter control of AI and datacentre construction – slowing development in one of the engines of global economic growth and corporate earnings on the stock market.

Challenging billionaire power and calling out Wall Street and big tech were the rallying cries of many Democrats in the midterm elections. Moratoriums on datacentre construction were effectively on the ballot in several states amid growing public opposition to the building of vast, resource-hungry facilities.

Highlighting the stakes, the SpaceX and Tesla CEO, Elon Musk, set a record for election spending after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans – and moved his personal residence to Texas, the leading state for datacentre construction. After the midterms shares in both his companies fell sharply.
Fears of an AI bubble have been growing for some time, given the astronomical rise in tech company valuations, which some analysts said had become increasingly detached from reality.

One measure of whether a market is overvalued, the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (Cape) ratio, had risen to its highest level since 2000, showing that the US stock market was unusually highly valued relative to profits.
Highlighting the disconnect, shares in Alphabet, the Google parent company, plunged last week after it reported lower than expected profits, wiping more than $500bn from its value.

Some form of a check on progress was also likely, amid a groundswell of public opposition to datacentre construction and worries over AI safety. Opinion polls show most Americans are opposed to US datacentre construction, while governments around the world have encouraged citizens to stockpile for multiple eventualities including cyber-attacks.
Ben Barringer, the head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said: “It is too easy to say that the Democrats will be bad for datacentres.

“Yes, there will be a pause in the buildout and delay in approvals, but if you go off the words of the new Texas governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, they are likely to be more pragmatic and ensure resources are more fairly allocated.”
What happens to the share prices of the US tech giants has enormous consequences for savers worldwide.

The “magnificent seven” tech stocks – Nvidia, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Tesla – account for more than a third of the S&P 500, meaning that funds that track this index are directly tied to their performance.
AI has been a big growth driver, with the tech boom helping to soften the hit to the world economy from the war in the Middle East.

The prospect of a sustained tech sell-off could prove a big setback, in a blow to countries that have pinned their hopes on the AI revolution creating jobs and generating a productivity boost to overcome years of relative economic stagnation.

In response to the inflation shock from the Iran war, central banks around the world have been raising interest rates. However, an economic slowdown could force a rethink amid the risk of stagflation, when weak growth is accompanied by fast-rising consumer prices.

Financial markets are prone to volatile swings and investors are divided about whether things will get worse from here. Many were, however, worried a big crash was overdue – and when investors begin to lose confidence, it can become self-reinforcing.
Barringer said: “A virtuous circle could quickly turn into a vicious one, and they [investors] must now ride it out until the direction of travel becomes clearer.”

For some, the latest tech rout represents a reset rather than a lasting downturn. Demand for AI and semiconductors will not vanish overnight: new tools will continue to be launched, and datacentres will be built.
Mark Haefele, the chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said the AI investment cycle should remain intact, despite the latest “market indigestion”.
“We do not think fundamentals justify a prolonged downturn,” he added.

items.title: Aluminium canopy encases waterfront pavilion in Providence by Architecture Research Office
paragraphs: Steel columns support the expansive canopy of this green-roofed pavilion at 195 District Park in Providence, Rhode Island, which has been completed by New York-based studio Architecture Research Office.

Conceived by the studio as a “year-round amenity” for the public, the 195 District Park Pavilion accommodates two local businesses, an indoor-outdoor dining area and public restrooms overlooking the Providence River.
The pavilion’s position at the park’s highest point led Architecture Research Office (ARO) to design its multifaceted structure as a “beacon” that would be accessible from multiple entrances.
“Centrally located within 195 District Park, the pavilion is a park amenity that welcomes and orients visitors while supporting park programming,” studio principal Kim Yao told Dezeen.
“The pavilion is located at the highest point within the park in response to the floodplain of the adjacent Providence River.”
“This positioning created an opportunity for the building to serve as a beacon, visible from multiple entry points to the park,” Yao added.
Fronted by a plaza, the pavilion is composed of a metal frame that has been cloaked with cedar wood in a nod to the area’s local architecture.
Its structure is wrapped by an expansive aluminium canopy, which is supported by a series of steel columns and extends over the plaza to shelter an outdoor seating space.
Atop the structure, the sloped green roof helps to blend the pavilion into its surrounding landscape, while also limiting stormwater run-off and screening the rooftop’s mechanical systems.
“As a year-round amenity, the pavilion opens to shaded exterior areas in the summer while providing shelter during colder seasons,” Yao said.
“It also provides occupants with views of the river and surrounding areas,” she added.
Inside, the 3,500-square-foot building opens up to the indoor seating area, complete with exposed wooden joists.
Flanking the space are the pavilion’s operable storefront doors, which open up to the adjacent plaza and enable passive ventilation throughout the space.
Additional facilities include public restrooms located at the pavilion’s southern corner.

Its structure is perched beside a curved pedestrian bridge completed by Inform Studio and Buro Happold in 2020 that stretches over the Providence River to link two parks on the east and west sides of the city’s riverfront.
Other pavilions recently featured on Dezeen include a temporary marketing space in São Paulo built from mass-timber scrap and a basket-like aluminium pavilion in New York.

items.title: European flights and broadcasters are targeted with another wave of bomb threats
paragraphs: Passengers arrive at the Henri Coanda International Airport pass under a Schengen Information sign, in Otopeni, near Bucharest, Romania, on March 31, 2024. Andreea Alexandru/AP hide caption

PRAGUE — Officials across Europe reported a fresh slew of bomb threats against multiple flights on Friday, following a string of hoaxes that have caused flight diversions this week. Three broadcasters also received security threats, in a possible sign the menace was spreading beyond the skies.

No suspicious items have been found and no one has been injured, but the threats have raised concern because they came on the heels of other European disruptions — including attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions.

Overall, the threats have caused minimal disruption to aviation, according to the European air traffic authority. Eurocontrol said it was aware of bomb threats against 14 flights on Thursday — only 0.05% of all of the nearly 26,300 flights across the European network that day — and seven on Tuesday. The European Union's transportation commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said there were 11 more on Friday.

Even so, airlines have to take every threat seriously because they are ultimately responsible for the lives of their passengers, said Robert Jordan, research director at Britain's Royal United Services Institute think tank.
Jordan told the BBC that there are more ways than ever to make threats against flights, and secure messaging apps have allowed for greater anonymity.

"The risk appetite for airlines is always going to be incredibly low," he said, noting the great strides that have been made in airport security in recent years. "It is baked into their safety procedures, and it's baked into their security procedures."

Tzitzikostas said after a meeting with Eurocontrol and the EU's Aviation Safety Agency in Brussels that security experts will meet in the Belgian capital next week to discuss measures needed to deal with the rash of bomb threats.
"Our priority here is clear. The safety of passengers and the smooth functioning of European aviation," he said.

In Hungary, the defense minister said fighter jets escorted three passenger planes Friday through the country's airspace within an hour after each received a bomb threat. Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said the escorts were for flights from Brussels to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, and from Prague to Cyprus and Romania.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's office said four bomb threats were made against aircraft flying over France. The planes landed safely at Paris' Orly Airport and bomb disposal experts conducted inspections. The office didn't specify which flights were affected.

Threats were also made against a Prague-to-Bucharest, Romania, flight operated by Romanian carrier Tarom, and a Ryanair flight from the Portuguese capital, Lisbon, to Rome. A WizzAir flight from Prague to Rome was diverted to Venice after a bomb alert, and passengers were evacuated after the aircraft landed.

Eurocontrol said Friday it was monitoring the situation and working closely with airlines, airports, navigation service providers and other groups across Europe "to mitigate any disruption to air traffic flows."

Nine of the affected flights were coming or going from Václav Havel Airport in Prague, airport spokesperson Denisa Hejtmánková said. They included flights from Denmark, Spain and Britain, and departures to the Netherlands and Britain, in addition to the ones to Cyprus, Italy and Romania. Czech police said security measures were taken that had "a minimal impact on the normal operations at the airport."
Diverting and inspecting flights is costly, though.

"I think it's a big problem for aviation that this is happening," Torstein Nymoen, a 52-year-old Norwegian traveler, said at the Prague airport. "It must cost a lot for the companies, the aviation companies. And I think that it's sad that some people are doing this."

In Denmark, police deployed to Copenhagen airport for a second consecutive day as a precautionary measure over threats directed at air traffic, and deemed there was no danger to passengers or others at the airport.
More than two dozen flights were affected by threats earlier in the week, with some diverted as authorities scrambled to rule out any danger.
Fake bomb threats are relatively common but it is unusual to see so many in such a short period.

It remains unclear who is behind the airline threats, which come at a time of increased geopolitical tensions and warnings from authorities that Russia may be ramping up so-called hybrid threats in Europe.

Authorities have not attributed the threats to any group or state actor, and no evidence has emerged linking the hoaxes to a government. An email containing the threat sent Thursday to airport authorities in Rome and reviewed by The Associated Press purported to come from a group describing itself as anti-feminist and claiming it was targeting a "feminist regime." Another European airport received a threat with similar wording, but it was unclear if it came from the same sender.

Bomb threats are on pilots' minds and create unnecessary tension, but crews are prepared to respond professionally, said Paul Reuter, vice president of the European Cockpit Association. Pilots review procedures with cabin crews, identify airports where they could divert and may carry extra fuel, he said.
Reuter called the use of civil aviation for geopolitical disruption or hoaxes "totally unacceptable."

In Ireland, the Dublin headquarters of national broadcaster RTE was evacuated Friday because of a bomb threat, and live broadcasts were replaced with prerecorded programs. Staff returned to the building after a few hours, once police with sniffer dogs had searched the area and declared it safe.
Ireland's police force, An Garda Síochána, said it has been liaising with Irish media organizations and that the threat will be investigated.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the threats to RTE and others "just illustrates how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and to undermine the normal operation of society through unconventional activities of this kind, which are designed to cause fear and anxiety."
He said there would be a "very significant security operation" in place next week when Dublin hosts meetings of the European Political Community and European Union leaders.

Separately, U.K.-based broadcaster Sky said it had also received a "security threat." In a statement reported by Sky News channel, it said that "we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure." Sky News remained on air.

Meanwhile, NOVA TV, a private broadcaster in Bulgaria, said it received an email Friday threatening it with a bomb. It said the sender claimed to be behind the threats to European air traffic, and that the broadcaster implemented its standard safety measures without any interruptions to its TV and radio broadcasts.

items.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
paragraphs: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

items.title: The 36 best Christmas gifts in the UK for every kind of teenager – chosen by teens
paragraphs: Because there is no doubt your teen thinks they know better than you, we took them at their word and asked what they think makes the perfect gift for Christmas (or other religious festival they celebrate).

To ensure the selection was truly tried and tested, we asked them only about presents they have already received, love and use constantly. We also made sure to ask a broad range of teens – from book lovers to tech fiends and plenty in between – to try to represent the myriad tastes of this age group.
Lego keeps you entertained for a long time. You can keep coming back to it, take it apart and rebuild it, and it’s really good to collect. Anon, 14

I love my Lego Lamborghini Huracán; the fun I had making the car is the real joy of it, plus putting it on display after hours of hard work is the best feeling, especially when friends see it. I think any kid my age who likes cars would absolutely love this for Christmas. I now have my eyes on the new Lego Formula One models. Ayush, 15
Boys of Tommen series by Chloe Walsh, six-book collection set
I’ve loved the Boys of Tommen book series. They’re addictive and emotional. I loved reading from all of the characters’ perspectives. Isabella, 16
Arc of a Scythe Series, four-book collection set

The Arc of a Scythe series by Neal Shusterman is perfect for fans of the Hunger Games and Divergent – it’s thrilling and impossible to put down once you’re immersed in the author’s dystopian world. Matilda, 13
The Heroes of Olympus: the complete five-book collection set
My favourites are the Heroes of Olympus books by Rick Riordan – entertaining, great for learning Greek mythology and particularly good for reluctant readers! Alisha, 14
A Natural History of Dragons: A Memoir by Lady Trent

I’ve been reading A Natural History of Dragons. It’s an interesting and well-written book that takes itself semi-seriously and is full of humour mixed with interesting speculative biology of dragons. It’s also, I think, accurate to the actual time period (outside the existence of dragons) and has a female lead! Solly, 18

I love my Sony wireless Bluetooth headphones; I’ve had them for several years and still use them all the time. I like listening to music (like Ed Sheeran) and think they would make a good gift for people my age who love music. I also love the light-up keyboard for my computer; it’s really cool. I like gaming with it and showing it to my mates. James, 14
Pokémon TCG: Mega Evolution – Pitch Black
I love this game. It’s not just whether you get anything good or not, it’s the surprise when you open them. With this, you get four packs and an extra 40 cards, so it’s good value. Ted, 13
Hy-Pro Fifa World Cup 2026 size 5 PVC football

My favourite things are my football – you don’t need any other fancy equipment, and you can play on your own as well as with friends – and my Bose SoundLink Flex portable speaker. I also recommend Nineteen Eighty-Four by George Orwell – it’s an amazingly interesting book that I think everyone should read. Stan, 14
Pokémon Brilliant Diamond for Nintendo Switch

I think people my age would definitely like this Nintendo Switch game, Pokémon Brilliant Diamond. You can get cool Pokémon and don’t need to upgrade to a Switch 2 – the game is available secondhand [for a more affordable] price too. Nathan, 13
SteelSeries Sensei Pro wireless gaming mouse

The SteelSeries Sensei Pro wireless gaming mouse is really good. Good polling rate [a test to see how fast and accurate a mouse is], two batteries and a dock. It doesn’t get interrupted by other devices, plus it’s lightweight. Dan, 16
Canon PowerShot SX160IS, refurbished model
Brother LS14s manual stitch sewing machine

I love my Canon PowerShot digital camera. I like to go to concerts and take pictures and videos – I can be in the moment. If I use my phone, I get distracted. I also love making things with my sewing machine. I recently altered an Alessi Rose top because only large sizes were left, and they were too big. I got them both secondhand as I’m really into recycling and reusing. Freya, 16
I recommend Beats’ headphones. These are so comfortable, and the sound quality is amazing. Aoife, 13
Yamaha PSR-E383 portable keyboard for beginners
I really like my Yamaha keyboard and think it’s something many teenagers would enjoy, especially for composing their own music. Ria, 14
Violator by Depeche Mode, Legacy vinyl edition

I love old vinyl, like Gary Numan and Depeche Mode. The sound quality and artwork are much better than streaming. I like my Polaroid camera too – I can make instant memories that feel more special than saving a picture on my phone. Martha, 14

The Elf Power Grip primer is one of my favourite products. I usually find all of my favourite products through TikTok videos, and everyone loves this one. It’s lightweight enough for someone who has just started wearing makeup, and I think it’s perfect for teen skin. Honestly, anything from Elf makes a perfect gift; I got a selection of products for my birthday, and there’s still so many I want to try.

items.title: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult is sentenced to 200 years in prison
paragraphs: Good News International Church pastor Paul Mackenzie, who has been convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult, awaits his sentence at the Mombasa High Court in Mombasa, Kenya, Friday. Brian Inganga/AP hide caption
MOMBASA, Kenya — The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult linked to the deaths of more than 400 people was sentenced on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people.

The High Court in Kenya's coastal city of Mombasa issued the sentence for Pastor Paul Mackenzie. He was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult after he ordered his followers to starve themselves to death in order to meet Jesus.
Mackenzie is also facing terrorism and manslaughter charges for the more than 200 other victims, as well as child abuse and torture charges in two other courts.

Justice Diana Kavedza said that Mackenzie, leader of the Good News International Church, bore the "primary criminal culpability" for relocating his followers to a remote location and ordering them to fast to death.

Mackenzie was charged with the murders alongside 28 of his followers, including guards who enforced his fasting directives and gravediggers who helped conceal the mass graves. All denied the charges, except for one person who confessed and pleaded for leniency.

Good News International Church pastor Paul Mackenzie, center, who has been convicted on 191 murder charges, arrives alongside fellow church members as he awaits sentencing at the Mombasa High Court in Mombasa, Kenya, Friday. Brian Inganga/AP hide caption
On Oct. 19, the court found all 29 of them guilty of the murder of 191 people.

In 2023, more than 400 bodies were exhumed from shallow graves on the 800-acre (320-hectare) Chakama Ranch in coastal Kilifi County, where Mackenzie's followers lived in mud huts, away from the scrutiny of local communities and authorities.
More than 60 bodies were positively identified and reburied by their relatives, while many others remain unidentified and unclaimed.
During the sentencing, Kavedza said that 183 victims died of starvation, defined as a complete lack of food, and the deaths of the other eight were classified as murder by direct homicide.

Kavedza said the killings were "cold and calculated" and dismissed claims by some of the accused that the loss of their own children altered the fact that they had participated in the killings of many other children.

The justice said that the perpetrators didn't show remorse and declared they were ready to fast to death as well. During the sentencing, Mackenzie often smiled and chatted with his assistant pastor, Smart Mwakalama, who was sentenced to 160 years in prison.
All of those who were convicted have been granted 14 days to file an appeal.
The prosecution had argued for the death penalty for Mackenzie and life imprisonment for his accomplices.

Defense lawyer Lawrence Obonyo, who represents Mackenzie and several others who were convicted, told The Associated Press that he had already launched an appeal. He said that the decision was "circling around the constitution to give a sentence that is unattainable" since the sentences of between 160 and 200 years amount to life sentences.

A father of seven, Suleiman Ziro, who traveled 120 kilometers (75 miles) for the sentencing, lost six of his children and his wife to the cult in 2023. He said that the sentence wasn't enough especially because he has yet to recover the bodies of his loved ones, calling for the death penalty in the case.

Mackenzie's son, Dan Mackenzie, said that he felt sorry for his father over the conviction, but it was "justice served to the victims." He said that he escaped by "rebelling" against his father's teachings and was often punished for it, but was glad he survived. Two of his younger brothers and three sisters were rescued and are currently at a children's home.
Those sentenced to death in Kenyan courts serve a life sentence. Kenya's last execution was in 1987.

items.title: Which is the best iPad to buy right now? After 16 years of using them, this is our take
paragraphs: Choosing an iPad used to be a piece of cake. Now there are four families, different processors, and prices that jumped up in June 2026. So it’s important to pick the right one, and not pay through the nose for power you don't actually need.

The good news is, for browsing, streaming, gaming and a bit of sketching, the classic 11-inch iPad (2025) does everything you probably need. If you have specific tasks beyond that, it might be worth shelling out for a more expensive iPad Air, iPad Pro and iPad mini. But for most people (including me) this is the best iPad to get.

Below, I’ve compared the latest versions of all four models – because they are the best versions of all the families – drawing on both my own experience and reviews by the Creative Bloq team, which has been using iPads since Gen 1 in 2010.
The basic iPad is the best choice for most people
Screen: 11-inch Liquid Retina LCD, 2360 x 1640, 60Hz, 500 nits
Stylus: Apple Pencil (1st generation), Apple Pencil (USB-C)

Our top pick for most people is what people often call the basic iPad. But don't let that put you off, because "basic" is purely a relative term here. So yes, this is the cheapest iPad Apple sells, but it’s still a lovely tablet to use every day. Web browsing, streaming, video calls, note-taking and email are all fast and easy, and the bright, colourful screen is big enough to be comfortable without weighing you down.

It’s a decent gaming tablet too, as long as you're not set on playing AAA titles at the highest frame rates. Call of Duty Mobile runs okay, for instance, until you go up to 120fps mode, while Infinity Nikki might need dropping to medium. The lack of an M-series chip also locks you out of some games entirely.

For drawing, though, it does the job nicely. Add an Apple Pencil and you can sketch happily in Procreate, although the first-generation Pencil is the one to get, as the cheaper USB-C model doesn’t have pressure sensitivity. As our reviewer Ian Evenden says: “You don’t get desktop-level processing power, but you do get one of the friendliest, most useful tablets around, especially if you combine it with a Pencil for sketching.”

A couple more things to point out: there’s no Apple Intelligence, the USB-C port is slow and the screen has an air gap beneath the glass, so it feels a little less refined under a stylus. In short, the compromises are there... but they won't be deal-breakers for most people. Finally, bear in mind that reports suggest a replacement could arrive in early 2027 – although Apple hasn’t confirmed anything so that's currently just speculation.
Price: 11-inch from $749 / £749; 13-inch from $949 / £949
Screen: 11-inch (2360 x 1640, 500 nits) or 13-inch (2732 x 2048, 600 nits) Liquid Retina LCD, both 60Hz
Stylus: Apple Pencil Pro, Apple Pencil (USB-C)
The Air costs $300 / £320 more than the basic iPad. In return you get a much faster chip, twice the memory, Apple Intelligence, Apple Pencil Pro support and the option of a 13-inch screen.

That extra power is overkill if all you want to do on your iPad is check emails and watch Netflix. But if you want to run demanding creative software or games, then it may be worth it. In our Geekbench 6 tests, the M4 Air’s multi-core score of 13,168 was more than double the 6,338 we got from the basic iPad. Its graphics score of 53,071 also matched the 53,252 of the previous M4 iPad Pro.

That will really make a difference, for example, if you want to run 3D software. Our reviever, Glen Southern, who has used iPad Pros for professional work since they launched, found that he could sculpt models of up to 16 million polygons in Nomad Sculpt. But he cautions that for some, all that power will be overkill. “For a lot of creative users, 12GB of memory and an M4 chip may be more iPad than they’ll ever actually need,” he says.

On the other side of the equation, the Air isn't quite as capable as the Pro. For instance, it has an LCD screen rather than OLED, and a 60Hz refresh rate rather than 120Hz. For many people, though, that line won’t be worth paying to cross.
Screen: 11-inch (2420 x 1668) or 13-inch (2752 x 2064) Ultra Retina XDR OLED, 120Hz, 1,000 nits (1,600 nits peak HDR)
Stylus: Apple Pencil Pro, Apple Pencil (USB-C)

The Pro is the absolute best tablet Apple makes, and so if price is no object then please, knock yourself out. It is very expensive, though, and for most people, it’ll be total overkill. However, if you have a specific work need for a Pro such as 3D modelling or video editing, then it may be worth the investment. And it truly is a lovely thing to have and use.

The tandem OLED screen is the best on any iPad, with deep blacks, high contrast and a 120Hz refresh rate. And it’s the most powerful iPad by a distance, scoring 16,443 for multi-core and 74,046 for graphics in our Geekbench 6 tests. “Whether it’s for building up a lot of layers in Procreate or Illustrator, video editing in Final Cut Pro or Davinci Resolve or crazy stuff in Zbrush or Nomad Sculpt, the M5 iPad Pro barely breaks a sweat,” says our reviewer Ian Evenden.

That price, though, is not to be sneezed at. And the cost climbs quickly once you add a Magic Keyboard, Apple Pencil Pro and extra storage. So unless you're certain exactly what the Pro would do for you, we'd say: get the Air.
The best iPad for portability and tight spaces
Price: 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR OLED, 2316 x 1512, 60Hz, 600 nits (1,200 nits peak HDR)
Screen: 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR OLED, 2316 x 1512, 60Hz, 600 nits (1,200 nits peak HDR)
Stylus: Apple Pencil Pro, Apple Pencil (USB-C)

The iPad mini is, just as the name suggests, small and light. That makes it a great choice if you want something you can carry easily in a small bag. It's also useful for using in tight spaces, like a crowded railway carriage.

If you’re a fan of small, and you want the best, the 2026 version is the one to choose. It's the first mini with an OLED screen, the first with IP67 water and dust resistance, and at 255g, it’s noticeably lighter than its predecessor.

We haven’t tested it ourselves yet, but our sister site TechRadar praised both its screen and fast performance. So if you want an iPad for reading, travel, note-taking and sketching on the go, it's a great choice; especially if you opt for the paper-like nano-texture screen, which costs an extra $100 / £100 on the 256GB and 512GB models.

The catch? It's a whopping $250 / £270 more than the basic iPad and only $50 / £50 less than the 11-inch Air, so you really are paying a premium for the smallness. The 8.5-inch screen is also stuck at 60Hz. However, if you want to save some cash and the upgrades aren't important to you, retailers still have the previous A17 Pro model, which has dropped to a record low.

The best iPad overall is the iPad Pro, which is number three on our list above. It's the fastest, most powerful and has the best screen. So if money's no object, this the one you should buy, unless you're mainly interested in something small and portable (in which case, go for the iPad mini, number four on our list.) However, if you don't have endless cash to spare, the iPad Pro may well be overkill, so it's worth deciding whether you really need all that power. The basic iPad is much cheaper and, as discussed below, is actually the best pick for most people.

The basic iPad (which is just called "iPad" on Apple's website and retailer listings) is the one most people should buy. It’s by far the cheapest way to get a new iPad, and handles browsing, streaming, email, video calls and casual gaming with ease. If you don't want to do anything more complicated with an iPad, there's no reason to pay more. It's number one on our list above.

The basic iPad, number one on our list above, is the best choice for most students, if you just want it for low-powered tasks like taking notes, reading, checking emails, listening to music and watching video. If you study a creative subject or use demanding apps, though, the iPad Air is worth the extra money if your budget allows.

The basic iPad with an Apple Pencil is the affordable way to start with drawing on the iPad. If you’d like a better drawing experience, the Air gives you a laminated screen, Apple Pencil Pro support and the option of a 13-inch canvas. For more detail, see our guide to the best iPads for drawing.

The iPad Pro, number 3 on our list, is the one to get if you need its OLED screen, 120Hz refresh rate or maximum power. But check that you really do. Many professionals will be just as happy with the 13-inch Air. Our guide to the best iPad for Procreate goes into more detail.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.
