items.title: Two Gloucester schools in lockdown after boy hurt in incident
paragraphs: Police were called to Chalford Road in Tuffley, Gloucester
ByHarriet RobinsonWest of England and Esme AshcroftReporting fromin Tuffley
Two schools are in lockdown as armed police search for a group of people involved in an altercation that left a boy injured.
One male was seen with a "long-bladed item" during the incident near St Peter's High School in Gloucester, police said.
Armed officers are now searching for a group involved who fled the area. The force said one boy had been taken to hospital with minor injuries and there was "no ongoing threat at the school".
Although pupils still cannot leave St Peter's High School alone, parents have now been told they can collect their children. Nearby Willow Primary Academy remains in full lockdown.
Pupil Jimmy who has now been let out of St Peter's, said the situation was "really scary" and he was still in shock.
After getting into school for the day, he said his friends came in and told him something had happened near his home.
He said the school's alarm then went off and the computer he was on displayed a message saying "This is a lockdown".
"The computers are not accessible at all and we've all had to turn the lights off, lock the doors, turn all the blinds down, and we've had to get on the ground," he said.
"At the time I was scared. My heart was racing," he added.
The incident happened close to two Gloucester schools
Jimmy said pupils were locked in their classrooms for two to three hours.
"[When police cars arrived] I thought this is getting serious, I'm getting worried, I don't know what's going on," he said.
The 15-year-old said he was able to message his mother when the school let students use their phones after about an hour.
"When I was able to eventually get out, she was giving me a bunch of hugs," he said.
"What I am is shocked. I'm surprised that this happened," he added.
Jimmy said the school had previously run lockdown drills but a real event had never happened before.
Adam, whose daughter attends the same school, said he felt frightened even though he had texted her and knew she was OK.
"I don't think this should happen at school. Thank God she is safe," he said.
The school had messaged parents to say everything was under control, he added.
Adam's daughter is a pupil at St Peter's High School
Another parent outside the school gates earlier, whose daughter is in Year 8 and nephew is in Year 7, said the family was "so worried".
"I'm slightly calmer now the police have told us they're safe but I want to take them home.
"I haven't heard from them because they aren't allowed phones in school," she added.
Addressing parents outside St Peter's High School, an officer said a police presence would remain at the site for the rest of the school day.
"That is not there for a safety reason, it is to provide reassurance to yourselves and answer any questions. It is not because there is any risk or threat to anyone," she said.

Lorraine Campbell, an independent councillor who represents the Tuffley area, said although police stressed there was no ongoing risk, the incident was still "very concerning" and there was "a great deal of uncertainty".
"There is always a big shock when we hear of something happening very literally on our doorsteps, it's of great concern. Hopefully it gets sorted out as soon as possible," Campbell said.
"Anything like this is extremely troubling and disturbing - we are all concerned but we do all stand together on these things," she added.
Police, who were called to Chalford Road at 08:50 GMT, said no other injuries had been reported.

items.title: Bomb threats against European flights ‘likely a coordinated campaign of disruption’, Ireland says – Europe live
paragraphs: The Irish government has warned against a “likely coordinated campaign of disruption” in a statement responding to the latest bomb threats against European flights after similar threats were issued against some Irish media organisations (11:22).
“The threats made this morning against media organisations here are very serious.

Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or coordinated effort.
However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.”

“The Gardaí, working in cooperation with the Defence Forces, and our cyber and aviation authorities, are working to establish who is responsible. The Gardaí and the Defence Forces are in ongoing liaison with their European security counterparts. Every effort will be made to identify those responsible and to hold them to account.
The main ⁠priority, however, is to ensure that people are kept safe, despite the unavoidable and unwelcome disruption that this may cause.
The Gardaí have been alive to the risk of disruptive threats such as these in the context of planning for EU Presidency events and are exercising the relevant protocols in response.”
Belgian government to have another go at finding compromise on budget
Another day of reported bomb threats against European flights
Ireland says bomb threats 'likely ... a coordinated campaign of disruption'
Dutch military police clears KLM flight from Prague
Hungary scrambles fighter jets to monitor three civilian flights, minister says
Two planes land safely after alerts en route to Sofia
Tell us: have you been affected by the bomb threats to flights in Europe?
Copenhagen police ends checks at Danish capital airport, concludes 'no danger to passengers'
At least eight flights to and from Prague affected by bomb threats this morning
Prague to Bucharest flight gets checked after false alarm
Four new bomb threats against aircraft flying over France, French PM's office says
Rome to Lisbon flight being assessed after bomb threat
Bomb scare forces diversion of Prague-Rome flight to Venice
Bomb threats against Irish media disrupt RTÉ's broadcasts, other media
Czech police investigating threats against planes landing in Prague
Copenhagen police present at airport following 'threats at air traffic' but assesses there is 'no danger to passengers'
Italy's Meloni complains against 'disorderly' process of talks on Ukraine
Morning opening: European skies on high alert after hoax bomb threats this week
I promised you an update on the situation in Belgium, and it looks like King Philippe has successfully pushed the government to resume talks on the next year’s budget.

Prime minister Bart De ​Wever offered to resign on Monday ‌following months of talks that ‌failed to yield an agreement on €10bn in spending cuts and tax increases ‌that he says are needed to stabilise Belgium’s finances.

After their second meeting today, the king’s office said talks would resume immediately as coalition partners seek ⁠to bridge remaining differences and reach an agreement to avert the prospect of early elections, Reuters reported.
The Royal Palace said that in conversations with the king this week all five parties in the government coalition had shown a willingness to compromise.
The king therefore tasked the prime minister with starting a new round of negotiations and with reporting back to the king on 16 November.
De Wever ‌did not speak to the press waiting outside the palace before and after his meeting with the king.
I keep monitoring the situation on European airports for you.

During an earlier disruption at Venice airport (11:33), a number of planes had to be diverted elsewhere: Brussels Airlines’s flight from Brussels and KLM from Amsterdam went to Trieste, whereas Air France’s service from Paris, Iberia’s service from Madrid, and Aegean’s from Athens went to Bologna.
Some of them have since completed their journeys flying back to Venice.

The Irish government has warned against a “likely coordinated campaign of disruption” in a statement responding to the latest bomb threats against European flights after similar threats were issued against some Irish media organisations (11:22).
“The threats made this morning against media organisations here are very serious.

Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or coordinated effort.
However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.”

“The Gardaí, working in cooperation with the Defence Forces, and our cyber and aviation authorities, are working to establish who is responsible. The Gardaí and the Defence Forces are in ongoing liaison with their European security counterparts. Every effort will be made to identify those responsible and to hold them to account.
The main ⁠priority, however, is to ensure that people are kept safe, despite the unavoidable and unwelcome disruption that this may cause.
The Gardaí have been alive to the risk of disruptive threats such as these in the context of planning for EU Presidency events and are exercising the relevant protocols in response.”
The Dutch military police has confirmed that it has checked a KLM flight to Amsterdam faced with a bomb threat and confirmed that no explosives were on board.

The statement did not identify the exact flight, but we know that a flight from Prague to the Netherlands was among the nine that saw bomb threats in Czech Republic, and local Dutch media said the affected flight was coming from the Czech capital, which means it was the flight KL1350.
While the number of bomb threats issued against European planes can sure be unsettling, it’s worth remembering it’s still a tiny, tiny, fraction of all flights taking place in Europe today.
Eurocontrol’s daily counter says there will be 26,709 flights in Europe today.

Hungary’s fighter jets have been scrambled three times this morning to escort civilian flights in Hungarian airspace after reported bomb threats, defence minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said on Facebook.

He said the first alert came in response to a threat issued against a WizzAir flight from Brussels to Sofia (that’s the W64328 we reported on earlier at 12:58), and two more for flights from Prague to Cyprus and Bucharest (the latter one is the Tarom we reported on earlier at 12:16).
Looking at Prague’s departures board, the Cyprus flight will be Wizz Air’s W64600 to Larnaca.
The Prague airport has confirmed to the Guardian that nine flights have been affected by bomb threats so far today, one up from the latest update (12:26).
“The Police have taken the necessary security measures in response. Operations at Prague Airport remain unaffected,” a spokesperson said.

Some other planes appeared to be disrupted too, with AJet’s service from Istanbul eventually diverting to Vienna after making several circles around Prague – although there is no suggestion that it was affected by this morning’s threats.

At least 17 flights have been reportedly disrupted today, but we are getting less detail from airports and national authorities about false alerts today, making it more difficult to keep track of all planes affected.

It’s also interesting to see civil aviation authorities’ planes or helicopters flying near some of the affected airports today, including Prague and Bucharest, keeping a watchful eye on what’s going on.

A Bulgarian transport ministry spokesperson told AFP alerts were also received for two flights to Sofia on Friday, and that both flights coming in from London Stansted Airport in Britain and from Brussels landed safely.
Looking at the airport’s arrivals board, that’d be W64328 from Brussels and FR1730 from London Stansted.
Multiple flights across Europe have been diverted or forced to make emergency landings following a series of bomb threats this week, prompting security checks and widespread disruption.

Are you on one of the affected flights or has your journey disrupted? What happened, and how did you feel? What information were you given by the airline or authorities, and how was the situation handled?
Meanwhile, Copenhagen police confirmed that it’s done with their checks at the Danish capital’s airport (10:48).

“We have been present solely as a security measure. It is therefore our assessment that there is no or has been any danger to passengers or others using the airport. We are investigating the new threats in line with the threats that arrived yesterday, and therefore have no further information.”
FlightRadar24 tracking service shows that some of these searches are making other planes circle near Prague Airport, with at least four planes currently holding near the airport.
We are also getting a bit more detail from the Prague airport authorities on disruptions that once again affected its operations this morning.
At least eight flights to and from Prague were hit by bomb threats, its spokesperson confirmed to AFP.
It concerned incoming flights from Denmark, Spain, and the UK, and outgoing flights to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy, and the UK, Denisa Hejtmánková said.

items.title: Russian opposition leader: release of political prisoners should be part of Ukraine ceasefire negotiations
paragraphs: Editor's note: This story was adapted from the original VOA Russian article.

Russian opposition politician and former political prisoner Vladimir Kara-Murza has called for the release of all prisoners of war in Russia, including Ukrainian civilians and Russian political prisoners. He also urged negotiators make their release a condition of any ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine.

He made the appeal October 30 following the Roll Call for Freedom, a ceremony in Washington marking International Political Prisoners Day. In his interview with VOA Russian, Kara-Murza explained that international attention helps prisoners resist the isolation that authoritarian regimes seek to impose on them.
“The worst thing for a political prisoner is to be forgotten. I have often quoted those words, but I only truly understood them when I found myself behind bars,” Kara-Murza said.

Kara-Murza was arrested in April 2022 for criticizing the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In 2023 he was convicted of treason and spreading “false information” about the Russian army and sentenced to 25 years in prison. He was freed on Aug. 1, 2024, in a major U.S.-Russia prisoner swap that also freed Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich and former Marine Paul Whelan.
People must be discussed first, said Kara-Murza calling for the release of prisoners of war and political prisoners to be included in any possible agreement on a ceasefire in Ukraine.

“In my view, a key element of any possible truce agreement, any possible agreement on a ceasefire in Ukraine, must be a provision for the release of all prisoners, all hostages of this damn war,” he said.

Kara-Murza said this should include Ukrainian civilians held in Russian prisons, children taken from Ukrainian territory, and Russian political prisoners persecuted for speaking out against the war and the authoritarian regime.

“When we periodically hear reports in the media that, during these regularly held negotiations, everything under the sun is being discussed — sanctions, frozen assets, territories, rare earth metals, God knows what else — people must be discussed first.”

Among the journalists, musicians, human rights defenders and representatives of religious minorities from different countries whose names were read at the October 30 ceremony, the only minors were Russian teenagers.

Their stories were presented by Sonya Kara-Murza, Vladimir Kara-Murza’s 17-year-old daughter. In an interview, she spoke about four teenagers between the ages of 15 and 17 who were imprisoned for anti-war statements and other forms of peaceful protest.

One of them was Arseny Turbin. In 2023, when he was 15, he was detained after distributing leaflets criticizing Russian President Vladimir Putin. Russian authorities accused the schoolboy of participating in the Freedom of Russia Legion, which Russia has designated a terrorist organization, and claimed he intended to join the group.

Turbin denied the allegations, saying he had distributed the leaflets on his own initiative. In June 2024, he was sentenced to five years in a juvenile penal colony. The human rights project Support for Political Prisoners Memorial recognized him as a political prisoner.

“Today I spoke about four teenagers who are roughly my age, between 15 and 17. They were all schoolchildren, passionate about something, with big dreams. They were approaching the end of school and were planning their futures, but they were arrested, and today they are all still imprisoned for absolutely nothing. Absolutely nothing. For using their voices or for graffiti,” said Sonya Kara-Murza following the ceremony.
She said stories about children fundamentally change the way people think about political prisoners:

“When we think of political prisoners, we imagine people who already have jobs, politicians or activists. But these are schoolchildren and children, athletes, aspiring scientists and mathematicians. These children should be spending time with their friends and worrying about getting into college, not about when they will see their families again.”
The Roll Call for Freedom ceremony was organized by the October 30 Coalition, established to draw international attention to the plight of political prisoners and support their families.

Its members include the National Endowment for Democracy, the 30 October Foundation, the Free Russia Foundation, Freedom House, the World Liberty Congress, the McCain Institute, the Lantos Foundation, the Raoul Wallenberg Centre for Human Rights, the Human Rights Foundation and Free Them One by One.
The organizers intend to hold International Political Prisoners Day annually and support joint efforts to secure prisoners' release throughout the year.

items.title: Anti-fire ant eradication activist convicted after using legal arguments ‘similar to sovereign citizens’
paragraphs: The Queensland leader of a group opposing the eradication of fire ants in Australia has been convicted of obstructing government officers, after a magistrate threw out his argument that the commonwealth-funded program is illegal.

Trevor Hold was fined $1,500 but a conviction was not recorded. Hold has described himself as an “ultrapreneur”, a mental health counsellor, an organic cattle farmer and the chief executive officer of the anti-program group the Australian Advocacy Group – and as self-employed.
He was convicted last month of two counts of obstruction for attempting to prevent fire ant treatment at his property, in what is believed to be a Queensland first.

His organisation and others held a series of well attended meetings last year across south-east Queensland to advise residents on what the group called their legal rights to refuse or prevent access to their properties to the program.
Under Queensland’s Biosecurity Act, landholders must permit program officers to access their property to treat fire ants, which are a declared priority pest.
But the organisations advised landholders to use a provision in the act allowing them to obstruct an officer if they had a “reasonable excuse” to refuse access, a provision in the Biosecurity Act.

On 16 April at about 9.20am, Hold prevented officers from entering his property in Adare in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane. The property was in the treatment zone and due for its annual treatment.

The eradication program had informed Hold in advance that it would treat his property that day. A small group of supporters gathered to film and yell at them while they did so, according to court documents.
The scene was later described as “an increasingly rowdy and crowded and dynamic situation” in the Ipswich magistrates court, which heard Hold’s charges last month.

He was arrested by Queensland police after about 40 minutes for obstructing them by not allowing a gate to be opened. He was then un-arrested. Despite being warned again, he was again arrested after another interaction with program officers.
Hold made three arguments to the magistrate, Leanne Scoines, in his defence.
He argued that he was intimidated by the police and the program officers and “withdrew his consent for their attendance”, describing himself as “frazzled”.
“It was put to Mr Hold that he was not frazzled, and that he had said on three occasions, as heard in the body-worn camera footage, that ‘this is the Trevor Hold show’,” Scoines said.
Through his lawyer, solicitor Beatrice Ludwig, Hold argued that the police had failed to take into account his “reasonable excuse” and were therefore acting outside their powers.

Hold based part of his argument on emails he sent to the Department of Primary Industries in December 2024 and January 2025, notices the magistrate described as “unilateral”, “quasi-legal documents … seeking tacit approval by non-response”. The magistrate found they were of no legal effect.
Finally, he challenged the validity of the program, arguing that the prosecution had not proven it was properly authorised under the Biosecurity Act, Scoines said.

All three arguments were dismissed and the magistrate found that the officers were entitled to proceed on the basis that the DPI officers were exercising powers conferred on them by the Biosecurity Act.
“I am not satisfied that Mr Hold was a credible or liable witness on the critical issues in dispute,” she said.
A police prosecutor told the court “In my respectful submission it was clear he was actually enjoying this incident”.
Hold has appealed against the judgment to the district court.
On his website, Hold advertises fundraising efforts for his defence, and also a mooted class action lawsuit against the program.

Southern Cross University professor David Heilpern compared some of the arguments used by Hold to sovereign citizen cases he used to judge as a magistrate in the NSW Northern Rivers region, particularly his claim that he hadn’t consented to fire ant treatment.

“That is a tried and tested argument in terms of many of those who are on the fringe of or deep into the sovereign citizen movement; that you have a right to remove consent from the operations of various laws,” Heilpern said.
“Whether you consent or don’t consent is completely immaterial under the biosecurity legislation.”

items.title: The Victorian Liberals’ campaign bus was supposed to be a reset. Instead it became the symbol of a rough week
paragraphs: Jess Wilson has barely put a foot wrong since becoming Victorian Liberal leader a little under a year ago. That was until this week, which ended with her campaign bus reversing into a small business.
The bus was launched on Friday, a few days earlier than planned, in what appeared to be an effort to reset Wilson’s relationship with the Spring Street press pack.

A day earlier, journalists had been left waiting for an hour as Wilson announced a $100m investment in medical research to an enthusiastic room of researchers at the Burnet Institute. But when it came to questions she stayed for just four minutes and 39 seconds – answering a single question from each of the nine journalists present before cutting the press conference short.
The pack had been keen to press Wilson on Labor’s claim that the Coalition’s election policies would cost $6.35bn more than they had disclosed.

The treasurer, Colin Brooks, had earlier spent 20 minutes taking journalists through a glossy booklet Labor titled “Jess Wilson’s Dodgy Costings”, which detailed 30 Coalition promises it claimed had not been costed and dozens it said the opposition had underquoted.

It was an interesting stunt given Labor has its own cost blowouts and financial problems – including net debt that is forecast to reach $199bn within four years. But they are not the only ones questioning how the Coalition plans to deliver a surplus by 2032 while making $8bn worth of election promises, offering tax cuts and vowing not to cut frontline services.
The Liberals have made much of their credentials as better economic managers than Labor and Wilson, as shadow treasurer, should have been prepared to stay and defend her own numbers.
The moment played into Brooks’s suggestion earlier in the day that the Liberals “don’t want to be subject to the scrutiny of having journalists … asking questions during the day”.
“They’re thinking they’re going to coast home to this election result, and that’s treating the Victorian people with contempt,” he said.
A similar thing happened last week, when Wilson’s team cancelled a press conference amid confusion over the Coalition’s plan to “pause and review” the multibillion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop project.

Then there is the debate brouhaha. Both News24 and Nine had requested a debate involving Wilson, the Labor premier, Ben Carroll, and the One Nation leader, Warren Pickering – given the latter is now commanding about 20% of primary votes in most polls.

Wilson has refused, instead insisting on a traditional one-on-one format with Labor, arguing that only the two major parties could form government. Carrollwants Pickering to be included, seemingly keen to keep alive the idea of a Liberal-One Nation coalition despite polling suggesting the Liberal-National Coalition should be able to win government in its own right.
Last week, News24 seemed to resolve the impasse by also inviting the Greens leader, Ellen Sandell.

But no agreement has been reached on Nine’s proposal. Wilson issued a statement on Thursday saying she had agreed to debate Carroll next week. This time Labor refused, claiming Nine has offered Pickering the opportunity to appear in a separate 10-minute segment during the same broadcast.
The Liberals reset on Friday, unveiling the “Jess Express” campaign bus.

Wilson was joined by her team and recruits from Canberra – including her close friend and federal Liberal senator James Paterson, and Kane Silom, who has taken leave from his role as communications director for the federal Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, to work on the Victorian campaign.
She chatted with journalists on the bus before it arrived at a Bentleigh cafe, where she made coffees and served brunch before a press conference, this time clocking in at more than 20 minutes.
Pressed again on her party’s costings, she said voters would have to wait until after early voting begins to see them.
“We cannot release our costings until the government has released its pre-election budget update,” Wilson said.

She batted off questions about the Liberals’ latest election commitment – to sell $1.3bn worth of government-owned land. Labor says this is more “dodgy costings” as it includes land earmarked for first home buyers, and a plot where radioactive cow carcasses were buried that would cost millions to clean up.
“Those costs have been factored in as part of the independent costings by the Parliamentary Budget Office,” Wilson said.
Then it was back on the bus and to the Centre Road shops – one of which became the victim of the Jess Express.
But perhaps there’s a glimmer of hope. Despite the damage, the store owner wasn’t too fussed, provided his awning is repaired.
Nor was it enough for him to rule out voting Liberal – he said he was still undecided.
It will take a little more to stop the Coalition momentum at this stage of the campaign.
Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

items.title: Parents take children out of big schools – level 1
paragraphs: Many parents in Denmark are taking their kids out of big schools. Normal classrooms are too loud and hard for some children.

A boy named Olav has autism. He only goes to school a few hours a week. He mostly learns outside on a farm with his family. Parents are starting local groups where kids can play, work with their hands, and feel safe without stress.
Experts say that schools need to change because kids learn in different ways today. These groups help families stay happy and keep learning every day.
Difficult words: loud (not quiet), autism (a change in a person’s brain which impacts thinking, speaking, and understanding the world), local (when something is in an area or neighborhood near you).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Parents take children out of big schools – level 2
paragraphs: In Denmark, more and more parents are keeping their children home from traditional schools. Many neurodivergent children, like 12-year-old Olav, who has autism, find normal classrooms too loud and stressful.

Because schools lack special resources, parents are creating alternative clubs. In these clubs, kids can learn outside by doing practical things, like working on organic farms or building boats, without feeling stressed.

While government officials worry about test scores in reading and math, experts say the school system is old and needs big changes. Parents hope these new groups will give their kids a safe space to grow, feel happy again, and slowly return to learning.

Difficult words: neurodivergent (thinking, learning, or behaving differently from most other people), lack (to not have enough of something, or to be completely without it), test score (a number or mark that shows how well a student did on an exam).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Parents take children out of big schools – level 3
paragraphs: More Danish parents are pulling their children out of mainstream schools. They argue that the traditional education system is far too rigid for neurodivergent kids.

Children with autism or attention disorders, like 12-year-old Olav, often struggle with noisy classrooms and fixed daily schedules. Because public schools lack resources and specialized programs, many families have turned to alternative support systems, such as parent-led clubs. These spaces allow children to learn at their own pace through practical activities, like organic farming, while giving them a safe environment free from pressure.

While politicians worry about falling academic standards in reading and math, educational researchers argue that the school system itself needs urgent reform rather than forcing children to fit into outdated models. These alternative clubs aim to rebuild confidence and help kids rebuild their relationship with learning.

Difficult words: rigid (unable to be changed or adapted; strictly set), neurodivergent (having a brain that processes information differently than what is considered typical), academic standards (the levels of quality, knowledge, and achievement expected from students in school).

items.title: Met chief says he wouldn't be surprised if more allegations made about Brand after rape conviction
paragraphs: The head of the Metropolitan Police has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about Russell Brand.
Sir Mark Rowley also told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that what he heard reported from Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court came very close to "victim blaming".
On Thursday, the entertainer and comedian was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. The 51-year-old will be sentenced on Monday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also spoken about the case, seeking to explain the Labour Party's previous association with Brand, saying "it's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life".
Some within the party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.
Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.
In 2014, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted in support of Brand on Twitter following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.

It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.
Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned with.
In his 2014 tweet, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".
Speaking on Friday, Burnham told the BBC: "His crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here.
"All I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do."
Speaking to the BBC on Friday, Sir Mark said that he "wouldn't be surprised if more people came forward" about Brand and said there were "two ongoing rape investigations" into him.
Brand has already been interviewed under caution in relation to those allegations.
In his interview Sir Mark praised the "bravery" of the women who came forward to tell "their story" to the police and during the trial.
"That's a real challenge for anyone having gone through something so ghastly and you have to admire them."

The head of the Met also said that whilst Brand's case "may look different because it's about celebrity, the majority of sex offending is about people abusing power", adding that victims will be believed.
"We will do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful person who are responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life.", he said.

It was put to Sir Mark during an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme that Brand's defence barrister "told jurors none of the complainants had in his words 'resisted, screamed or even tried to leave'".
Sir Mark said that what he heard reported from the trial was "very close to victim blaming".

Asked whether he would support the Victim's Commissioner's call for a legal duty in the Courts and Tribunals Bill that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

He said he would "strongly support" that call, adding: "It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case."
Brand was refused bail following his conviction on Thursday and will now spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to the same court on Monday for sentencing.
He is expected to face a substantial prison sentence.

Once the trial was over, it was reported that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has already been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Metropolitan Police said its investigation "remains ongoing".

Details in legal documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court before Brand's criminal trial began suggest that one of the women was 16 years old at the time and featured in a Channel 4 documentary.
The actor and comedian denied the allegations.
None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.
During a pre-trial hearing in October, Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.
His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer could not receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.
During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.
The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.
The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.
A man who was accused of laughing while Russell Brand sexually assaulted a woman in 2009, has been asked "to step back" from his employer while they consider the verdicts.
Jack Bayles was part of his entourage in 2009 and was said to be present when one of the sexual assaults took place.
Brand had been working on a Channel 4 project when he laid his head into the groin area of a woman who was helping him at the time.

During the trial, the victim told the court Jack Bayles and another member of staff of Brand's had asked her to give the comedian a massage, and said he wouldn't continue unless she did. Shortly after - he sexually assaulted her.
She had complained to her manager - who told the court through a statement at the trial that the victim had described how the men had laughed while the attack took place.
In recent years, Jack Bayles has been working for the TV production company, Various Artists Ltd, as their head of comedy.

In a statement, they told the BBC: "We have asked Jack Bayles to step back from the company whilst we consider the verdict and events surrounding the trial. Our thoughts, though, are primarily with every one of Brand's victims at this time."

According to his biography on the Various Artists Ltd website, Bayles commissioned shows for Channel 4 including two series Derry Girls and Aisling Bea's This Way Up, plus Back, Year Of The Rabbit, Frank Of Ireland and Hullraisers.
In a statement, Mr Bayles said he was sorry but doesn't remember the sexual assault.
"I am appalled and sickened by Brand's actions and have co-operated fully and voluntarily with the investigation and endeavoured to assist as best I can," he said.

"However, I do not remember the incident that took place 17 years ago in 2009. But I acknowledge that I clearly missed something at the time and did not see nor recognise that it caused distress. For that I am sincerely sorry."
He said at the time of the offence he was in the early stages of his career, calling it "a frantic, pressured and toxic working environment".
He described Brand as someone who was "chaotic, dismissive and manipulated the people around him".

The producer said this was why he decided to stop working with him in 2010, adding he "has not had any contact with him since", and that when he worked with him, no complaints were made to him about Brand's behaviour.
"I am unaware if any were raised to anyone else more senior to me," he said.

"I would never willingly or proactively wish to make anyone feel uncomfortable, unsafe or unsupported at work. If I was ever present when Brand acted inappropriately and I failed to spot it and step in, then I sincerely apologise".

items.title: EU charges TikTok with failing to protect users’ mental health
paragraphs: TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of content that risks worsening eating disorders and anxiety in a case that strikes at its business model.
Issuing a preliminary ruling on Friday, the EU regulator said TikTok’s algorithm “can be harmful” and was leading young and vulnerable users “down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from”.

The Chinese-owned short-video platform, which has 189 million users in the EU, was found to have failed to prevent users from being served up repetitive content on themes such as body image or isolation, which can lead to anxiety, sadness, worsen existing eating disorders or mental health problems.

Officials said their investigation focused on legal content, where a single video might not be problematic, but the cumulative effect of watching scores of them on one theme could damage users’ mental health.

TikTok’s safeguards to mitigate the risks of “rabbit-hole effects” – where users are served narrow and repetitive content to keep them engaged – were found to be ineffective. For example, officials said, if a user checked a “not interested” button on a video about eating patterns, the algorithm would still offer them similar content on diet and body image. Similarly, refreshing a feed only provided a brief respite from a stream of content on one topic, it found.

“Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” said the European Commission’s lead official on tech policy, Henna Virkkunen. “TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ wellbeing, including those of minors.”
In response, a TikTok spokesperson said: “The commission has made a series of statements that are fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety.
“We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience.”

The company argues that its policies prohibit content that promotes disordered eating and risky weight-management behaviours. It also says that more than 79 million users in the EU used its “not interested” or keyword filters to screen out unwanted content in the first six months of 2026.
The EU investigation strikes at TikTok’s business model, which is built on keeping users scrolling as long as possible.
EU officials want TikTok to change the design of its ForYou feed, to give users greater control over the content they see.

“We are addressing a business model,” a commission official told reporters, saying that a business model focused mainly on engagement “can potentially create a risk” especially for minors and vulnerable adults.

The findings are part of a broader investigation launched in February 2024 under the Digital Services Act, which obliges large internet companies to take action to prevent a wide range of harms, from disinformation to damage to mental health.

The commission has already found the company violated EU rules over its “addictive design” for features such as infinite scroll. The company said at the time “the commission’s preliminary findings present a categorically false and entirely meritless depiction of our platform” and that it would challenge the findings.
A complaint about lack of transparency over who paid for TikTok’s advertising was resolved when the company made binding commitments to change its policies last December.
TikTok, which now has a chance to examine the investigation file and mount a defence, could agree to change its recommender system to avoid a fine.
If EU officials uphold the finding, the company could be fined up to 6% of its global worldwide turnover.

items.title: Further bomb threats disrupt at least another 18 flights across Europe
paragraphs: A fresh wave of bomb threats has disrupted air traffic across Europe but the affected planes landed safely and searches revealed no explosive devices.

The latest alerts affected at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria, Czechia, France, Italy, Hungary, Cyprus, Romania, the UK and Portugal. Danish police investigated a threat against Copenhagen airport but the airport said it was operating normally.

The warnings followed separate threats on Tuesday and Thursday that forced at least 35 flights to be diverted or searched, raising questions over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.

The latest threats affected at least nine flights to and from Prague, four flights over France, two flights en route to Sofia and a flight from Lisbon to Rome. Hungary scrambled fighter jets three times to escort civilian flights in its airspace, the defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, said on Facebook.

The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny percentage – just 0.0674% – of the 26,709 flights that according to the air traffic control agency Eurocontrol were scheduled in Europe on Friday.
A separate spate of threats on Friday against media organisations in Ireland disrupted broadcasts and prompted staff evacuations and police searches of offices and newsrooms.
The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, told RTÉ Radio 1 after it resumed scheduled broadcasting that such threats had to be taken seriously and were an effort to sow fear and anxiety.

“It shows how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and undermine the normal operation of society.” European security agencies would seek to identify those responsible and hold them accountable, said Martin.
The British broadcaster ⁠Sky said on Friday it had also received a ⁠security threat and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.
Earlier this week, cyber-attacks targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

Investigators have said there was no evidence that hoaxes against airlines and other targets were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, but that inquiries continue.
Some of the threats on Thursday were signed “fighters of the Male State”, a reference to a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016.
Some officials suspect the waves of disruption are linked to European support for Ukraine in its war against the Russian invasion.

Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, said authorities needed more time to identify culprits but that there appeared to be a pattern. “It ⁠cannot be mere coincidence that so many incidents with exactly the same modus operandi are happening across Europe,” he told the national broadcaster TVE.
“The ​most reasonable assumption is that we are facing ​an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form ​of psychological warfare,” he said, adding that Europe must be prepared for more such challenges.

items.title: Katherine Ryan says she feels 'grief and relief' after Russell Brand conviction
paragraphs: Speaking about the guilty verdict of his trial, on the latest episode of her podcast Telling Everybody Everything, Ryan said: "It really made me feel just quite dysregulated again, caught off-guard, emotional, in awe of the survivors who also had nothing to gain.
"They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money, and a legion of fans ready to attack them."
She added: "I will never be someone who like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There's a level of relief, but there's grief alongside relief.
"Everything's nuanced, and it was proved in court that a terrible thing happened, and that means that a terrible thing happened.

"I just think again and again about people who have been hurt, and who have to carry that, who've carried that around long enough, and will continue to carry that in some way, regardless of what justice is done."
Brand is now also being investigated over further rape allegations made by two women, police have now said.

Details in legal documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court before Brand's criminal trial began suggest that one of the women was 16 years old at the time and featured in a Channel 4 documentary.
Brand was accused by four women of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint Channel 4 Dispatches, Times and Sunday Times investigation in September 2023.
The actor and comedian denied the allegations.
None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.
On Thursday it emerged that Brand was facing further rape allegations made by two women. The Metropolitan police said he had previously been interviewed under caution in relation to them.
During a pre-trial hearing in October Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.
His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer couldn't receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.
Prosecutors opposed Brand's application to have his case stopped.
It was during that hearing that the prosecution said one of the complaints made in the documentary was being investigated.
Riel Karmy-Jones KC said: "Of the four women in the Ch4 documentary, two concern events outside the jurisdiction.
"One did not disclose any offence. The other is being investigated.
"There had been some interaction in 2018, she did not report the matter until 2024, after the documentary was aired."
In documents submitted to the court for the hearing prosecutors also said it was "plainly incorrect" to say there had been a decision not to investigate.

"The outstanding charges against RB in respect of 'Alice' from Dispatches demonstrate that there has been no such decision – rather that the police will and have responded appropriately once a formal allegation is made."
The head of the Metropolitan Police has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about Russell Brand.
Sir Mark Rowley also told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday that what he heard reported from Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court came very close to "victim blaming".

items.title: Flávio Bolsonaro battles to remain relevant as he speaks at rightwing conference at Mar-a-Lago
paragraphs: Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right politician who lost Brazil’s presidential election last month, has insisted his defeat is not “the end for Brazil” as he battles to maintain political relevance after fleeing to the US.
Bolsonaro absconded early last week shortly after losing the 25 October election to the leftwing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than 4m votes.

On Thursday night Bolsonaro made his first major public appearance since arriving in the US, speaking at a rightwing gathering at Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property where he claimed “great things” were still to come.

“I know this wasn’t the end for Brazil and I know it wasn’t the end for America,” Bolsonaro, 45, told a gala dinner at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC)’s four-day “gathering of visionaries” event, where the former British prime minister Liz Truss is also due to speak.

“Even when what seems like the end isn’t what we’d hoped for, we must thank God and have even more faith that this isn’t yet the end,” he added. “No one shuts the door that he opens – and the door he shuts, no one opens.”
Earlier, in his first post-election interview, Bolsonaro made a series of unsubstantiated claims about election fraud and insisted he received “help from absolutely no one” to flee.

“It was all me,” Bolsonaro told the New York Times, contradicting reports that he was helped by the Trump adviser Jason Miller and Santiago Caputo, a close aide to Argentina’s rightwing president, Javier Milei.

He said he would “take to the grave” the full story of how he had fled Brazil, where he faces federal police investigations for money laundering and corruption. Bolsonaro is a member of congress who has held elected office for more than 20 years but he will lose parliamentary immunity early next year when his term ends, meaning he could then be prosecuted.

Brazilian analysts agree that by skipping the country after an election in which he received 59m votes, Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, abdicated leadership of the opposition and sabotaged his political future.

Thomas Traumann, an author and pundit for the TV network GloboNews, said: “Flávio was foolish enough to throw away the leadership of the opposition that he could have exercised had he stayed in Brazil. But the [Bolsonaro] family is still a player.”

Flávio Bolsonaro’s brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, also lives in self-imposed exile in the US and will have to serve a four-year sentence for coercion if he returns to Brazil. Four other members of the Bolsonaro family were elected to congress in last month’s election, including their brothers Carlos and Jair Renan and stepmother, Michelle Bolsonaro.

Traumann believed it was not inconceivable that Jair Bolsonaro would attempt a political comeback if he managed to negotiate his way out of his 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. However, as things stand, the 71-year-old is banned from running for office until 2060 and must live under house arrest.
Many doubt the Bolsonaro family can continue to control Bolsonarismo, the populist political movement that takes their name, with two key members in exile and one imprisoned.
“[The movement] is mortally wounded because of its mistakes and its crimes,” the political scientist Sérgio Abranches told the newspaper O Globo this week.

Abranches said democratic rightwing politicians now had a chance to “detach” themselves from the Bolsonaros’ anti-democratic movement and break off in a new direction before the next presidential election in 2030.
Flávio Bolsonaro told the New York Times he would “obviously” be a candidate in future elections but said his future lay in the US “at least for now”.

It is unclear where Flávio Bolsonaro, who has been granted a US visa by Trump, will live. His brother Eduardo set up home in Southlake, Texas, after leaving Brazil last year – although some expect him to move after the traditionally conservative state elected the Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor in this week’s midterms.

In a video posted on CPAC’s social networks before Thursday’s event, Eduardo Bolsonaro played down the risk posed by the “blue tsunami” to their ability to stay in the US. “They [Democrats] will try [to make trouble for us] – but it’s not up to Congress … to revoke visas or citizenships,” he said.
Likening their plight to that of a female asylum seeker fleeing Iran for fear of being killed after refusing to wear a hijab, he added: “I am 100% legal – as is my brother and his family.”

items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?
paragraphs: It is Thursday night and I am sat blurry-eyed and runny nosed outside the Argos on Oxford Street. Incredibly, I am far from alone. This is not some strange protest against the popular retailer. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills.

These days, of course, most video games are bought as digital copies that download straight to your PC or console on the day of release. You don’t even have to get out of bed to start playing. But in a bygone era, when we used to go to shops to buy games, midnight launches offered a space for likeminded enthusiasts to gather and celebrate their fandom. Every Call of Duty, Halo or Grand Theft Auto release would have fans queueing outside branches of Game or Electronics Boutique, many dressed as favourite characters.

As one of the few Brits deluded enough to spend six hours queueing at the Wii U’s midnight launch, I have a certain fondness for the game launch as a cultural event rather than just a weird display of performative consumerism. There was something heartwarming about seeing the video game hype cycle transformed into a shared experience.

In our age of downloads and streaming services, however, you might wonder why anyone would bother queueing for hours in the November chill. Well, myself and hundreds of others have made the pilgrimage for one infuriatingly irresistible reason: those attending the launch would not only get a copy of the game but also a limited ocarina-shaped keyring and an exclusive replica of the original 1998 N64 box. To you, perhaps, a worthless piece of cardboard – but to us, a highly collectible, nostalgia-soaked … piece of cardboard.

Arriving at the queue for 22:45, bottle of water in hand, it’s not long before I realise I may have already blown it. With midnight launch events now few and far between, I had no idea whether people would still show up. Yet London’s Zelda fans had answered the Ocarina’s hymn and assembled en masse – snaking all the way around the corner.

Thankfully, we’re soon informed by staff that everyone will be receiving a precious exclusive box regardless. Even if the stock runs out tonight, they say, we will all be posted one. Cue the Zelda treasure chest fanfare. I befriend a popcorn-munching man behind me who regales me with tales of the GameCube launch, as confused gen Z queuers regard us elderly Nintendo fanatics with disdain. The throng shuffles ever closer from the sidestreet into the back street, but when the clock strikes midnight, the shop is still a world away. A parade of men with cameraphones clutched to their chests circles the snaking queue, recording our suffering for future generations.

At 2am, progress halts and frustration grows. Reluctantly, I scout to the front to investigate. It transpires that the store will soon shut, and the hundreds of queuers that remain will need to leave their details to receive the feted box by post. By the time I scrawl my name and address, I have been queueing for four hours.

As I wait for my taxi, questioning my life choices, I see a fellow cardboard enthusiast peering into the shuttered window, wistfully admiring the Zelda display. He tells me that his partner attended the Paris midnight launch where the queues were similarly enormous. Not only did she walk away with nothing, but Nintendo France were not taking details or promising to post boxes out to unlucky queuers. As my lift pulls up, the nostalgic appeal of the midnight launch has all but dissipated. I take small comfort in knowing one thing – at least we’re better off than the French.

items.title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
paragraphs: The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.

The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.

The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.

The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.

In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.

With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.

Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.

The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.

With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

items.title: US rockets firm could take over mothballed Highland spaceport
paragraphs: HIE and Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn have welcomed the agreement.
The site is on Melness Crofters Estate, an area of small-scale farms on the A' Mhoine Peninsula in Sutherland in the north-west Highlands.
Chairwoman Dorothy Pritchard said the estate was delighted to welcome Leap as a potential launch operator.

She said: "We believe their presence here will be an important step towards establishing a thriving and sustainable spaceport that can bring long-term benefits to Sutherland and the UK's growing space industry.

"Alongside other UK launch sites, both developed and emerging, an operational Sutherland Spaceport will become an integral part of a resilient and diverse UK launch ecosystem, securing the UK position within the global space economy, something we welcome and support.
"Melness Crofters Estate looks forward to seeing the spaceport become a driver of economic opportunity."

items.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production as Elon Musk focuses on robotics and AI
paragraphs: Elon Musk has announced that Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck, marking the end of a failed effort to take a chunk of the lucrative market for pickups in the US.

The billionaire chief executive said production of the car would stop in about the middle of next year at the company’s factory in Texas in order to use the plant for the Cybercab, its self-driving taxi.
Musk did not say whether Tesla had plans to produce the vehicle in another factory, although that would probably require significant investment for the specialised tooling needed to make it.

Musk has pinned hopes for Tesla on robotics, artificial intelligence and an autonomous driving fleet rather than following the traditional carmakers’ approach of developing a steady stream of new models to entice private buyers.

It caps a tricky week for the world’s richest person, after Republican candidates he had backed with $446m (£332m) in donations lost in the US midterm elections. The paper value of Musk’s fortune fell by $113bn after the extent of the rout became clear, as stock market investors questioned whether a Democrat-led Congress could slow the pace of the AI boom.
Tesla shares fell by 11% on Thursday, while his AI and rocket launch company, SpaceX, dropped by 9%.

Tesla started deliveries of the Cybertruck in late 2023, after several long delays as the company tried to cope with the technical challenges of producing such an unusual vehicle – and particularly its steel shell.
The Cybertruck never made it on sale in Europe because it did not reach the required safety standards.

Even before sales began, Musk acknowledged how difficult it would be to make it a success. In a 2023 earnings call, he said: “We dug our own grave with Cybertruck,” and noted “enormous challenges” in increasing production and earning money from it.

Musk had said the company aimed to sell 200,000 Cybertrucks each year but it never approached that target. Tesla does not report sales of the trucks separately but in the third quarter of 2026 it delivered only 8,300 “other models”, which include the Cybertruck. The vast majority of its sales were the Model 3 saloon and the Model Y SUV, with 478,000 combined deliveries during the quarter.
Tesla also this year stopped production of its Model S and Model X, its premium saloon and SUV, amid declining sales for ageing products.

Tesla’s automotive focus has shifted to the Cybercab. Tesla has started offering paid trips in the car, which has space for two passengers and no steering wheel, in limited parts of Austin, Texas. However, it is unclear how quickly the company will be able to roll out the taxi service around the US or further afield amid close regulatory scrutiny of driverless car technology.

As well as the Cybercab, Tesla is still ramping up production of its long-delayed Semi electric lorry. Musk is also aiming to produce one other new model: the Roadster sportscar, which Musk revealed with a demonstration of a “flying car” version that used thrusters developed by SpaceX to drive up a curved ramp before flipping and landing. Tesla is aiming to start production of a road-bound version in 2028. Analysts do not expect the Roadster to make a large difference to Tesla’s future profits.
Beyond vehicles, the Texas factory will also be used to build Tesla’s Optimus humanoid robot.

Musk posted on X, the social network he owns: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

items.title: 'We have our own fair playing field': 1Xtra launches first ever UK rap chart
paragraphs: British rap artists will step into the spotlight later when BBC Radio 1Xtra launches the first ever dedicated rap chart based on UK listening figures.
DJ Kenny Allstar, who'll host the countdown on Friday nights, has one word: "Finally".
"If we have our own fair playing field where we can all be celebrated... it then feels fair and it feels exciting," he tells BBC Newsbeat.
Currently artists compete across genres for a spot in the Official Singles Chart, but Allstar says this is dominated by pop music, making it harder for other genres to be heard.

Perhaps with the exception of heavyweights like Central Cee and Dave, who broke chart records with Sprinter back in 2023, "it's not easy for any artist to go against Sabrina Carpenter and Taylor Swift every week," he says.
Compiled by the Official Charts Company, 20 rap singles from British artists will be ranked each week based on streams and sales in the UK.
It follows the launch of other genre-specific charts including for R&B, 'homegrown' albums and British Asian music.

Allstar hopes it'll give UK rap a boost as he acknowledges it has taken a bit of a beating recently with prominent artists like Skepta and Digga saying the quality of music coming from the scene has dipped.
"Future broadcasters and talent will benefit from this forever, I'm super gassed."
Allstar has long been a champion of UK rap and currently presents the Rap Show on BBC Radio 1, which he describes as "the show I always wanted as a kid".
This new role is "a pinch me moment," he says.
The Official Charts Company previously listed the 40 top selling R&B and hip hop tracks on its website, but there had been nowhere for fans to listen to the chart.
"It was literally just a bunch of numbers and text, so it kind of existed but not in this capacity," Allstar says.
Each week will likely see at least three or four new artists in the chart, giving emerging talent a chance to be heard by hundreds of thousands of listeners.
"What we can finally have is UK rap having its dedicated space where artists can just be celebrated," he says.

Eric Hunter, from the Official Charts Company, says the countdown will be "an amazing opportunity to shine a light on more artists, document the culture and give emerging talent a way to track their progress alongside their peers".

The company says UK rap is "one of the country's most influential and fast-moving music scenes" and the chart will celebrate both established names and the next generation of rappers driving the scene.
The debut show coincides with Skepta's long-awaited sixth studio album and Allstar says he expects to see the rapper feature in the chart.
"It's looking promising, but the only way you can find out is if you listen in," he says.
The Official UK Rap Chart will broadcast on 1Xtra each Friday from 22:00-23:00 and will be available after on BBC Sounds.

items.title: Most Europeans want action to tackle climate crisis but not at any cost, poll shows
paragraphs: Europeans believe human-made climate change is real, a survey has shown, with most feeling action must be taken soon – as long as they do not have to sacrifice too much to achieve it.

The YouGov poll of six European countries showed between 69% (Germany) and 80% (France) of respondents believed the climate was changing, with few (1%-4%) denying it and 14-20% believing it was changing, but not as a result of human activity.

Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent and scientists say human-driven climate breakdown through the burning of fossil fuels is increasing the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and destructive storms.

Days before the Cop31 climate conference in Turkey, the polling showed vast majorities (79-89%) in Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK thought countries would combat the crisis more effectively by working internationally.

Those in the EU were more likely to say that climate action decisions should be made at EU rather than national level, a feeling shared by 50-54% of respondents in France, Italy and Germany as well as 61% in Denmark and 64% in Spain.

Majorities of between 65% and 83% in each country surveyed said they were worried about the climate crisis, including 23%-42% who were “very worried”. YouGov noted an uptick in concern during this summer’s heatwaves.
In April, 74% of respondents in France said they were worried about the climate crisis but that figure was up to 83% by mid-August and still at that level last month.

The number of French people who were “very worried” about climate change also rose, from 28% in April to a record high of 42% in August, a level it held last month. Concern in other countries spiked in August but has since dipped.

In Germany, for example, the number very concerned rose from 27% in April to 40% in August but has now fallen back to 31%. Concern remained relatively stable in Denmark, at 66%-69% “worried” and 20%-23% “very worried”.

Across the six countries surveyed, respondents mostly (45%-63%) thought it was not too late to avert the worst impacts of the climate crisis but that it would require a drastic change in approach. Only 11%-24% believed it was already too late.

Between 9% and 20% said they thought current measures would be enough to prevent the most serious impacts. But in terms of what climate actions had support, those not directly affecting people’s lives were the most popular.

Measures such as planting more trees, subsidising energy efficiency, banning single-use plastics and taxing big emitters were all favoured, while increasing fuel duty, limiting meat and dairy, taxing air fares and banning new petrol and diesel cars were opposed.

A similar pattern emerged when respondents were asked what steps they would be prepared to take: cheap and easy actions such as creating green space at home and eating only seasonal fruit and vegetables were popular, but not shopping exclusively secondhand or paying more for flights.

items.title: How 2000s lad culture helped Russell Brand to hide in plain sight
paragraphs: Russell Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault
Warning: This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual acts
No British celebrity navigated the cultural changes of the early 21st Century better than Russell Brand.
His life has been one long personal rebrand.

He morphed from provocative stand-up comic to TV star and Hollywood actor. He became a YouTuber and political activist, taking up left-wing causes around issues of inequality in the 2010s, then Covid conspiracies and in 2024 supporting Donald Trump for president. That same year he was baptised as a Christian in London's River Thames.
Now he has a new persona to try on: convicted rapist.
On Thursday, the disgraced comedian was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.
As he faces jail, it's clear that the behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution is the same behaviour that helped elevate him in the first place.
Brand performing at the MTV Video Music Awards a year after his memoir was published
Brand shot to fame as a sexually outrageous libertine whose risque humour thrilled audiences.
He cultivated the image of an insatiable, shameless womaniser. Sex, drugs and excess were central to his comic material.
Over the decade of his offending, Brand sold out stand-up comedy venues and theatres, broadcasters - including MTV, Channel 4 and the BBC - started to throw money at him.
With his backcombed hair and drainpipe black jeans, Brand regaled audiences at his stand-up comedy gigs with the graphic details of his sexual exploits: anal sex, prostitutes and orgies.
He simulated masturbation and sex on stage. He said he liked oral sex with women "where it goes in their neck a little bit" and their "mascara runs a little bit," acting it out on stage.
Even Brand's own barrister called the humour "a product of its time," reminding the jury in the trial that this graphic sexualised comedy was viewed as "radical and different" back then.
Barely a generation later, many will view it as deeply rooted misogyny dressed up as humour. But these were different times.
Back then lads' magazines ruled - with their covers and double page spreads full of topless glamour models and half-naked female celebrities
The late nineties and early noughties in Britain were an era that celebrated casual sexism and often elevated celebrities who espoused it.

In 1999, FHM projected a naked photo of the Scottish TV presenter Gail Porter on to the Houses of Parliament. She only found out when she saw it on the news, and spoke later about how it deeply affected her mental health.

What might now be termed toxic masculinity was often deemed funny, seen by some as good old-fashioned male humour. By others it was viewed as palatable because they believed it was being done with an apparently ironic eyebrow raise.
"There is no question he was a very talented stand-up," says Sarah Ditum, author of Toxic: Women, Fame and the Noughties. "There was an appetite for taboo breaking.

"I think it looks very old hat if you look back on that stuff. It's dated horribly and I don't think many people are going to be keen to defend Brand's act now knowing that it reflected his real world behaviour rather than an ironic performance."
My Booky Wook topped the Sunday Times bestseller chart for seven weeks in 2007
But there were clues at the time that his outrageous stage act did not stop when the show ended - most publicly in his 2007 bestselling memoir, My Booky Wook.
"I'm a bloke from Grays with a good job and a terrific haircut who's been given a Wonka ticket to a lovely sex factory 'cos of ol' fame."

Of course, many of his sexual partners consented. As his defence barrister told the jury "he devoted himself for many years to a highly promiscuous life", reminding them that "having lots of sex is completely lawful".

My Booky Wook, which topped the Sunday Times bestseller chart for seven weeks in 2007 and sold 600,000 copies in hardback in the UK, opens with him checking into a clinic for sex addiction. He writes about going to lap dancing clubs and having "a lot" of oral sex in toilets and many threesomes.
"The rules change when you're famous. In that case two is often better than either none or one."
He writes about how an MTV PR "reminded me that I put lap dances and prostitutes on her gold card and got the hotel to give me cash on her account without her prior knowledge".
The Observer called it "a scandalous, libidinous memoir that is better written and more entertaining than any number of celebrity autobiographies that clog the shelves".
Heat said: "You come away from the book feeling like you really know - and like - the real Russell."

You can't imagine a celebrity these days writing a memoir in which he claims that at stage school a primetime actress, whom he names, "kissed me once in a corridor" and for years afterwards he'd tell people "'I had sex with her… And by sex, I mean bumming'".
But it's all told in a jokey, revelatory way, by "a bloke from Essex who likes birds with big bottoms and big boobs…. Lovely dolly-birds".
Meeting crowds backstage in Sydney in 2010
In light of his offending, writing that was celebrated for being frank, honest - and very funny - now looks anything but.

People "are willing to mistake irony and self-awareness for truth telling and trustworthiness," says Ditum. "The idea that he made these jokes about being this kind of sexual monster was supposed to convince you that he wasn't actually a sexual monster in real life."

Did normalising his behaviour allow him to hide in plain sight? Were the media companies who embraced him, the comedy venues who promoted him, the audiences who laughed at his humour, in some way complicit?
A former TV boss who didn't want to be named explained the thinking of his peers like this: "You've got this charismatic presenter who appears to be very, very good and you don't want to lose that.

"The women who were being persecuted didn't feel empowered to speak up and the few who did feel empowered might have been classed as troublemakers but certainly weren't really listened to because you didn't want to lose the star. That was the process."
Indeed, in Brand's trial, one of the complainants told the court she didn't report what had happened to her because she didn't think she would be believed in "those laddish culture times".
"It was my word against his," she said in her evidence.

Jo Caulfield, a contemporary of Brand's on the early noughties stand-up circuit, says she initially found him "utterly charming" but she sees that he was "enabled and nobody will say anything against it".

"People have people around them, promoters, assistants in TV. It's in the hierarchy of TV. If a runner [an entry-level production assistant] goes to his dressing room and he gets his knob out, it's like, 'oh, come on, don't make a fuss.'"
And while safeguarding standards have been heavily tightened in some parts of the entertainment world, she says it "still goes on".
"Nobody wants to upset the star. This person is making them money so everybody down the food chain better not say anything if they behave badly," says Caulfield.
At the end of My Booky Wook, Brand writes "I have done some terrible things over the course of this booky wook… I mean, over my life."

items.title: Measles, mumps and misinformation: how Crunchy Moms became ‘the most dangerous’ group on Facebook
paragraphs: As a measles outbreak spread through Lancaster county, Pennsylvania, in August, a parent turned to a massive public Facebook group, Crunchy Moms, for advice. They were considering getting their three-year-old vaccinated, in part to protect their six-month-old.
