“I’m nervous for my baby,” the parent wrote.

“First of all your children cannot die of measles. It is literally impossible,” one member responded. “Do not do it,” advised another. Others said the vaccine would spread measles or that it would be like “injecting poison”.
At the end of the post, Facebook’s AI system – run by its parent company Meta – summarized the 589 responses, writing in part that commenters “claim the vaccine is unnecessary or even harmful”.

None of those claims are true. Pennsylvania has reported six measles-associated deaths this year, including two babies in Lancaster county. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is safe and effective. Health officials say it is the best defense against measles spreading and injuring or killing people.

Scientists, doctors and advocates for health and children’s safety told the Guardian that what they see in Crunchy Moms and similar groups is alarming. They worry children could be getting hurt and that mothers are getting pulled into an online community that rejects science and fact-based medicine. One scientist who spends her free time monitoring the platform to highlight harmful health misinformation calls Crunchy Moms “the most dangerous group on Facebook”.
Meta did not comment on that characterization.

The spread of misinformation on Facebook has been a problem for years, but in the past, the company took steps to curb it. During the Covid-19 pandemic, for example, Facebook recognized it had a problem and changed its policies to “prioritize connecting people with accurate health information”.
But last year, shortly before the inauguration of Donald Trump, Mark Zuckerberg, Facebook’s billionaire founder, said there was “too much censorship” on Meta’s platforms.

Meta changed course; it eliminated factcheckers in the US and dialed down active moderation of anything but the most severe or illegal content. The company still maintains a policy that prohibits harmful health misinformation, but it is not known how Meta enforces it, and how its new permissive approach affects users at a time when measles and other infectious diseases are making a comeback.
In response to questions from the Guardian, Meta claimed nothing has changed in the policy or how it is enforced since 2023.

A Guardian investigation has found that dangerous medical misinformation is flowing freely on Facebook in groups like Crunchy Moms – now more than 490,000 members strong. What’s more, the company appears to have helped spread such ideas by promoting Crunchy Moms into users’ feeds, even when they do not seek it out.

Zuckerberg previously suggested that waiting for users to report “bad stuff” – rather than having automated systems catch them – would strike a better balance between what he termed censorship and free expression. But the Guardian found that following Zuckerberg’s suggested approach appears to have little to no discernible effect on false information that circulates on Crunchy Moms.

Facebook took no action on more than 50 posts and comments a Guardian journalist reported to the platform from her own Facebook account. The posts appeared to violate Meta’s own standards, including that vaccines caused autism, that measles is not deadly, or that “miracle cures” like the caustic agent black salve that destroys skin tissue can treat cancer. Facebook did not acknowledge or respond to a single one of the Guardian’s reports, made in May, July and September.

In a response, Meta said its misinformation policies allow people to discuss personal experiences and scientific research. It said it removes misinformation when it is likely to directly contribute to the risk of imminent physical harm. But Meta did not respond to detailed questions about Crunchy Moms or experts’ assessment that such misinformation is commonplace in the group.
Meta’s revenue last year exceeded $200bn.

Doctors, researchers, former employees and public health advocates said the Guardian’s findings show that the pendulum at Meta has swung back to a time when there was little moderation of false health information.
“We were documenting Facebook recommending anti-vaccine groups to parents almost a decade ago,” said Renée DiResta, a professor at Georgetown University who studies online manipulation.
She and others have shown how that approach harmed children. Back then, there were stories of children being hurt or dying after their parents turned to Facebook groups for health advice.
“I’m afraid that we’re going to see that same kind of dynamic all over again.”
A Guardian journalist was scrolling on her phone in March when something caught her eye. Her Facebook feed recommended she join a group called Crunchy Moms: Natural Living & Clean Products.
The group was created in March 2025, less than three months after Zuckerberg announced Meta’s new hands-off approach.

Crunchy Moms’ administrators describe it as “a supportive space for moms who want to raise their families using toxin-free products, low-tox alternatives, and clean ingredient solutions.” But a quick check of the group revealed, and experts confirmed, it was a hotbed of false medical information that could hurt people – especially children and their mothers, who turn to the group for community, advice and affirmation.

The group focuses largely on health, though some posters also come to seek parenting tips, product recommendations and other non-medical questions. Many posters appear to take it as a given that group members are – or should be – against vaccinating their children. They frequently describe vaccines and their ingredients as deadly, toxic or poisonous.

“We don’t vaccinate in this group. It’s the foundation of becoming a crunchy mom,” one anonymous member explained last month, in response to a question about the vaccine for RSV, a respiratory virus. A group administrator responded to a different post that “As a crunchy community we are generally against v@cs” – a code for vaccines.
Crunchy Moms has more than doubled in size since January, and receives hundreds of posts a day, and thousands of comments and replies.

Sara Rupe launched the group in March 2025. It was less than three months after Zuckerberg announced Meta’s new hands-off approach. The Connecticut mom said in an interview that her intention in creating the group was to share product recommendations for things like personal care products and makeup, but it turned into something bigger.
At least part of Crunchy Moms’ success, she said, was because it does not block “free speech”.
“Everybody has a right to say what they want to say as long as it’s within community standards of Facebook,” Rupe said. “I don’t censor things.”

Rupe added: “If somebody wants to say something, then I usually let them. But I mean, within reason, if I really think it’s going to hurt somebody, I don’t. But I also think letting some information get out there could be good.”

Crunchy Moms is the largest group in a network of groups that collectively has over 1 million members. Rupe runs them with the help of several administrators and moderators, including her husband, who is a registered nurse, a pastor and wife couple in upstate New York, and a woman whose Meta-verified account describes her as a doctor of holistic health.

They post often with links to supplements and other products for sale on an Amazon store, with links to another administrator’s skincare line, or with affiliate links to products that provide a cut of sales to the person sharing it.

Rupe said she and another administrator use multiple accounts to run the group, which lets them maintain access to it if Facebook restricts her account. Her daughter was in seventh grade last year when Rupe used her account to post a listing of over three dozen products, including herbal remedy bundles that run over $100, non-fluoride toothpaste, $25 tallow balm and red light therapy panels that cost $200 or more.

A second administrator, Dawn Mannion, said she doesn’t make any money from the group, though others make a small commission that’s “not even minimum wage”. She said she frequently recommends that members seek medical attention from holistic or other qualified healthcare professionals. She added: “We do not discourage people from seeking medical care. We encourage it.”
Other administrators and moderators contacted by the Guardian did not respond to Facebook messages and texts seeking comment.
Many Crunchy Moms members were already into “natural living” and questioning vaccines when they come to the group, and group leaders don’t try to sway anyone’s mind, Rupe said.
Rupe has a child with autism that she now believes is connected to vaccination, and said many others in the group believe their children were injured by vaccines.
“We don’t want anybody to be hurt at all,” she said. “We want everybody to be as happy and healthy as possible.”

While Crunchy Mom posters often vehemently counsel against vaccines and modern medicine, Rupe said she does not think the group is harming anyone. Instead, she said it is helping people make their own decisions.

Some members say vaccines are so dangerous that it is safer to get a deadly or life-altering vaccine-preventable disease than it is to get immunized. They tell other members that catching a disease like measles or chicken pox “naturally” can be more healthy than getting vaccinated. Others repeat US Health and Human Services secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr’s unproven claims that Tylenol is linked to autism. One recent comment said that catching measles makes your body stronger, trains your immune system and results in a lower risk of cardiovascular disease and cancer.
Many posts spread the false assertion that vaccines cause autism and sudden infant death syndrome (Sids) – even though Meta specifies in its own policies that posts saying so violate its terms.

New or soon-to-be mothers looking for help and advice are frequent posters, and targets for swarms of comments telling them not to follow science-backed health recommendations for their children, like giving their newborns a Vitamin K shot that can prevent brain bleeds.

One woman asked about a link between vaccination and Sids, suggesting she feared she was putting her baby at risk of death if she followed the recommended vaccine schedule. She said she was considering spacing out her infant’s vaccines to lessen the risk. She ended her post: “I’m terrified.”

“Delaying poison won’t do anything beneficial. Injecting poison WILL increase the likelihood of SIDS,” one woman replied. Another, labeled an “All-Star contributor” by Facebook, weighed in: “SIDS is vaccine death. SIDS was invented to cover up the fact that vaccines kill infants.”

Scroll through a post asking whether vaccines cause autism, readers will find comment after comment saying that they do. In one post, a frequent commenter offered a false statistic that 79% of autism is caused by vaccines. She replied to a person who said they were neurodiverse: “Your parents caused this with their vaccines. I am sorry.”

The same commenter later counseled the Lancaster county parent who was worried about their community’s measles outbreak that “It is not worth risking death or a disabling lifelong neurodegenerative condition, such as autism, for a vaccine that is ineffective, at best, at preventing measles.”

The group includes a mix of views. Some commenters will offer encouragement to seek medical care and to vaccinate their children. The Guardian spoke to people who became members of Crunchy Moms to try to provide a counterweight to the false information shared there.
Mannion said they do not endorse every statement made by individual members.

One of the Crunchy Mom rules that is supposed to govern the group is that the information shared is not medical advice, and that members should consult a healthcare provider before making any health or medical decisions. But in the many posts from parents asking for advice or sharing what their doctors told them, commenters often urge them not to follow what the doctor suggests, or say there is no need to speak to a doctor at all.
Rupe said she believes many of the comments are from “trolls” trying to get the group in trouble, and that people are simply posting their opinions.

Dr Alok Patel, a pediatrician who reviewed the group at the Guardian’s request, pointed to those kinds of comments as particularly concerning. It is a time-honored tradition for mothers to turn to fellow mothers for advice, and Patel believes it is important for people to use social media to find connection.

“But when people are outright dismissing modern medicine and putting their foot down and saying don’t get vaccines, don’t get the vitamin K shot, don’t see a doctor, and instead promoting a product, that is outright misinformation and potentially dangerous,” he said.

Patel has built up his own following on Meta’s Instagram platform to deliver science-based medical information to people. Social media companies, he said, should show it is more important to provide quality information than it is to keep people on their apps.
“Prove to us that you are prioritizing public health as much as you prioritize profits for your investors,” Patel said.
Research has shown that health misinformation shared on Facebook can have a real-world impact on people’s decisions.

Jennifer Allen, a professor at NYU Stern who worked at Facebook from 2016 to 2018, has researched the effect of misinformation and vaccine-skeptical content on Facebook. She and her colleagues have estimated that exposure to vaccine skeptical content on the platform during the Covid-19 pandemic reduced people’s intention to get vaccinated. Without that exposure, they estimated 5 million more Americans would have been vaccinated, saving approximately 21,000 lives.
While people should be able to express themselves, Allen said, there is evidence that the kinds of expression she saw in Crunchy Moms can be dangerous.

“The fact that this group seems to exist and is being recommended to people, and there is so much clear misinformation in it, it seems to me that that means that there’s a failure along the way of Facebook,” Allen said.

During the pandemic, she said Facebook got pretty good at identifying and taking down egregiously false information and also not recommending it to people. She said she was surprised to now see such explicit misinformation being shared in a public group, and Facebook recommending it to users.

One scientist who spends her free time trawling Facebook to highlight the harmful information she sees there spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity because she has received harassment and threats. She said Crunchy Moms stands out among the worst, but is far from the only group where these problems are happening.

“Meta, and specifically Facebook, is allowing for these things to continue,” she said. She cited posts she has seen that counsel mothers not to get the Vitamin K shot for their newborns and others that sell unregulated supplements. She said she believes it is more dangerous than any other groups she monitors.
“Everybody should have the freedom to talk about what they want to talk about,” Rupe said when given the opportunity to respond to that criticism.
Given the volume of the posts, Rupe said she and other administrators can’t vet every single post.
“I’m assuming that if Meta sees that it doesn’t agree that it will just take it down. So I don’t really worry about that part,” she said.

In 2019, Facebook announced it would stop recommending groups that spread misinformation about vaccinations, saying it was “fully committed to the safety of our community”. DiResta said the company responded to public pressure as it became clear anti-vaccine activists were using Facebook to undermine public health in places like Samoa, where a 2019 measles outbreak killed 83 people, mostly children under age five. Facebook’s regional policy director said at the time that its teams were “proactively scanning for any health-related misinformation and are taking action to prevent its spread on our platforms”.

Later that year, Zuckerberg was pressed on the issue by a Republican congressman who complained Facebook was censoring users’ speech about vaccine risks and injuries. Zuckerberg, whose wife Priscilla Chan is a pediatrician and who donated $75m to a major San Francisco hospital which now bears their name, acknowledged the concern. But he said “we also hear consistently from our community that people want us to stop the spread of misinformation” and that he understood “scientific consensus is that it is important that people get their vaccines”. While users would be allowed to post anti-vaccine content or join such groups, Zuckerberg said Facebook would not “recommend or go out of our way to show people content that would encourage people to join those groups”.
After Covid hit in 2020, Facebook stopped recommending health groups altogether, explaining that “it’s crucial that people get their health information from authoritative sources.”

Anti-vaccine activists complained of censorship and joined with Republican politicians and others who took issue with Facebook’s response to false information about elections and other civic matters. Then Trump was elected to a second term. His pick to lead the nation’s health department was Kennedy, a longtime leader in the anti-vaccine movement who has accused Facebook of censoring him and the group he used to run, and sued over it. The case was dismissed.

Shortly before Trump was sworn into office, Zuckerberg and Meta announced the end to third-party factchecking in the US as well as rollbacks to moderation. A few weeks later, Zuckerberg and tech CEOs attended Trump’s inauguration.
Still, Meta retained a misinformation policy.

The current policy says it removes what it calls harmful health misinformation that is “likely to directly contribute to imminent harm to public health and safety”. It lists several specific examples of what it does not allow – much of it about vaccines. Among those are claims that vaccines cause autism or Sids; that vaccine ingredients are deadly, toxic, poisonous, harmful or dangerous; that vaccines are not effective; and that measles is not deadly. Meta’s policy also says it bars promoting or advocating for harmful miracle cures, including black salve which is peddled online as a skin cancer treatment without evidence that it works, and it has disfigured people or left their cancer to grow.
Though Facebook issued a report on how it has enforced its community standards this year, it did not discuss how or whether it has enforced its standards that govern misinformation on health.

The Guardian spoke to several people who had reported Crunchy Moms posts to Facebook or who had tried to report posts outside the group that similarly contained dangerous health misinformation. They said they had little success.
“My own personal post reports have universally been ignored by Facebook,” said Dr Frank Han, a pediatric cardiologist in Connecticut.
“While Facebook claims that they moderate, the practical effect is that medical misinformation propagates much faster than medically correct information,” Han said.

Another Crunchy Moms member, Emily Loving-Rodriguez, said she had made dozens of reports to Facebook, and possibly hundreds, since she joined earlier this year. The Idaho resident has a personal interest in child welfare and misinformation, and noted a post she had seen recently in Crunchy Moms where someone said herpes could be cured with the dietary supplement zeolite. She said her reports rarely had any effect.
Kasey Kramps, another member, said she had made reports to Facebook in the past for medical misinformation but said she could no longer find a way to report it.

“Their health misinformation rules are very explicit. They’re still up there,” said DiResta, who reviewed the group at the Guardian’s request. “They have a policy and they actively choose – at this point – it does not seem that they are enforcing it.”

To test how Facebook enforces its harmful medical misinformation policy, the Guardian reported 55 Crunchy Mom posts, comments and replies and one video reel to Facebook that appeared to violate the policy.
It is the approach that Zuckerberg endorsed when he announced Meta’s changes in January 2025.

“We used to have filters that scanned for any policy violation,” Zuckerberg said then. “Now we’re going to focus those filters on tackling illegal and high severity violations. And for lower severity violations, we’re going to rely on someone reporting an issue before we take action.”

The Guardian’s reports spanned a range of content. One post stated in part that scientific research shows “vaccines cause autism”. A comment said: “The MMR vaccine CAUSES measles.” Another: “Vaccines are extremely toxic and unnecessary as well as NOT safe or effective. They all poison.”

In a video shared in the group that downplayed the dangers of tetanus and urged against vaccines, a caption included the line “High-dose vitamin C led to 100% survival in tetanus-infected children and reduced death rates in adults.” Meta’s policy prohibits saying Vitamin C is as effective as a vaccine.

On a post asking: “What are we using to get rid of skin cancer?” the Guardian reported several replies suggesting black salve. It also reported a post asking for a brand of black salve to use on a “questionable mole/mark”, as well as the reply from a group administrator providing an affiliate link to purchase a black salve product, as well as to another administrator’s Amazon store.
The Guardian also reported the entire Crunchy Moms group on 1 October, given that similar content is commonplace within it.

There is no way to report content specifically as harmful health misinformation. Instead, the user making a report must first select a broad category: “scam, fraud or false information”. Then, content can be reported under the heading “Sharing false information”.

The Guardian did not receive a single confirmation from Facebook to any of its reports, even though the company says it alerts users to the outcomes of their reports. Loving-Rodriguez said when she reports comments for hate or Nazi content in other Facebook communities, she gets a message from Facebook confirming her report. But not when she flags content that seems to violate Facebook’s rules in Crunchy Moms.
Nearly all of the content the Guardian reported to Facebook was still up when Meta was approached for comment.

While the repeated reports of policy violations by the Guardian didn’t receive any responses, Facebook invited the journalist to join the platform’s community notes program. The program replaced third-party factcheckers in the United States after the 2025 rollbacks. Meta has said it was already testing the program in several countries and plans to roll it out and eliminate factcheckers once it was confident it was working well.
The Guardian this week provided Meta with examples of content found on the group. Meta said it was reviewing those links and would take action on posts that violate its policies.

Recommendations have become an important source of content on Facebook, now representing 36% to 39% of what users see in their news feed, according to the company’s most recent reports. That content comes from sources they are not connected to but which Facebook determines might interest them. By contrast, content from friends makes up only about 20% of users’ feeds.
Facebook says it makes such personalized recommendations to help people “discover new communities and content”.

When Facebook chooses to promote a group, DiResta claimed, it is using its editorial discretion, exercising its speech and making a value judgment. In the past, she said, Facebook had acknowledged that recommendations create a different level of responsibility from simply allowing people to speak.
The Guardian found several people who encountered Crunchy Moms in their feed as a result of Facebook’s curation choices.
“It came across my feed, and I engaged,” said Kramps, who joined the group about six months ago. “I did not seek it out.”
“It was offered to me organically in my feed,” said Dr Casey Husser, an anesthesiologist in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. “I didn’t look for Crunchy Moms.”
A Minneapolis mother of two children, ages two and five, told the Guardian Crunchy Moms showed up in her feed for months, even though she was not part of the group and did not seek it out.

Meta told the Guardian its approach to misinformation is to create an environment that reduces its distribution. It did not address specific questions about why it was recommending Crunchy Moms to users’ feeds.

Facebook also has taken the step of adding titles or comment summaries to some posts. Generated by Meta’s AI tool, they are meant to “help people catch up” on conversations on the platform. The comment summaries it offered on some posts conflicted with good science, critics said.

For example, Meta’s AI entitled one post: “What vaccines are recommended or skipped during pregnancy and infancy?” It summarized the comments by stating: “Hepatitis B and flu vaccines are commonly suggested to skip, while some recommend delaying or picking and choosing vaccines.”

That conflicts with recommendations from doctors’ groups in the US, which recommend universal hepatitis B vaccination for all infants at birth, as well as flu vaccine for children six months and older and for pregnant women during influenza season.

On the Lancaster measles post, which asked for ways to “detox” from the MMR vaccine, Meta’s AI summarized the discussion as: “No detox needed, some commenters cite vitamin A deficiency as a measles risk factor, while others claim the vaccine is unnecessary or even harmful.”
Meta’s AI system could be adding context to that post to clarify that a vaccine detox is not a scientifically valid idea, DiResta said.
“It’s very easy for an AI to do that,” she said, pointing out that Meta uses AI for some notes on Threads. “But it seems, again, that they’re choosing not to do that.”

Meta told the Guardian on Wednesday evening it had gotten rid of AI summaries of discussions in September. But the Guardian took screen shots of more than 10 such summaries in October, some going back as far as December 2025.
Meta did not respond to specific questions on the issues the Guardian raised about the substance of the AI-generated content.
Husser said he makes it a habit to pay attention to bad medical information circulating online so he won’t be surprised at work if patients ask him about it.
“[Facebook is] way more permissive,” Husser said. “Since 2025, it’s become a totally different environment.”
Crunchy Moms’ administrator Rupe said she has noticed a change as well. In the past, she remembers getting Facebook strikes or removals for mentioning the word vaccines.
“It seems like we’re not getting in trouble for a lot of things like we used to,” Rupe said.

In the past, she recalls that Facebook would flag posts it deemed as containing misinformation before they were approved, and said she usually would not approve them if she saw such a message. But she doesn’t remember getting any this year. Rupe said Facebook only takes down about one post per month from Crunchy Moms.
Meta’s AI will alert her when someone uses a swear word, or a variation of one, in the group. But Rupe said it doesn’t give her any alerts about what some might call medical misinformation.
DiResta said the fact that Facebook is recommending this group to people is significant.

“Meta is pushing this thing unsolicited into the feeds of particularly new parents” who naturally have concerns and fears about their childrens’ health, DiResta said. “They want to feel that they’re doing the best for their kids.”

items.title: Simple nudes, priceless fakes and riches from an emperor’s palace – the week in art
paragraphs: Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires From the tulips and silks of the Ottoman court, back in time to the Emperor Constantine’s palace, this is a sumptuous and haunting mystery tour. V&A South Kensington, London, 7 November to 9 May

Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant Two modern painters, one complex relationship in an exhibition that takes you to the heart of the early 20th century Bloomsbury Group. Tate Britain, London, from 12 November

Ida Applebroog Angry Birds of America, a series of animal images that updates Audubon for the Trump era, and naked portraits of people that celebrate human variety. Fruitmarket Gallery, Edinburgh, until 11 February
Glenn Brown The superbly decadent contemporary painter takes on the luscious genius of Thomas Gainsborough. Gainsborough’s House, Sudbury, until 18 April
Alexis Kyle Mitchell An exhibition about health inequalities and the way people’s bodies are judged. Site Gallery, Sheffield, until 21 March

The aficionados among you will immediately recognise this screenprint: Marilyn Monroe was recreated countless times with infinite variety by Andy Warhol. Only the very keenest cognoscente, however, will recognise that pop art’s king of reproduction has himself been reproduced here. Elaine Sturtevant’s Warhol Black Marilyn (2004) is just one example of a feedback loop the conceptual forger has created with artists such as Jasper Johns, Keith Haring and her beloved Warhol, by copying their work to such a degree that it makes us reflect on how meaning is created around art. Her exhibition is at Raven Row in London until 20 December.
Comedian Andy Field drew a horse a day until he mastered it
Visiting art galleries is good for you but we do we need another self-optimisation prescription?
A rare Renaissance masterpiece hidden for 70 years could fetch £5m at auction
British modernist painter Wilhelmina Barns-Graham is finally getting the recognition she deserves
CJ Reay is fighting the system with quilts
You can make great art by putting a traffic cone on your head
The Bloomsbury Group helped shape how we think about mental health – and illness
Art imitates life imitating art imitating life … if you consider Rocky art
The Virgin and Child by Giovanni Bellini, c1480-90

The Bellinis not only dominated Venetian art in the later 15th century but spanned east and west, linking Italy with Istanbul. Giovanni’s brother Gentile travelled to the capital of the Ottoman Empire and portrayed its Sultan – as seen in the V&A blockbuster Constantinople to Istanbul – as well as other places and people he saw in the eastern Mediterranean. Giovanni was more of a homebody but you couldn’t entirely avoid global influence in Venice, capital of a great trading empire, with its golden Byzantine mosaics in St Mark’s. Is there perhaps a hint of a Byzantine icon about this painting with its eerie spiritual calm and the subtly luxurious hanging behind the Virgin? You feel the air warming and vibrating around her, the stillness of those clouds, the rich veined purple marble of the parapet in front of her. Bellini makes you meditate with his music of colour. National Gallery, London

items.title: e.l.f.’s stop-motion Christmas ad is a win for human creativity
paragraphs: The fight for the Christmas advert crown is on, and brands have set standards high this year. From hand-drawn animation to immersive storytelling, there's been a wonderful display of hand-crafted creativity, and among the ranks, beauty brand e.l.f. did not disappoint.

As the brand's first-ever holiday campaign, the beautiful stop-motion animation is a sparkling debut that captures the joy of the festive season. A masterful display of tactile craftsmanship, the 'e.l.f. Made to Stand Out' campaign carries many of the traits of the best Christmas adverts, proving that analogue storytelling is the perfect tool for sparking festive joy.

Narrated by iconic actor Alan Cumming, the campaign follows friends Kit, Echo and Cleo as they reunite in their hometown for a holiday get-together. What could be an uncomfortable hangout turns into a celebration of the qualities that make them extraordinary, spreading festive cheer.

“For a campaign about the power of standing out, the medium needed to stand out too, and stop motion felt like such a natural fit for this story," explains Oshiya Savur, chief marketing officer at e.l.f. Beauty. "We're seeing a real appetite for nostalgia and a return to simpler times, with 72% of Americans saying nostalgic memories inspire them when life feels complicated.
There's an incredible level of craftsmanship and character that comes from building an entire world by hand

There's something about stop motion that takes you right back to the holiday specials you grew up watching, but we saw an opportunity to give that familiar art form a uniquely e.l.f. twist. There's an incredible level of craftsmanship and character that comes from building an entire world by hand, and when you combine that with our signature wit and wink, you create something that feels both familiar and completely unexpected.”

Created by Apartment D Films, each element of the ad reads as a love letter to analogue craft, from individually moulded characters to intricately constructed miniature sets. "We used a wide variety of different materials! It's truly a mixed media project," Cami Kwan, Creative Director of Apartment D, tells Creative Bloq. "The puppets have aluminium and steel wire armatures inside, which makes them posable. Their hands and heads are made of printed resin, which we then painted and finished with actual e.l.f. products! The cheeks and mouths of the puppets are colored using a combination of e.l.f. Powder Blush Palette, e.l.f Perfect 10 Eyeshadow Palette, and e.l.f. Halo Glow Silky Powder Highlighter.

All the characters' hair is made with different weights and textures of yarn, to call back to super nostalgic toys, but with a modern sensibility. The eyebrows and eyelids of the characters are made of a mix of wax and clay, so they're super mouldable to get big expressions in the performance, and also so you can literally see the animators' fingerprints on the characters as they emote.

A lot of the world around the character is made of wood, but with hand-painted textures so the wood grain is more painterly and stylized. The mini products and bottles the characters use are all hand-sculpted out of clay, and then finished with a variety of nail art techniques, like cured acrylic, gels, and powder shimmers! The mini bottles are really so, so small; none of them is more than 1 inch tall."

It wasn't a project without some difficulties, as Cami explains. "One of our challenges was integrating real beauty products intended to live on human skin with stop-motion puppets. Unlike real humans, our puppets don't have pores and don't have a body temperature, both of which e.l.f. beauty products are chemically formulated to interact with.

On top of that, stop motion puppets are designed to be handled and touched constantly during the animation process, so the treatments and colors on them need to be incredibly resilient to constant wear and tear. We spent a good deal of time on the material testing of the e.l.f. beauty products to see which ones would integrate best with our fabrication techniques.
We're seeing a renewed appreciation for the analog, and I think that's a natural response to an increasingly digital world

It was actually really interesting to let our puppet team dip into their extensive knowledge of material science! We've found that generally anything based in a powder pigment merged really well with our typical techniques, and those combinations were really successful in getting puppets with a lot of character and a lot of dynamic color and shimmer on screen!"

Honouring such a tactile animation style is a time intensive practice, but are audiences hungry for analogue creativity? “Absolutely," says Oshiya. "The more purely AI-generated content we see, the greater the opposite and equal reaction from people craving something real: human connection and creativity they can actually feel.

We're seeing a renewed appreciation for the analogue, and I think that's a natural response to an increasingly digital world. At e.l.f., we're human first, human last. AI can be an incredible tool, but taste, discernment and original ideas come from human ingenuity. At the end of the day, we want to make people feel something, and that human element is what makes it possible.”

"The thing I'm most proud of is how kind and collaborative our crew on this project was. It's not something you can point to on screen, but it's something you can feel in how much care was taken with every frame, and how lively the animation is. There was so much joy in the creation and filming of this project, and I do think you can feel that in how kinetic and inventive everything is. It's a little zany, a little imperfect, and really so captivating when all seen together!" says Cami.
Every quirk and detail adds personality to the story, and there's no expectation of perfection.

"For a more specific on-screen detail, though, I love the smear frames we used when Echo is zooming between the tables and getting everyone amped up! Smear frames are an animation technique that's most typical in 2D animation – they're moments when, for just a few frames, you distort the character and literally smear them to give a sense of speed, mimicking the way something moving too fast on a live-action camera will appear blurry.

You hardly ever see smear frames in stop motion, but one of the things that we really focus on at Apartment D is pushing the stylistic boundaries of stop motion and finding ways to bring 2D animation techniques into our three-dimensional medium. So, in that Echo zooming scene, we actually used pieces of cut paper to create practical, dimensional smear frames! Jen Prokopowicz, the animator of that shot, curved the paper smears to get an extra sense of dimension, and created smears of different sizes to get a sense of speeding up and slowing down. It's just so cool, and something that generally only real animation nerds will notice," Kami adds.

“At e.l.f., we've never been interested in being part of a sea of sameness. We're a brand that celebrates the unexpected, embraces individuality and believes that what makes us different is what makes us extraordinary. That's what I love about stop motion. Every quirk and detail adds personality to the story, and there's no expectation of perfection. Just as no two handcrafted creations are exactly alike, no two people are either. It's a playful way to bring our belief in celebrating every eye, lip and face to life, and a reminder that your difference is low-key your gift,” says Oshiya.
For more creative inspiration check out Prada's Disney inspired Christmas campaign or take a look at Dior's festive ad that ruffled some feathers.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: Sydney's Powerhouse Parramatta revealed ahead of public opening tomorrow
paragraphs: The Powerhouse Parramatta museum in Sydney by architecture studios Moreau Kusunoki and Genton, which is described as the largest cultural project in Australia since the Sydney Opera House, is set to open tomorrow.

Located on the banks of the Parramatta River in western Sydney, the distinctive Powerhouse Parramatta museum is wrapped by a lattice exoskeleton of steel that acts both as facade and structure. It was designed to “pioneer a new museum model” that redefines contemporary museum practice and culture.

“We designed the new Powerhouse Parramatta with the mission of calling the museum paradigm into question and conceiving a platform with limitless potential that evolves over time and through its users,” said Moreau Kusunoki.
Paris-based architecture studio Moreau Kusunoki, in collaboration with Australian architecture firm Genton, split the 30,000-square-metre museum into two blocky forms connected on the upper levels.

A system of three-layered steel lattice wraps the exterior of the building, referencing the iconic structure of Sydney Harbour Bridge while also connecting to the industrial heritage and manufacturing traditions of the site.

“Together with engineer Jun Sato, we developed the concept of ‘lattice’ for the structural exoskeleton – a system of intricate lattices that are wrapped around the spaces of the museum and support their dynamic programming, providing total interior freedom,” Moreau Kusunoki explained.

“Through the dissolution of the structure into a fine, efficient three-layered lattice, we conceived an envelope that transcends scale in order to exist simultaneously as both intimate and iconic, becoming the museum’s most recognisable design element.”
The lattice exoskeleton serves as the building’s facade as well as structure, which enables column-free interior exhibition spaces that support the museum’s diverse programming.

These include Exhibition Space 1, which is described as the largest column-free exhibition space in Australia. At 18 metres high and spanning over 2,000 square metres, it features a mechanical hoisting door in five sections, allowing it to open to the public riverside terrace.
Along with seven more traditional exhibition spaces, the institution contains 30 residential studios, numerous co-working spaces and other community-led learning facilities.

Beneath the lattice exoskeleton, much of the facade is fully glazed to filter natural light into the interiors. These interstitial spaces are informed by the Japanese concept of mâ – the interval between things, people, and time – shaping moments of pause that foster reflection and informal interaction.

“The concept of ‘in-between’, or mâ in Japanese, is central to the design approach in all our projects,” said Moreau Kusunoki. “We carved these spaces throughout the museum’s design as an indispensable factor of placemaking.”

“In contrast with the opaque nature of the presentation spaces, we modelled the mâ spaces as transparent and full of natural light, looking over the Parramatta River below and onto the horizon and country beyond,” it continued.

“The potential of the interstitial spaces gives way for life and meaning to evolve and to naturally appear in between the defined spaces, while events and interactions arise ‘through the cracks’, thereby organically enhancing the impact of the project.”

The two blocks, which were designed to open up on the ground floor, stand on two sides of a riverside terrace that sits above a garden that slopes down to the river. According to the museum, two-thirds of the site is dedicated to landscaped public space, with indigenous plant species planted under the guidance of the local First Nation community.

A rooftop terrace features a garden and a greenhouse, while an observatory with telescopes sits beneath a retractable roof. The museum’s ING Garden Pavilion will be used for hosting talks and workshops alongside community and industry programmes.
The neutral palette continues from the exterior to the interiors, with internal walls clad with glassfibre-reinforced concrete (GRC) panels of various textures.
They were made with quartz aggregate, waterglass-finish concrete and hand-applied oystershell render, adding tactile surfaces to the interior to create a calm exhibition viewing experience.
The building has been designed to operate at net-zero carbon.

Sustainability is embedded across the project, from renewable energy and water systems to zero-waste exhibition principles, making it the first public building in Australia to be assessed as a 6 Star Designed project under the Green Building Council of Australia‘s new Green Star Buildings assessment tool.

Five major international exhibitions will open tomorrow as part of the opening programmes of Powerhouse Parramatta, including Task Eternal, an immersive exhibition exploring humanity’s journey into space, which will be presented at Exhibition Space 1, and designed by Chinese architecture studio Open Architecture.
Dezeen is partnering with Powerhouse Parramatta to host two talks exploring the design and making of the landmark new museum. as part of the opening celebration.

The first brings together the architects, engineers and construction teams behind the building, while the second sees Dezeen co-CEO Benedict Hobson in conversation with OMA/AMO managing partner David Gianotten about The Mall – an ambitious exhibition examining the evolution of shopping centres and their influence on architecture, retail and contemporary culture.

A total of 179 events will take place across three weeks following the opening day as part of the opening festival programme, showcasing over 3,000 objects, including over 1,600 from Powerhouse Museum’s own collection.

Dezeen will also publish an exclusive video interview with architects Moreau Kusunoki and Genton, alongside four social videos exploring the museum’s inaugural exhibitions, including Task Eternal, The Mall and Es Devlin’s The Turning, showcasing the breadth of design, creativity and ideas behind the museum’s opening programme.

The creation of the new Powerhouse Parramatta museum, and the expanded research and public facilities at Powerhouse Castle Hill completed in 2024, form the $1.3 billion infrastructure renewal programme for the largest museum group in Australia. The renewal of the heritage Powerhouse Ultimo is still on going and expected to complete by late 2028.

Other recent landmark projects completed in Sydney include the Western Sydney International Airport, open to public last month, and Sydney Fish Market, which claims to be the largest fish market in the southern hemisphere.
Photography by Rory Gardiner, Powerhouse Studio, Christina Yao

items.title: Olivia Rodrigo's Christmas song sounds familiar... on purpose
paragraphs: Pop star Olivia Rodrigo unwrapped her first-ever Christmas song on Thursday night, alongside a festive music video starring Sex and the City star Cynthia Nixon.
The track, called Take Me Home (4 Christmas), finds the pop star asking her boyfriend to "show some serious commitment" by bringing her to his parents' house for the Christmas break.
As soon as it was released, fans noticed similarities to The Waitresses' 1981 festive hit Christmas Wrapping... And it turns out that was by design rather than mistake.
Chris Butler, who wrote The Waitresses' song, posted a message on Facebook, external, saying Rodrigo had contacted him to seek permission for the song; and praising her "phenomenal" writing.
"About two months ago, I received a weird email from someone claiming to be 'Olivia Rodrigo'," he said. "Said she'd written a Christmas song, and invited me to hear it."
Admitting he'd never heard of the pop star before, Butler said he assumed the email was a fake.
But after researching her career, he became a fan - not just of her music, but of the fact she'd hired an all-female band, and negotiated control of her master recordings.
In the end, he decided to reply to her email - and posted the text to his Facebook profile.
"If you really are you, thanks for contacting me. And your comments are really sweet, and very flattering," he said.
"They're really sweet and flattering... even if you AREN'T you.
"If you really are Olivia Rodrigo: I like you, I like your music. I like the arrangements especially. Soft-loud-soft, etc. And that your recordings sound like people are playing on them.
He continued: "I like that your lyrics are intense, real, and poetic. I like that you "got" my songwriting, and that you like our band."
Butler also accepted the invitation to hear Rodrigo's Christmas song, and told his followers: "Her song was/is great.
"It's going to be a smash, maybe even that elusive Christmas number one contest they have every year in the UK."

Although the song is indebted to the Waitresses' new wave and post-punk sound, Butler does not receive a writing credit on Take Me Home (4 Christmas) as it neither samples nor interpolates any of his music.

Posting on social media, Rodrigo said it was written last summer with her longtime collaborator Dan Nigro, and Amy Allen, who has previously contributed to songs by Harry Styles, Sabrina Carpenter and Tate McCrae.
Meanwhile, the Christmas jumper-tastic video, external follows the single's storyline, with SNL star Ben Marshall playing her feckless boyfriend, and Nixon starring as her prospective mother-in-law.
Rodrigo's track arrives in the same week as several other major contenders for this year's Christmas number one.

Singer-songwriter Sam Fender has covered the Rolling Stones' You Can't Always Get What You Want, external for this year's John Lewis Christmas advertising campaign; while CMAT has teamed up with Elton John for a countrified version of his festive classic Step Into Christmas., external
Alanis Morissette is releasing an album called Good Weather for Immaculate Conception, while Sufjan Stevens is issuing a compilation of his festive output, titled Worst Christmas Ever.

Chic legend Nile Rodgers has also teamed up with X Factor star Rebecca Ferguson to cover The Christmas Song (Chestnuts Roasting on an Open Fire), although the duo have received a backlash for using AI to create the song's video.
And Kate Nash has written a track called Christmas Eve, external, which tells the story of the night her grandparents met in Dublin.

However, all the new Christmas songs have the unenviable task of going up against Wham's Last Christmas and Mariah Carey's All I Want For Christmas Is You, which typically dominate the festive charts.
The two songs entered the UK's Spotify top 10 on 1 November, two weeks earlier than last year.
Wham secured the Christmas number one slot in both 2023 and 2024 - and could receive a sales boost this year, as fans mark the 10th anniversary of George Michael's death.
Last year's festive chart-topper was Kylie Minogue's XMAS.

items.title: The Cabinetmakers’ Autumn Exhibition features a rug-wrapped chair and a giant candle holder
paragraphs: The 2026 edition of the Danish furniture show has opened at Museum Ordrupgaard, with works by 36 designers on show alongside historic paintings and sculptures.
For this year’s edition of the Cabinetmakers’ Autumn Exhibition, or Snedkernes Efterårsudstilling, designers were invited to contribute works that explore the relationship between light and form.
The theme was chosen to reflect this year’s venue, the Snøhetta-designed galleries of Museum Ordrupgaard, which house important works of French and Danish art from the 19th and 20th centuries.
“In both impressionism and furniture design, light becomes a means of shaping an atmosphere and creating a sense of presence,” the exhibition overview stated.

“While the painters explored the impact of light on colours and atmosphere, designers examine the encounter between light and form, materials and surfaces, as use, function and aesthetic fuse into one, and even minor details and variations in light influence our perception of the furniture.”

The results include a 1.8-metre-high floor lamp that looks like a candle holder, by designers Karen Kjærgaard, Nanna Gram and Peter Skrzipczyk, and an elm wood chair wrapped in a patterned wool rug, by designers Karin Carlander and Christian Street.

Other eye-catching works include a cube made out of squashed ceramic vessels, by ceramicist duo Claydies, and a heavy bronze piece designed to look like a lightweight woven chair by designer Hans Sandgren Jakobsen.
The Cabinetmakers’ Autumn Exhibition has been an annual fixture since 1981, but its origins go back even further.

It began as a revival of the historic Cabinetmakers’ Guild Exhibition, which ran from 1927 to 1966 and debuted some of Denmark’s most iconic furniture designs, from Børge Mogensen’s Spanish Chair to Hans J Wegner‘s Round Chair.
Most of the works are contributed by members of the association, which is made up of over 80 designers, architects and manufacturers, although a handful of guests are invited to join each year.
One of this year’s most attention-grabbing works was contributed by guest exhibitor Matteo Fogale, a Uruguayan designer based in Copenhagen.
Fogale partnered with lighting brand Astep on a family of curvaceous ash wood lamps of different heights, topped by rotating discs that double as both lights and dimmer switches.

August Ostrow’s Soft Structure Lamp is another of the guest works. The American designer took cues from folded metal forms found in heating and ventilation machinery to create his copper and paper table light.
Timber craft is well represented in the show, with one particularly impressive piece by designer Andreas Lund and cabinetmaker Søren Risvang Snedkeri.
The pair collaborated on a table with an experimental frame of slender pine rods and 3D-printed joints.
Anna Søgaard designed a pair of cherry wood frames with opposing curves, while Claus Landry Bjerre crafted a pine wood cabinet incorporating 3D-milled replicas of 3D-scanned hazel branches.

Notable works in other materials include Carlo Volf’s wire-frame lamp, Zeyu Rong’s curvy translucent screen, and a light formed of four triangular glass tubes by Jonas Trampedach and Viola Heyn-Johnsen.
The Cabinetmakers’ Autumn Exhibition is on show at Museum Ordrupgaard in Charlottenlund from 23 October to 13 December 2026. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events around the world.

items.title: "More than an absence of colour": 4 artists reveal the keys to working in black and white
paragraphs: With a whole spectrum of colours only a few clicks away, perhaps it’s not surprising that working in black and white is sometimes overlooked.

But whether you’re working monochromatically to draft an illustration or using it for a finished piece, a black and white approach is full of benefits. It can even make you stand out in an art world that's saturated with vibrant talent (if you need the tools for your own art, see our guides to the best drawing tablets and the best pens for artists).

Foregoing colour can be an intentional creative choice rather than the result of a limitation, but for illustrator Sarah Koudelka-Mason it was born out of convenience. “After trying out all sorts of tools, I found pencils to be the simplest, least fussy medium,” she says. “All you need is a pencil and paper, which you can bring anywhere. Perhaps because pencils were also my first and most consistent tool in my art journey, I feel the most comfortable with them.”
For character artist and illustrator Joe Vriens, a black and white approach was the result of a fear of colour theory mixed with a dash of impatience.

“I’d always get excited to see the bare line work of a comic, too; it seemed much more achievable,” he reveals. “I could grab a pen and paper and make a comic without expensive markers, paints or digital tools.
“I’m also old enough to remember King Kong in black and white. I made my parents rent that thing probably once a month. In retrospect, maybe King Kong informed my approach all along?”

Illustrator Isabella Mazzanti points out that working in black and white plays into a long tradition of art styles, including her own influences which range from Gustave Doré’s engravings to contemporary manga.
“They seemed accessible and reproducible to me,” she says. “These early experiences were fundamental, because they shaped my aesthetic sensibility and my approach to drawing.”
Seeing as working in black in white is a deliberate approach, it also depends on specific considerations.

“You have to make sure the shading values are balanced well,” Sarah advises. “It’s easy for your shading to look flat or ’muddy’ if your tones are too similar, so you really have to figure out your darks, mediums and lights, and then tie them together with the between shading. I personally like to work lighter and work my way to the crisp dark lines at the end. So satisfying.”

“Line weight and shape design are also key,” says concept artist Alexander Joseba, who has worked for Epic Games, HBO, Ubisoft and more. “A strong silhouette can communicate a character or object very quickly, and different line weights can help separate forms and create depth. Since you cannot use colour to separate materials or planes, you need to do it through values, textures, edges and rhythm.”

“For me, black and white forces you to be more disciplined, although I also like to play with a more wild and instinctive approach. If the image works in black and white, it usually means that the composition, lighting and structure are solid.”
Alexander grew up looking at the work of great artists such as John Buscema, Mike Mignola, Alberto Breccia and many others.

“I was fascinated by the way they were able to communicate so much with ink: how they separated planes, created depth, controlled light and shadow, and made the whole image work so clearly, each one with their own very distinct style,” he explains
Some extra considerations are required when working in black and white, however. Alexander believes the most important consideration is readability.

“Without colour, you have to rely much more on values, contrast, shapes, silhouettes and composition to guide the viewer’s eye. Everything needs to be clear from the beginning: what the focal point is, what belongs to the foreground, middle ground and background, and where the main light is coming from.

“Working in black and white forces you to focus on the foundation of the image. You need to solve composition, lighting, values, silhouette, volume and overall readability properly. I think any artist who works well in black and white will also improve their colour work, because they understand values, light and structure better. Colour does not replace that foundation; it complements it.”
Isabella also warns against assuming that working in black and white is a simpler approach.

“A solid grasp of the visual language is essential in order to use it effectively,” she argues. “Black and white is not simply the absence of colour; when working with chiaroscuro, one chooses to tell a story based on duality, contrast and the exaggeration of ambiguity. I believe it is vitally important for an artist to understand this element, which has the power to intensify the viewer’s emotional engagement.”

When it comes to making black and white art work professionally, Isabella stresses that economic forces may be influencing publishers just as much as aesthetic considerations. “It lends images a classic, refined and timeless quality,” she says.

“Even when telling a certain type of story – for example, Gothic literature – black and white seems to be the most natural choice. It can be a risky choice, because one is foregoing the emotional appeal of colour, but when used in the right way and in the right context, it’s a winning decision.”

Sarah claims that black and white art is underrated, and that it’s not the usual approach commissioners are looking for. “But at the same time, if there are clients specifically looking for works of that nature and you’ve established yourself in that niche, you will find them. This applies to any unique niche of art, and I personally enjoy the challenge of going against the grain!”

For Alexander, black and white artwork is useful for both commercial production pipelines and for final illustration styles. “It depends on the project: sometimes it is a practical development tool, and sometimes it becomes the final artistic language,” he says.

Even if artists don’t gear their black and white artwork towards clients, focusing on it can still improve their overall craft. “Balancing tones in a final image is super-important, so if you can master greys then moving on to colour will feel easier,” says Joe.

“You can guide the viewer’s eye with tones alone, so it can help your compositions greatly. Focusing on greys or even black and white can take a lot of the pressure off as well, which allows you to really dig into lighting and form.”
Meanwhile Sarah is a firm believer that practising black and white art is one of the best ways to strengthen your understanding of the fundamentals.

“Without the distraction or support of vibrant colours, you are encouraged to look at your work in a simpler and more intentional way,” she says. “You start to see shape language, values, lighting, contrast, composition and depth a lot clearer.

Isabella agrees: “The absence of colour changes the way an image is perceived,” she says. “Rather than depriving the image of something, a black and white approach reveals its essential and most intimate nature; it speaks to the viewer in a more universal, almost archetypal language.”

items.title: RuPaul's Drag Race UK crowns winner as BBC axes the series
paragraphs: Queens Alik, Flesh, Naya Thorn and Mocha made it to the final episode
Warning: This article includes spoilers for the finale of RuPaul's Drag Race UK.
After 10 weeks of toe-to-toe lip-syncs, fierce runways and shady remarks, the time has come for one queen to be named the UK's next Drag Race superstar.
For the final time on the BBC, 12 contestants were whittled down to just one after the broadcaster announced it was axing RuPaul's Drag Race UK due to budget cuts.
On Thursday night, RuPaul crowned Flesh as the series eight winner.
The London queen snatched the title from Mocha, Naya Thorn and Alik who also made it to the final episode.
Flesh was awarded the £25,000 cash prize after impressing the judges in the final maxi challenge, which saw the last four queens perform a megamix of previous girl group anthems from past series.
The 26-year-old was crowned by last year's winner, Bones, who is also her best friend and drag sister, with the duo performing together as Heavenly Bodies.
"To be here with Bones is just the perfect moment, this is everything I have ever dreamed of and more," Flesh said as she won.
Flesh was crowned by last year's winner, and her drag sister, Bones
Flesh has stood out across the series as a fashion queen, bringing looks to the runway that RuPaul said would go down in the franchise's history.

Speaking to RuPaul and judge Michelle Visage during the final episode, Flesh said the series "tells people it's not only OK to be them but it's a gift and a dream, and to be crowned the UK's next drag race superstar would be mine coming true".
She made it through the series without ever being in the bottom two and only had to lip-sync for the first time in the final when the top three queens battled it out for the win.
After Alik was eliminated, Flesh, Mocha and Naya Thorn performed a rendition of David Bowie's Modern Love.
Posting on Instagram after missing out on the crown, Mocha said she was "so proud" of herself.
"Not everything can go your way and whilst I wanted to believe it was mine I respect the decision made."
Final three Flesh, Mocha and Naya Thorn lipsynced to David Bowie's Modern Love after Alik was eliminated
The decision to shelve the programme was announced shortly after the latest series began airing, with the BBC saying it was facing "very difficult choices" amid "significant financial pressures".
The franchise will continue but will instead only be broadcast on Wow Presents Plus, a streaming platform owned by the production company behind the show.

While some fans have welcomed the prospect of a new chapter for the series which might include bigger cash prizes, like in other spin-offs, others fear leaving the BBC will mean less representation for LGBTQ+ culture.
It wasn't only the UK's next Drag Race superstar recognised by RuPaul during the finale episode - the Miss Congeniality title is typically awarded to the friendliest and kindest queen.
This year that title was awarded to Paris Baby, who created more than her fair share of drama across the series, in particular her spats with Staffordshire queen KY Kelly.
Miss Congeniality is decided by a secret cast vote and the queens were visibly shocked when RuPaul said Paris had won by a landslide.
At the start of the series, Paris said she had been blocked on social media by some of her competitors, including Flesh, but said they were now "besties".
"Hopefully the world can now see there's a lot more to Paris Baby," she said.

items.title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
paragraphs: Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.
He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."
With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.
Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".
Musk responded to the user, external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise, external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date, external" in April.
But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.
It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.

items.title: Low pressure in US midwest brings unseasonable heat to New York and Boston
paragraphs: Despite the rapid descent into autumn in the northern hemisphere, parts of eastern North America have experienced an exceptionally late taste of summer in recent days. Temperatures approached 23C (73F) in New York and Boston, about 7-10C above what is expected in early November. The unseasonable warmth spilled into parts of eastern Canada, with temperatures exceeding 20C, about 10-15C above normal for the time of year. The balmy conditions were caused by an area of low pressure in the US midwest, dragging up exceptionally warm air from the Gulf of Mexico along its eastern flank. This area of low pressure will gradually drift eastwards, allowing temperatures to fall closer to the average.

Further south, severe thunderstorms have resulted in numerous flood warnings and evacuation warnings being issued this week across many states, with disruptive weather affecting polling stations in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado. The powerful thunderstorms even resulted in a tornado touching down in Keyes, Oklahoma, forcing the relocation of a polling station. The tornado caused extensive damage, although no causalities have been reported. Officials across many states have requested federal funding assistance after the extreme weather resulted in widespread damage to homes and infrastructure.

Across the Atlantic, a number of authorities in the Mediterranean regions of southern France, Corsica and Sardinia issued severe flood warnings this week, as an area of low pressure caused thunderstorms and torrential rain. As much as 50-100mm (2-4in) of rain is expected over the coming days with more localised totals in excess of 100mm possible in the southern French regions of Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur and Occitanie, as well as Corsica. Where torrential rain is most prolonged, up to 70-80mm of rain could fall within a 24-hour period. More rain is expected next week as low pressure continues to dominate the region.

items.title: Library by Collective Architecture breathes new life into Scottish high street
paragraphs: The conversion of a dilapidated high-street building into a public library in Paisley, Scotland, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.
The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to Paisley Central Library, designed by Scottish studio Collective Architecture to serve as a welcoming community space with reading areas, event spaces and a study room.
According to studio director Ewan Imrie, Paisley Central Library was conceived as a civic space for “people to dwell”.
“The client was very clear from the outset that the building had to be as welcoming to all different types of people from all aspects of society,” Imrie said.
“Encouraging people to dwell was the most important thing and if they pick up a book and read it then that’s a bonus.”
Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS said this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “important conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Paisley Central Library is the Edinburgh Futures Institute by Bennetts Associates and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.
Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.
The film and photography is courtesy of Jim Stephenson.

items.title: Global stocks plunge amid AI slowdown fears after Democrats’ midterm triumph
paragraphs: European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry.

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets on Friday morning. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market is poised for its worst day since March.
The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down 207 points, or 1.9%, at 10,575 points in mid-morning trading.
Germany’s Dax index fell by 1.9% in morning trading, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 1.5% and Spain’s Ibex lost 1.1%.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe.

“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”
On Thursday the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.

Chip stocks led the slump, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by 61% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 8%.

“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets. “[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come.

“Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”
However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year.
The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 4.6% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 6.9% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”.

He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.”
Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper set for its biggest weekly fall since March.
Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week.
Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.
