items.title: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI
paragraphs: The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.

MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.

“Critical minerals are the alpha of the new economy,” said the committee’s chair, Liam Byrne. “We cannot rearm Britain, build AI or deliver net zero unless we secure the minerals these technologies depend on.
“Yet 16 years after China first weaponised its chokehold over rare earths, Britain remains dangerously exposed.”
It is the second time in a week that the government’s policy on China has been criticised by Byrne’s committee.

China has a stranglehold on the world’s supply of rare earths and other critical minerals, as well as their refined byproducts that are used in everything from military jets to car-locking systems and consumer products such as fridges and washing machines.

The committee heard that “the processing stage” was where the bottlenecks were, with China dominating the refining of seven categories of minerals, including refined lithium needed for electric vehicles and rare earths used in the fuselage and wings of military aircraft to help withstand temperature extremes.
MPs were told that demand for lithium alone would increase 45-fold between now and 2030, leaving the UK in a high-risk dependency relationship with China.
The demand for rare earths needed for permanent magnets used in military jets and other applications would rise 16-fold in the same period as Britain was seeking to rebuild its military capabilities.

But with China capable of suddenly turning off rare earth supplies, as it did in 2025, a dependency on Beijing was a strategic vulnerability for the UK economy and national security, the committee found.
Separate restrictions on legacy chips after a row over a Dutch intervention in the China-owned Nexperia left the European car industry “days away” from stoppages last October.

The EU, the US and other countries faced the same risk of supplies of rare earths being cut off by China, and the committee said the UK was not putting enough effort into finding alternative supplies.

Donald Trump secured a one-year reprieve on global export restrictions on rare earths from Xi Jinping in October last year. This was extended to January 2027 after the Chinese president’s recent visit to Washington.
However, the reprieve means the UK is at the mercy of US-China relations, the report suggests.
The most “realistic” solution was for the UK to work closely with G7 partners, the rest of Europe and Indo-Pacific countries, to “aggregate demand” and bring in new suppliers.
The committee said its investigation was frustrated by lack of transparency by the government.
“Parliament has no visibility of the capabilities the government is seeking to protect, the vulnerabilities it has identified, or the projects it is backing to reduce risk,” it said.

The committee has drawn up a 10-point plan that includes: working to identify domestic mining; refining and recycling opportunities and their costs; a strategy to encourage business to reduce procurement from China; a plan to unlock investment; and assess planning and permitting processes that may prove a barrier to mining.
As it stood, the committee said it could not be confident the government could satisfy any of its 10 tests.
“The UK requires new institutional and financial muscle,” it concluded.
A government spokesperson denied it did not have a critical minerals strategy saying it was delivering £400m “to ramp up domestic production and recycling” and forge new international partnerships.

“Our strategy also sets clear goals for 2035, including meeting 10% of demand through domestic production and 20% through recycling, with no more than 60% of any critical minerals coming from any single country,” they added.

items.title: Elon Musk’s nearly half a billion dollars in midterms spending was a flop
paragraphs: Elon Musk set a record for election spending this year after pouring nearly half a billion dollars into backing Republicans in the US midterm elections. It turned out to be a poor investment.

The SpaceX and Tesla CEO contributed at least $446m to Republican-aligned Super Pacs and groups over the course of the elections, specifically targeting several key Senate races in an effort to help the Trump administration retain Republican control of Congress. He outdid his own 2024 spending of nearly $290m. Yet as Democrats swept to power across the country on Tuesday night, it became clear that Musk would get nearly nothing in return for his hundreds of millions in spending.

Democrats won every one of the five Senate races where Musk’s America Pac spent the most money backing Republican candidates. In Texas, where Musk’s empire is based and where he directed most of his political efforts, Republicans lost the Senate race, governor’s office and are expected to relinquish control of the state house.

After months of Musk posting attacks on Democrats and amplifying election conspiracy theories on X, the tech mogul was unusually quiet on election night. He jokingly posted “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” but the top Republican mega-donor was otherwise largely silent on the results.

Musk’s losses from midterms go beyond the enormous sums that he dumped into failed campaigns, however, potentially ending an era of lax regulation and cozy relations with state officials that has benefited his companies. The world’s richest person will soon face a House, Senate and Texas government filled with Democrats that have vowed to take a tougher stance on tech and specifically scrutinize his operations in particular.

Altogether, Musk’s political spending this midterms flowed into at least eight Republican-aligned Super Pacs that targeted races across the country, with the largest donation of at least $216m going into his own America Pac. He also gave $168m to the Senate Leadership Fund, which backed a series of candidates that included the Texas Republican Ken Paxton.

Out of all of Musk’s political activity in midterms, the contest where he put the most money and focus was the Senate race in Texas between Paxton and Democrat James Talarico. America Pac spent at least $28m on anti-Talarico ad buys and messaging alone, while Musk repeatedly posted attacks on X, his social media platform, such as “Talarico wants to trans your kids and destroy the border.”
After Talarico achieved a commanding win on Tuesday night, the Democratic senator-elect referenced Musk in his victory speech.
“We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas,” Talarico said. “We just sent a message to every billionaire mega-donor, every trillionaire mega-donor.”

Senate races in Michigan, Maine, Ohio and Iowa similarly went for Democratic candidates after America Pac spent tens of millions supporting Republican campaigns. The Pac’s money had gone into attack ads that focused on transgender rights or accused Democrats of being radical socialists.

Even if Musk’s spending was not successful, it doesn’t mean it wasn’t impactful. Musk and the Super Pacs’ expenditures created several of the most expensive races in US history and set a potential precedent for how much spending will take place in the 2028 presidential election. It will also probably spur months of analysis around the limits of what money can buy in politics.

Musk’s businesses have benefited greatly from lucrative contracts with the Trump administration, as well as Trump’s hands-off approach to regulating artificial intelligence. In Texas, the state legislature and Governor Greg Abbott have provided him a friendly environment to do business while passing laws backed by the billionaire’s lobbyists.

Gina Hinojosa, the incoming Democratic governor in Texas, will probably take a more critical stance towards Musk and his businesses. Hinojosa has called for a datacenter moratorium and has been in a legal battle in recent months to gain access to unredacted emails between Abbott’s office and Musk. Meanwhile, House Democrats have called for launching investigations into Musk’s conduct while he was leader of the so-called “department of government efficiency” last year and vowed to scrutinize federal funding for his companies.

items.title: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
paragraphs: Fishermen return to sea under a crimson sky in August after China's Jiangsu province is hit by Super Typhoon Dolphin
ByJoel GuintoBBC NewsReporting fromSingaporeKurumi MoriTokyo correspondent and Darren BettLead weather presenter
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.

A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.

In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.

Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.

It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.

In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.
This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm Narra
August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.

The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.

The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.

Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El Niño predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.
China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El Niño.
Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.
China has seen back-to-back typhoons as the 2026 El Niño intensifies

In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.

To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.

They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.

In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.
Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.
Tide of rubbish blankets Philippines river in August after weeks of monsoon rains

Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season, and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.
The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.
But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El Niño is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.

"How severely a community experiences an El Niño is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.
"Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

items.title: UN warns of worsening humanitarian situation in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.
One-third of the population in Afghanistan faces crisis or worse levels of food insecurity, according to a U.N. update released Wednesday.

“Food insecurity and acute malnutrition continued to worsen in Afghanistan, with 15.9 million people facing crisis or worse levels of food insecurity (IPC Phase 3), including 3.4 million in Emergency (IPC Phase 4), while child wasting reached its highest recorded levels of the August-October period,” the United Nations Children’s Fund or UNICEF report said.

The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification is put together by representatives of national and local governments, U.N. agencies and non-governmental organizations to measure the severity of food insecurity and acute malnutrition in a country.

The IPC ranges from Phase 1, minimal or none, to Phase 5, famine. IPC 3 indicates crisis or serious food shortages, where households cannot meet their minimum food needs and either suffer from food shortages or adopt coping strategies that harm their ability to access food in the future.

The U.N. report said the humanitarian situation in Afghanistan remains critical, driven by worsening food insecurity and malnutrition, outbreaks of diseases, the return of millions of Afghans from neighboring countries and recurring climate disasters.
“Funding shortfalls and pressure on essential services further compounded humanitarian needs, particularly among children, women, returnees and disaster-affected communities,” the UNICEF report said.
According to the United Nations, Afghanistan will remain one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises in 2026, with nearly 22 percent of the population needing humanitarian assistance.
In October, UNICEF warned that more than four million Afghan children, the highest number recorded in the past five years, could need treatment for acute malnutrition in 2027.
The U.N. agency said that acute malnutrition is worsening across the country and is expected to rise further next year.
It added that nearly 1.1 million Afghan children will suffer from severe acute malnutrition in 2027 and about 3 million others will experience moderate acute malnutrition.
Some 1.3 million pregnant and breastfeeding women are also projected to suffer from malnutrition, UNICEF said.

It warns the number of Afghan provinces facing critical levels of malnutrition has increased from seven in 2025 to 10 in 2026 and is projected to reach 14 provinces in 2027, affecting more than one-third of the country.
UNICEF noted that some of the most severe levels of malnutrition continue to be recorded in southern Afghanistan, and that humanitarian needs are outpacing available services.
U.N. agencies warn that without urgent financial support; the country’s malnutrition crisis is likely to worsen.
Furthermore, the return of millions of Afghan refugees from Pakistan and Iran has put pressure on the available resources in the country.
The United Nations Development Program in Afghanistan said last month in a post on X that the large-scale return of Afghans has added “pressure on jobs, essential services and infrastructure.”
The U.N. said that nearly 1.3 million Afghans have returned, including those deported, from Pakistan and Iran, the two countries hosting most Afghan refugees, to Afghanistan so far in 2026.

items.title: Elon Musk will face scrutiny from Democrats in Washington and Texas after midterms
paragraphs: Elon Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, political action committees and outside groups, according to federal election filings but most of the candidates he backed on Tuesday lost. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images hide caption

Elon Musk wasn't on Tuesday's ballot, but he stands to lose a lot from Democrats' sweeping midterm victories in the House and Senate. In no state was this more acutely felt than in Texas, home to the headquarters of Musk's companies and where he spent more than $200 million, according to federal filings, in a mission to sway the Senate race in the Republican candidate's favor.

With a Democratic majority in Congress, the billionaire, who controls Tesla and SpaceX, will likely face investigations into the billions of dollars of government contracts his companies have been awarded since President Trump returned to office and his role leading the Department of Government Efficiency at the beginning of Trump's second term.

Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, political action committees and outside groups, according to federal election filings analyzed by OpenSecrets, a nonprofit that tracks campaign spending. That makes him the top donor in the midterms and among the very largest political donors in American history.

The central question Democratic lawmakers say they want answered is whether Musk used his influence inside the Trump administration to benefit his own businesses, and whether taxpayer money, government data and public institutions were put at risk in the process.

During the four months Musk led DOGE, he received at least $6.3 billion in government contracts. Since then, he has gained at least another $10 billion in government contracts, according to the Democracy Defenders Fund, a legal advocacy nonprofit.

"The DOGE chickens are coming home to roost. Elon Musk waved a chainsaw on stage and laughed while firing public servants and gutting the services Americans rely on. Then he lied to the American people about the savings. He must answer for it under oath," Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) wrote on X.

Musk's foreign dealings are also under scrutiny. Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware posted on X that Musk's links to Russia's President Vladimir Putin are "One more thing to add to the list of questions for Musk when I subpoena him."

U.S. Rep. Mike Levin of California highlighted that Musk restricted Ukraine's use of his Starlink satellite internet service days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia and began buying Russian diesel in October. Starlink and its military-grade counterpart, Starshield, are vital for Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, frontline communications and drone operations in its war against Russia.

"How on earth did we get to this point? How is it possible that Musk can disrupt an American ally's military operations whenever he chooses, maintain a clear line to the Kremlin, and face zero accountability to the American people or the U.S. government?" Levin wrote on X.
Musk did not respond to a request for comment from NPR.

While leading DOGE, Musk was a part-time special government employee, and as such was subject to a federal law prohibiting covered executive branch and related personnel from participating in official matters affecting their personal financial interests, said Richard Painter, former chief White House ethics lawyer in the George W. Bush administration.

"SpaceX is a big contractor and gets a lot of money from NASA and the Department of Defense. If [Musk] touched anything that he knew would have an impact on SpaceX, he would've committed a crime," Painter said.

Texas in particular has become a big focus of Musk's efforts to exert political power, as he has made the state the nerve center of his sprawling business empire. Tesla's corporate headquarters and a major vehicle manufacturing facility are in Austin. X, formerly Twitter, is based outside of Austin. SpaceX, which makes rockets and satellites, is based in southern Texas. Musk's Neuralink and The Boring Company are also headquartered in the state.
Much of Musk's estimated wealth is tied up in his ownership stakes in his companies. Even as markets rose Wednesday after Democrats' midterm wins, SpaceX shares fell nearly 4% and Tesla dropped 3%.

SpaceX is reportedly exploring several possible Texas sites for large data centers. Tesla owns and operates its massive Giga Texas data center in Austin. In August, plans for a $16.8 billion SpaceXAI semiconductor fabrication project in Texas were announced.

Musk directed at least $225 million of his midterm spending to Texas, according to OpenSecrets, including supporting Republican Ken Paxton's bid for U.S. Senate and Gov. Greg Abbott's reelection campaign.
But Paxton and Abbott both lost, suggesting Musk's money wasn't enough to overcome a wave of enthusiasm that saw Democrats capture every statewide office in Texas.

"Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas," said James Talarico, who defeated Paxton in the Senate race, at a campaign rally in Lubbock last month.
Elon Musk's own posts on X about Talarico were often personal and incendiary. "Talarico will vote to trans your kids," he wrote on Nov. 1.
Talarico addressed Musk in his victory speech on Tuesday.

"We just sent a message to every billionaire mega-donor, every trillionaire mega-donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system in this state, in this country. Power belongs to the people," Talarico said. "The real fight in this country is not right versus left; it is top versus bottom."
As results came in on Tuesday night, Musk wrote on X, "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," followed by a shrug emoji.

items.title: Ontario house by Brian O'Brian takes cues from farm buildings
paragraphs: Canadian architect Brian O’Brian has completed a rural weekend house in Ontario that features a slanted, corrugated-metal facade and an angled roof covered with greenery.
The Hemlock House sits on a 72-acre (29-hectare) property in the southern town of Markdale.
The project grew in scope over time. Originally, the plan was to renovate an old farmhouse, but the client ultimately decided to create an entirely new house.
“What started as a modest renovation evolved into a full replacement of the small, 1930s farmhouse,” said Brian O’Brian, a Toronto-based architect.
The commission came about after the client saw another project by O’Brian in the area – a 19th-century schoolhouse with stone walls that had been converted into a cottage.
For the Hemlock House, O’Brian took cues from the region’s agrarian buildings to conceive the design.
Set on a flat site surrounded by woods and farmland, the house is composed of a long bar and adjoining box, and totals 3,250 square feet (302 square metres).
A long entry driveway “traces the lineage of the site”, passing by an old farmhouse and century-old barn.
The new house draws upon these earlier buildings and “extends the language of agricultural buildings into a contemporary domestic form”, the architect said.
The home’s bar-shaped volume is topped with a sloped, metal-clad roof, while the attached box has an angular green roof.
The north side of the house is lined with a slanted wall made of corrugated metal.
Cut into the wall are three windows, which can be covered by external, perforated steel panels that slide up and down. This elevation also features a boxy protrusion with wood cladding.
“This is meant to feel like an agrarian building at first view, but one that begins softening and opening on approach,” said the architect.
The southern elevation – which overlooks patios and a swimming pool – features hemlock siding and ample glazing. Various roof overhangs help shield the building from sun and snow.
The house also has a carport, which is sheltered by a canopy made of wood and metal.
Within the home, there is a division between public and private spaces.
The linear volume, which spans two levels, contains a principal suite, a secondary suite, and two bedrooms with a shared bathroom. The adjoining box holds a kitchen, dining area and living room.
Rooms feature neutral colours and a mix of earthy and industrial materials.
“Concrete and hemlock define every surface, carrying a steady material logic through the house,” the architect said.

Other projects in Ontario include a 1970s chalet that was renovated and expanded by UUfie to conform to its steep site, and a black cabin by Barbora Vokac Taylor that includes wedge-shaped clerestory windows.

items.title: Lapalma presents a cross-section of its catalogue on Dezeen Showroom
paragraphs: From colour palettes and modular seating to outdoor furniture and tables, Italian brand Lapalma has listed a selection of its most recent products on our Showroom section.
The brand collaborated with architect and designer Raffaella Mangiarotti on a new palette of colourways that can be applied across its offering of products.
Nine new shades join seven rethought existing colours in what the brand describes as a “chromatic alphabet”, which can be mixed or matched across seating, tables and accessories.
When designing the collection, Mangiarotti considered each colour’s capacity to work seamlessly whether applied to metal, wood or plastic.
The brand’s Kipu Club outdoor chair presents a new iteration of Anderssen & Voll‘s original design and can withstand life outdoors.
A curvilinear backrest partially wraps a pebble-shaped seat, creating a comfortable and friendly seat for al fresco lounging.
A family of tables have been developed for the brand by designer Mario Ferrarini, who created and named the collection after the conical profile of Mount Kilimanjaro.
Aptly named Kili, the tables are designed to be sculptural as well as functional, coming in various sizes and tabletop shapes, with each element carefully aesthetically considered.

Snaking lengths of seating are created in this new modular system designed for the brand by Francesco Rota, who wanted to make “welcoming islands for meeting, working, waiting or simply taking a pause”.
The HUB modular system is reconfigurable, allowing users to reorder the modules to create evolving landscapes in open-plan spaces.
Designer Francesco Rota collaborated with Lapalma to extend the Plus modular outdoor seating system, which now comprises additional sun loungers and facilitates all-new combination options.
Round-cornered, lozenge-shaped modules available in various bright and neutral-coloured upholstery make up the range, which creates opportunity for open-air lounging and socialising.
Lapalma is an Italian furniture company with a forty-year history of designing and manufacturing tables, seating and other furnishings for both indoor and outdoor use.
It frequently collaborates with eminent designers, both fellow Italians and those from further afield, to develop cutting-edge furniture solutions for contemporary interiors.

items.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK
paragraphs: A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.

“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”

The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters.

A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.
The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

The current outbreak, declared on 15 May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases, and 5,000 deaths. It is the 17th in DR Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus, and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history. The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way.

Since the outbreak started, it has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last month Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She, along with a close contact, were evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.

In an interview with the Guardian last month, Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said the “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak meant it could reach the UK and other countries.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented.”

Other patients who have been medically evacuated for specialised care since the start of the outbreak include two sent to Germany and one to the Netherlands. Another case was reported in France in July.
British health authorities say the risk ⁠to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the NHS has procedures in place to manage suspected and confirmed infections.
There have only been four confirmed cases recorded in Britain since 1976, ‌according to the UK Health Security Agency.

items.title: Inaugural Walker Design Triennial features flesh-like speakers and post-apocalyptic scenes
paragraphs: A set of speakers with flesh-like exteriors was among the conceptual design work shown at the first Walker Design Triennial in Minneapolis, USA, which curator Joseph Grima said reflected on the meaning of design in a world fixated on optimisation.
Filling a series of galleries at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, Minnesota, the exhibition was called Beyond Materialism and featured numerous examples of conceptual design.

The pieces ranged from the historical works such as Italian radical designer Alessandro Mendini’s 1970s Lassù – paired with depictions of the performance of the chair on fire – to an international set of design studios representing the field today.

Grima, who has served as a curator and educator for several high-profile institutions including Design Academy Eindhoven and international exhibition series Alcova, said the show was meant to challenge mainstream conceptions of design.
“We live in an age that is conditioned to think that anything and everything can be designed, and often what is that everything can be optimised,” said Grima.
“And it’s precisely this association between design and optimisation that this exhibition intends to question.”

With objects of various scales on display, the Walker Design Triennial featured a room with large-scale conceptual installations. Many of the participants were international, with a cohort of contemporary US designers, including Germane Barnes and Theaster Gates.
Terracotta plinths were included as part of the exhibition design, supporting many of the small and large objects.
Some of the pieces were commissioned directly for the event, mainly in the large-scale section.

Among these was Spanish designer Lucas Muñoz Muñoz’s All Ears, a set of latex-covered speakers that were programmed to play sounds recorded in the months before in Minneapolis. A sleek soundboard allowed users to play the tracks, with multiple tracks routed through the amorphous, fleshy speakers all at once to cacophonic effect.
Muñoz told Dezeen that the installation was designed to be a “microphone” for the city itself and “make visible the act of listening”.
The broadcast from the soundboard was also projected out of the gallery as a radio sequence.

Also commissioned for the event was a work by Vessel, featuring two massive rolls of fabric spooled over a kiosk. The fabric was based on Vessel cofounder Navine G Dossos’s paintings of her and her partner James Bridle’s self-built home.

Also in the large-scale room was a series of post-apocalyptic appliances made from found objects by Brussels-based Espace Aygo, derived from the studio’s 2022 transformation of a derelict apartment building into a home and art space.
The themes of fleshy objects, post-apocalypticism, and reuse continued into the rooms with smaller objects.

Here, London-based studio Superflux showcased objects from its Relics of Abundance series, showing objects created by a future civilisation that may someday use our objects today in a time of scarcity, including a chair made from straw and rebar.

Austro-Canadian designer Christoph Wimmer Ruelland created a series of furniture pieces with found objects that are extraordinarily colour-matched, while Korean designer Jonghoo Jeong utilised jerrycans to create a fountain, a reference to his past practice of dumping the objects in his process.
Athens-based studio Astronauts showcased inflated metal works informed by the autobody shops, creating love seats, chairs and even a seesaw that are iridescent while still familiar.

Italian-German designer Maximilian Marchesani created a structural piece made of smartphone glass that refracts metal-coated leaves as well as a chandelier that combined LEDs with branches. South Korean studio Wknd Lab created a series of stools made from discarded shells.

Dozens of other designers took part in the installation, including Moon Seop Seo, Studio Ker, Objects of Common Interest, Stef Fusani, Kevin Quale and Kostas Lambridis, representing a who’s who of avant-garde design, refracted through the lens of Grima and the event’s artistic director, Asli Altay.
It was an “opportunity to stop, take stock for a moment, and reflect on what design is today,” said Grima.
Other recent design showcases include a show of wood furniture by Armadillo and furniture made from fragments of New York buildings by Rafael Prieto.
Beyond Materialism is on show at the Walker Art Center from 17 October 2026 to 14 February 2027. Find out more about design and architecture exhibitions, talks and fairs at Dezeen Events Guide.

items.title: This super-comfy higher-end budget ergonomic office chair has $70 off for Black Friday
paragraphs: We've reviewed a lot of office chairs over the years, and there's a brand we often come back to at the budget end of the spectrum. Sihoo is known for its fantastic-value M18, the cheapest ergonomic office chair we recommend, but it also makes some higher-end offerings. The Doro C300 Pro is the one that's most impressed us, and it's now reduced by $70 from $509 to $439 on the Sihoo website.
That's a lot cheaper than most of the best office chairs for back pain, and the Doro C300 Pro has a wide seat, breathable mesh, lumbar support, lots of adjustability and fantastic armrests.
We recognise that the C300 Pro is not the most beautiful office chair, and, like all Sihoo chairs, it takes some patience with assembly. But once you've got it set up, it is very comfortable.

The highlight is the lumbar support, which is one of the more comfy that we've tested, helping to support the back's natural 's' shape without making you feel like it wants to break you into submission.

Most of the chair's adjustability is as you'd expect from a higher-mid range ergonomic chair, but the armrests stand out. They go up/down, forward/back, and tilt and, most impressively, move laterally in and out from your chest. This is no minor detail: it provides more options for how you sit and allows you to freely move your arms as you want.
Not in the US? See the best budget office chair deals in your region below. Once you've made your choice, make sure you know how to sit properly in a chair.
Subscribe to the Creative Bloq newsletter for details of expert-curated offers, bringing the tools you need to create – and products perfect for the design-obsessed.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time reviews are in, and critics agree on one thing
paragraphs: Early reviews of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time are out, and most reviewers are certain this one has avoided the pitfalls of some remakes – no weird visual redesigns here. Our review will come a little later, but for now, let's look at what some are saying about how Nintendo's 1998 Nintendo 64 adventure, often held up as one of the greatest games ever made, has made it to the Switch 2.

The response has been pretty spectacular. The remake is sitting at 96 on Metacritic, with a hefty collection of perfect scores and very few critics finding much to complain about. That's quite an achievement for a game whose original version already has such a place in gaming history.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launches on 5 November, and Nintendo has done rather more than give Link a fresh coat of paint. Hyrule has been rebuilt with a striking new visual style (while staying tonally true), the soundtrack has been re-orchestrated, and the original's occasionally clunky controls have been updated. Now it offers free jumping, a modern camera, and fully voiced cutscenes, alongside redesigned dungeons and expanded character interactions.

It's a substantial overhaul, even if the adventure itself remains reassuringly familiar to those who grew up on this classic Nintendo game. If you're a fan, take our Ultimate Zelda quiz and test your knowledge.

GamesRadar+ awards the remake five stars, calling it "a remake for the ages". Reviewer Anna Koselke is particularly taken with how Nintendo has brought Hyrule to life without losing the original's charm, praising its "stunning visuals" and newly voiced dialogue.

TechRadar is equally impressed, awarding five stars and describing the remake as "a thoroughly well-thought-out retelling of one of the most loved video games of all time". Reviewer Josephine Watson highlights the redesigned locations, enemies and puzzles, as well as the refreshed soundtrack. There is a little caution, though, with TechRadar suggesting the remake could have been more ambitious and that some of the original's difficulty has been lost along the way.

Game Informer awards the remake 9.25/10, describing it as "a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one." Reviewer Kyle Hilliard likes the visual overhaul and improved camera but feels Nintendo has played it relatively safe with the changes. It looks new, he argues, without necessarily feeling like an entirely new adventure.

Shacknews is considerably more enthusiastic, awarding a perfect 10/10 and calling the remake "a tour de force that redefines what remakes can be". Its review highlights how Nintendo has made familiar mechanics feel fresh, from the reworked combat to the redesigned dungeons. It also singles out Navi, who has been given a much bigger role as a companion rather than simply popping up to shout "Hey! Listen!"

Destructoid also hands out a 10/10, calling it "one of the best examples of how to properly reimagine an enduring masterpiece". The review praises the improved visuals, 60fps performance, and updated controls, though it agrees the remake can feel a little too easy in places.

The Guardian's Keza MacDonald is similarly impressed, scoring the game five stars and describing the remake as "a dream come true". Her review makes an interesting observation about the new art direction, comparing Hyrule to detailed theatre scenery and Link to a handmade doll, with his equipment looking like exaggerated props. It's a more stylised approach than simply chasing photorealism, and one that suits the fairytale quality of the original.

Reviewers are highlighting the lack of Master Quest is a notable omission for returning players wanting a tougher adventure, while the more generous clues and quality-of-life improvements have softened some of the original's challenge.

GamesRadar+ also flags the absence of Master Quest and the single-save-file restriction as drawbacks. Game Informer, meanwhile, feels the remake could have been a little more adventurous in how it reinterprets the original.
These aren't deal-breakers, but they're worth considering if you've spent years exploring Hyrule and know the N64 version inside out.

For anyone who grew up with the original Nintendo 64, this remake is clearly wrapped in an enormous amount of nostalgia. But Ocarina of Time is more than a fond memory for those of us who played it back in 1998. It helped establish the language of 3D adventure games, from lock-on combat to sprawling interconnected dungeons, and its influence still runs through modern game design.

Nintendo has had to do a lot of work to bring the adventure up to date, but it hasn't had to fix what made it special in the first place. The world design, the sense of discovery, and that slightly odd fairy-tale atmosphere are all still there, only now with the visual detail and fluidity the original hardware could never manage.
And Nintendo is very good at this too, with the recent Star Fox remake also proving popular on Switch 2, and the many Metroid and Mario updates and remasters proving a reason to buy Nintendo Online.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches on Nintendo Switch 2 on 5 November.

items.title: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
paragraphs: French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.
"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.
Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.

Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.
Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.
But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.
While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.
Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.
Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.
In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.
By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.
According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.
"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.
The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.

But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.

"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.
Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.
It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.
Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.
"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.
A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.

In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.
But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too.

"Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.
According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.
Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing.
"To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC.

"Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."
Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.
Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.
None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.
But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.
Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats.

items.title: ‘I put a smoke bomb in a road cone and stuck it on my head’: Delton Barrett’s best photograph
paragraphs: I grew up on New Providence in the Bahamas, and still live on the south side of the island. After leaving school, I worked with my dad in construction, and that’s where I started taking photos. For the first couple of years, I used my flip phone, playing with images of nature and flowers on the sites we were working on, but in 2010 I bought my first DSLR (digital single-lens reflex) camera and started teaching myself about photography.

I started doing a lot of landscapes. I tended to shoot at sunrise or sunset, and became interested in taking photos of people in vacant spaces. Because I didn’t have a model, I used a tripod and a timer to include myself in these very fantasy-looking naturescapes.

This shot came about on a day when I woke up feeling I needed to try out something new. I took three or four different outfits to the western part of the island along with a few props, one of which was this cone. I often keep random items I find, sometimes incorporating them into images.

The road I was on leads to a dead end, so cars don’t drive along it much. It was a pretty safe space – I almost felt like I was in my own back yard. I’d been playing with ideas, and putting the cone on my head was the last one I tried that day. I just liked the way it looked but, as you can imagine, it was quite suffocating.

Then I remembered I had a smoke bomb in the car and it just happened to fit into the tip of the cone. Looking back, it’s a wonder I survived. I’d tried many shots and was getting tired. But it occurred to me that this shot really did look like someone losing their mind, going ballistic. The way I’m gripping the cone makes it unclear whether I’m trying to throw it off or hold it on. Perhaps I’m trapped inside, perhaps I’m in there intentionally because there’s something I don’t want to see.

Either way, there’s some kind of struggle happening. Maybe the smoke is giving a signal, calling people nearby for help, like: “Hey, something’s up here!” I call the image Stop the Madness. We pass people every day who give off signs that they are struggling, or not in their right mind. Maybe we walk past, maybe we help.

The island inspires me a lot. It’s the only backdrop I’ve ever really known. In 2024, I went to Madrid, which is highly developed compared with the Bahamas. When I came back to Nassau after, I thought: “Wow, we have so much more colour, so much more green.” I hadn’t really understood that until then. As an artist and photographer, what stimulates me are my surroundings. The beaches are a five-minute drive away – my images tend to have seas or a sunset or some type of bush involved. I use the elements around me to express my ideas.

Some of my images are manipulated to fit the concept or tell the story I want. If I need a seagull to be in a precise spot, for example, I won’t spend all day waiting for that to happen. One of my favourites shows me standing on top of the sea opposite another version of me in a different costume – and our fingers are almost touching, like in Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam. It’s an image I’d thought about for a long time, so when everything came together it was like a mother who’d waited nine months to have her baby. But often a scene is perfect as it is – all I need to do is frame it and adjust the lighting and maybe the contrast. That’s all that was needed for Stop the Madness.

Born: Manchester, Jamaica, 1991 High point: My first solo show in 2018 at D’Aguilar Art Foundation in Nassau. The Bahamas has been a lasting high point. It set the sail for me to continue to create great images that can inspire others in a way I’d also want to be inspired Top tip: Create what makes you feel. Sit with your ideas and think about them until you’ve found the right way to execute them. We can become so excited in photographing the idea that we miss out the small details that make the image worth taking in the moment. In a nutshell I would say: “Take the pressure off shooting and focus more on what you want to shoot and how you want it to feel”

items.title: Canva's mass layoffs are a warning sign for creative tech
paragraphs: Artists and creatives are familiar with the fear of AI. Illustrators and graphic designers have watched in dismay as increasing numbers of businesses decide that AI slop is good enough for their branding and marketing needs. And many put the blame on companies like Canva and Adobe, who have been aggressively rolling out AI tools in their software.

Canva's just revealed another side of the story: the tech companies driving the change aren't immune to its impact. The Australian design software giant has announced the biggest restructuring in its 12 years of history, with plans to eliminate or relocate more than 1,200 jobs. That's almost a quarter of its global workforce, and it will include staff who helped to build the platform.

Canva aims to “collapse layers” in its organisation and bring “more teams together in person”. It's handling the layoffs in the classiest way possible, promising six months of salary and 12 months of healthcare to those affected, alongside career support, a fund for those who want to start their own business – and it's letting people keep their MacBooks.

But the layoffs highlight an inescapable contradiction. Even those responsible for the ubiquity of AI image generation are suffering from its expansion. Rather than a push for growth and innovation, Adobe and Canva's rollout of AI tools feels more their own desperate fight for survival, and it's a fight they might not be able to win.

"Success in our first chapter doesn’t guarantee success in the next," Canva CEO Melanie Perkins writes in an update to staff. "This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade."

There's been talk of an “SaaS-pocalypse” as AI becomes advanced enough to make specialised software redundant. We've already seen the release of an open-source vibe-coded Adobe alternative, and it works to an extent. Generating your own software is only going to get easier, as is asking an AI bot to generate design assets directly.

Despite its heavy investment in AI, Adobe's stock price has fallen by around 25% in the past year and over 60% in the past five years. It's not clear that even AI leaders like OpenAI and Anthropic, the makers of ChatGPT and Claude, can become profitable as Chinese rivals emerge delivering similar technology at a cheaper price.

Some creatives opposed to AI might feel a twinge of satisfaction at seeing a prominent proponent floundering. But Canva has also been a positive force, even if you don't use it's AI tools. As well as its premium platform, it has one of the best free Adobe alternatives in its free Affinity app, providing much-needed competition.

Creatives using the app might have cause to worry about how long it will be offered as a loss leader. Canva's shown a strong commitment to it so far, recently adding new raw editing tools and an iPad app. But its recent decision to pull the previously free Remove.bg into its paid suite shows that the structure and availability of creative software is constantly in flux as developers try to work out how to respond to competition from AI.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: World of Warcraft: Forever is bringing Azeroth back to life, "as it lives in our heads", without losing what made it special
paragraphs: When we return to a game after years away, we tend to remember it as bigger and more vivid than it ever looked on screen. The forests, the mountains, and the little settlements along the way to somewhere more exciting all grow a little in memory. Blizzard Entertainment is building World of Warcraft: Forever around that effect.

WoW: Forever, the new version of the iconic MMORPG, released today, takes players back to the original Azeroth, with reworked environments, lighting and atmosphere. It won’t get a full visual overhaul or take on the look of the recent expansions. Blizzard wants it to feel like coming home to a place that’s more alive. That's a tricky task, given that World of Warcraft is one of the defining video game art styles many look to and love.

“We believe WoW Classic’s art style is timeless,” says Matt Heyman, lead environment artist at Blizzard Entertainment. “Which is why our focus was not on changing the game art but on small ways we could push specifically things like the environmental effects. Such as the way rivers now flow in Elwynn Forest, or the way the fog rolls in the Duskwood at night. Or the way the moonlight breaks through the leaves in the Ashenvale. It’s the same original Azeroth that players fell in love with all those years ago, with just a few small but powerful effects and updates to make it more immersive than ever.”

World of Warcraft: Forever is designed as a permanent home alongside modern and Classic WoW. It returns players to the original continents and the level 1-60 journey while adding new stories and experiences, and Blizzard says it will keep expanding this version of Azeroth over time.

For this unique release, the team needed to build something new without disturbing the memories players already hold. The work covers around 40 existing zones, new locations such as Zephras Isle, home of the new Skyborne race, and changes to familiar places including Dalaran.

“We asked ourselves, ‘What does it mean to evolve a timeless world?’” says Heyman. “We wanted to take that original ‘Vanilla’ version of Azeroth and combine it with the version that lives in our heads. Where our experiences, nostalgia and imagination all shape the ways we remember it.”
Each zone has its own colour palette, mood and atmosphere. “We often talk about the world as the main character of World of Warcraft, but I like to imagine it as a cast of characters,” he says.

Duskwood shows the problem well. Players remember a gloomy forest full of spiders, wolves, undead and skeletons, with the Night Watch patrolling Darkshire by torchlight. “However, while it’s an awesome and iconic zone, it’s probably not as dark and creepy as people remember,” says Heyman.
For WoW: Forever, the team is leaning into the remembered version, with moonlight cutting through the branches around Darkshire and fog drifting through the graveyards.

New tools can tempt artists to change things just because they can, so Blizzard has set a guiding rule. “Changing a world that players have cherished for such a long time has risks. We approach it carefully and responsibly,” Heyman explains. “We developed a central artistic principle that everything must be authentic. That’s both authentic to our world but, most importantly, authentic to the memories we have of Azeroth when the journey began in WoW.”

He points to Durotar, the arid, vibrant homeland of the Orcs. A cool blue atmosphere would look natural and realistic there, he says, but it wouldn’t be authentic. “The correct approach is to go in with purpose and to lean in and push the fantasy that the region already has.”

Most of the changes sit in the rendering technology, according to lead software engineer Jason Scott, who describes work on fog, lighting and water. Fog has been part of WoW’s look since the beginning, creating depth and gloomy vistas. Blizzard has replaced the original distant fog with volumetric technology, which gives artists much more control.

“We can control fog like we never have before,” says Scott. “Now we can increase the sense of creepiness in Dustwallow Marsh, and we can see the effect of wind in a zone. The texture of dust as it sweeps across plains.” It also extends sightlines across the map, which adds to the sense of scale.

Lighting has changed too. Until now, the sun and moons didn’t cast light into the world, a gap that would have been obvious once volumetric fog went in. Light now shines through the fog in a process called scattering, with the size and shape of the rays set by whatever blocks it, whether trees, mountains or other terrain.
“Now in WoW: Forever, when the sun comes up at dawn, there are streams of light that now cascade down the mountains, and we created similar rays for the moons as well,” says Scott.

To make that work, the team had to be sure the world properly blocked light and that the sun and moons lined up with the illumination on the ground. “There are still creative and artistic choices that we make, but it altogether makes the world feel much more alive,” he adds.

Rivers used to move simply, without resembling a river. For Forever, Scott says, the team studied how water moves, how wind and waves affect its surface, and how light interacts with its colour, transparency, and reflections. Rivers now follow their course, bend around rocks and produce foam where they hit them. Artists have full control over the effects, so different kinds of water can be tuned to look the way the team wants.

The models and textures remain the foundation of Warcraft’s look, even though the style has shifted with each expansion. Heyman says Forever is deliberately holding on to the character of the original assets.

“There’s an edge and grittiness to the way those assets look, and it just feels like Warcraft,” he says. “It’s a little bit of old, and a little bit of new. It’s maintaining that timeless iconic look matched with new rendering updates that breathe life into the world.”
World of Warcraft: Forever is available from today on Mac and PC (Pacific Time).

items.title: Elon Musk's millions fail to deliver Texas for the Republicans in fierce midterms
paragraphs: Talarico's victory marked a key turning point in the midterms, helping solidify the Democrats' control of the US Congress in a wave of wins across the US.
Musk has increasingly made Texas the hub of his companies, from Tesla's Austin headquarters to SpaceX's Starbase launch site.

As well as backing Paxton through outside groups, the X owner took to his own platform to spread conspiracy theories about the Democrat, posting: "There is something deeply wrong with Talarico" after he briefly disappeared from the campaign trail in October.
"There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator," Talarico posted in response.

On top of contributing to one of the most expensive Senate races ever, the SpaceX owner also became the top individual donor in this year's midterms overall, contributing an estimated $446m in backing Republican candidates.
Musk's money went through Super Pacs, groups which can raise unlimited sums but can't give directly to candidates or coordinate with their campaigns.
Individuals, parties and traditional groups face legal limits on direct donations.
Super Pacs get around this by spending independently, such as on ads backing a candidate.
Musk became one of the Republican Party's biggest donors in 2024, pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Donald Trump's winning presidential campaign.
A similarly eye-watering amount was not enough to do the same for Paxton this time around.

items.title: OEB Architects channels 1980s interiors for London extension
paragraphs: Glossy ceramic tiles, a glass-block wall and a leafy garden were intended to evoke tropical modernism and 1980s interiors for London Tropical, an extension to a Victorian terrace designed by local practice OEB Architects.
OEB Architects was tasked with creating an open-plan kitchen and dining space at the rear of the three-storey terrace in Southwark that would feel “surrounded” by its garden.
“The project considers how an extension to a typical Victorian outrigger can connect to its modest urban garden,” Gabriel George, project architect at the studio, told Dezeen.

“It explores the layering and overlaying of translucent and reflective materials and bold, graphic objects to give a nuanced and varied space through all seasons, contributing to a feeling of living surrounded by the garden,” he added.

Instead of filling the width of the site, OEB Architects pulled the extension back from the southern boundary, allowing it to be lined with both a glass-block wall and full-height windows that address a courtyard and side return.

This openness continues around to an end wall with full-height sliding glass doors, not only framing the garden but allowing the space to be entirely opened up to a patio surrounded by leafy planting.
“The clients were keen not to have a conventional top-lit infill extension, with a roof light sloping down to the boundary, as is common among extensions to Victorian terraces,” George told Dezeen.
“This expansion is set back from the boundary, providing both a passage and a new outlook from inside,” he continued.

“This results in two new external spaces, a courtyard addressing the main house and the rear garden serving the extension. Each is wrapped in full-height glazing with a range of transparencies responding to each view.”

The extension’s interior is defined by a kitchen island clad in glossy green tiles and a column clad in shiny red tiles, acting as spatial anchors that contrast the otherwise minimalist, white-painted surfaces, stone floors and pale timber carpentry and ceilings.

Both the glossy tiles and translucent glass-block wall were used to create a changing quality of light throughout the day, with the south-facing courtyard able to be screened off via translucent curtains that further add to this effect.

“The material and spatial ideas were driven by conversations with the clients discussing architectural precedents along with art, graphic and design references, including mid-century West Coast American case study houses, 80s interiors and tropical modernism,” George said.
The extension’s floor level steps upwards to meet the back of the main home, where the connecting corridor has been flanked by a bathroom and pantry space.

OEB Architects was founded in 2018 by directors Tessa Baird and David Eland, and has offices in London and Brighton. The studio previously completed another extension for a home in Tottenham, which expanded a semi-detached home with a simple blockwork and timber structure.
