items.title: Review: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is superb, streamlined and safe
paragraphs: Link, the Hero of Time, grown-up and newly awoken from a magical seven-year slumber. Nintendo hide caption

With its tale of an idyllic world despoiled by the lust for power, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time feels as relevant today as it did in 1998. Nintendo's new remake, out Thursday on the Switch 2, enshrines its place in the gaming canon for generations to come. But despite its stupendous production values and painstaking details, the game left me feeling oddly bereft.

Perhaps I should have expected as much. Ocarina of Time weaponizes nostalgia even within its narrative, as the protagonist Link ventures to save his post-apocalyptic world as an adult after first working through it as a kid. You'll uncover old characters enduring new catastrophes. You'll try to rescue everyone you meet. You'll strive to bring things back to how they were before — no, better than they were before.

Seven years stretch between Link's childhood and adult adventures. 28 years yawn between the remake and the original's release. Both in and out of the game, Ocarina of Time makes us yearn for an idealized past.

Decent remakes evoke how you remember a game rather than re-create dated controls and chunky graphics. In myriad small ways, Nintendo has brought Ocarina of Time up to contemporary standards while (mostly) preserving its soul.
In one of the game's most poignant scenes, kid Link answers to the call to adventure, leaving his friend Saria and the Kokiri Forest they called home. Nintendo hide caption

I miss the thoughtfully-composed camera angles from the original, but quickly got used to the over-the-shoulder camera the remake employs (though I was irked that it abandoned the top-down view when you sneak into Hyrule Castle). The new jump and sprint buttons made navigating the world feel more natural. Combat's smoother too, though it's still not easy to switch between targeted enemies (unlike modern third-person games like Elden Ring, where you can toggle between foes by simply flicking the right stick).

You can, thankfully, swap between items in a quick menu — the same system introduced to the series in 2023's Tears of the Kingdom and continued in 2024's Echoes of Wisdom. It's still not as fast as I'd wish (I'd have preferred a customizable wheel), but I vastly prefer it to constantly pausing to access my equipment. It made it easy to change my strategy on the fly. I'd often cast Naryu's Love and deploy Bombchus, for example, where before I'd mostly stick to the Longshot and Bow.
The villain Ganondorf, on the precipice of his initial triumph over Princess Zelda, Link, and the whole of Hyrule. Nintendo hide caption

If you get stuck, a new "Threads of Time" quest log can point you in the right direction (though you'll likely still need to look up a guide for the convoluted Biggoron Sword quest!). And yes, the notoriously frustrating Water Temple is much more tolerable this time around. But mind your rupees! Inflation's hit Hyrule. While wallets can now carry double the cash that they used to, Great Fairy upgrades are no longer free. They can cost up to 500 rupees!

It's the remake's aesthetic changes that stand out most. The game's astonishingly ornate textures can jar with its cartoony proportions. Ninety-eight percent of the time the translation is a clear upgrade, but other times it leads straight into the uncanny valley (Nabooru looks bizarrely yassified with huge red lips and golden eye-shadow, for example).
Gerudo thief Nabooru, flanked by the malicious witches Kotake and Koume. Nintendo hide caption

The animations are much more extensive — so much so that the new cutscenes, particularly in the game's opening hours, can drag down the pacing. The game also fleshes out unspoken implications and flattens rough edges. Mido, the jerk who blocks your progress in Kokiri Forest, has been subtly rewritten from bully to overbearing but well-intentioned boss. Kaepora Gaebora, the talking owl who guides your path, won't repeat himself at the slightest provocation. Navi, your fairy companion, no longer chimes in with an incessant "Hey! Listen!"

Such changes risk eroding the game's character. Still, it ultimately stands as one of the most faithful adaptations I've seen — less than the Demon's Souls remake but far more than the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy or even the Resident Evil 4 remake. It gives me hope that Ocarina of Time's surreal sequel, Majora's Mask, could receive such treatment in the future.
Sheik, Link's ally in the fight against Ganondorf, demonstrates one of the many songs you'll play by pressing buttons or humming directly into the Switch 2's microphone. Nintendo hide caption

Yet this remake will never eclipse my memories of the first Ocarina of Time. Of course it couldn't — that game helped launch a new 3D era and defined the childhoods of a whole generation. Where once it innovated, now it represents the safest of safe bets.

But by lavishing such attention on an all-time classic — ahead of a Zelda movie next year — Nintendo has ensured it won't go out of style for at least another few decades. I look forward to sharing it with my nephews and, eventually, my own toddling son. As much as I detest how media giants can't seem to move past the hits of yesteryear, some harmonies are worth turning back time for.
Editor's note: This story initially and inadvertently published 24 hours before its embargo lifted. Nov. 4, 2026

items.title: Celebrity hairstylist John Frieda dies aged 75
paragraphs: British celebrity hairstylist and beauty brand entrepreneur John Frieda has died aged 75.

Frieda became a firm favourite with celebrities throughout the 1960s and 1970s, and is known to have cut hair for clients including British model Twiggy, US First Lady Jackie Kennedy and Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger.
He was also known for the range of hair products bearing his name, and the iconic Purdey bowl cut which he created for The New Avengers actor Joanna Lumley in 1976.
His death was announced by his hair salon in an Instagram post on Tuesday., external
"It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our dear John passed away peacefully ….surrounded by his family", the statement said
"John was more than a mentor to us; he was a true icon of the hair industry. He was the person who taught us everything, believed in us, and made us better.
"Rest in peace, John. You will be forever in our hearts."
Throughout his career, Frieda worked with other famous clients including Diana, Princess of Wales, Madonna, Nicole Kidman and Scarlett Johansson.
Born Alan Howard Frieda in London in 1951, his father was a hairdresser who owned a salon in Ealing, west London, while his grandfather had also been a Fleet Street barber.
After having gone into the family business, Frieda later joined Leonard Lewis's star-studded salon House of Leonard - famous for having created Twiggy's famous crop - becoming his assistant.
He went on to work for fashion magazine's British Vogue and Harper's Bazaar.
In 1976, Frieda opened his own salon in central London which became massively successful and booked up months in advance as his reputation as an influential stylist grew.
He subsequently opened branches across the world, including in Barbados, Ibiza and Los Angeles.
In the 1990s, Frieda stepped back from cutting hair and concentrated on developing his own brand of hair products, including Frizz-Ease hair serum which he created in 1988.
His business empire grew rapidly over the following decade as it expanded into the US and across the world.
In 2002, he and his business partner Gail Federici sold the company to a Japanese conglomerate Kao for $450m (£334m).
Speaking to the British Beauty Council, external in June, Frieda gave his advice for future generation of British hairdressers.
"If you have a client in front of you, rather than thinking about the money or what you're getting from cutting their hair, just think about the action," he said.
"The reward is giving her the best haircut she's ever had. That is your reward."
Model and TV personality Jo Wood, the ex-wife of Rolling Stones guitarist Ronnie Wood, described the news of his death as "so sad".
"When I was 16 and John worked as an assistant at Leonard's he would do my hair," she recalled. "He was so great..."
Cetera Lamb, creative director at Frieda's London salon said the industry had lost "a true legend, a real maverick in hairdressing".
"For 50 years, he led our wonderful salon, leaving behind an incredible legacy of passion, creativity, vision and outstanding hairdressing.

"We will continue in his honour, celebrating his achievements and keeping his memory, values, vision and love for great hairdressing alive. His legacy will live on through us, and we will make sure of that."

items.title: SOM unveils design for luxury waterfront development on Australian pier
paragraphs: International architecture studio SOM is set to transform a historic pier in Geelong, Victoria, into a waterfront destination culminating in a rounded high-rise.

SOM recently won the competition to design the 10,000-square-metre development for developers Gurner Group and Costa Property Group, which will add public space, apartments, a 200-room hotel, shops and restaurants over the water at Corio Bay.

The project will involve transforming and extending the existing Cunningham Pier, which was originally built in 1855 to give railway access to docking ships. It underwent major refurbishment in 1929, and now acts as a stretch of car parking spaces culminating in a restaurant and event space.
Envisioned as a pedestrianised waterfront destination, visitors will enter SOM’s revamped pier through a public square with water features.
A 34-storey building will rise at the end of the pier, which will surpass the 21-storey Miramar apartment tower to become Geelong’s tallest building.
Trefoil in plan, the tower’s form will resemble three combined cylinders that taper towards the top and bottom.
Lining the length of Cunningham Pier will be a series of buildings with rounded edges and layered terraces, designed by SOM to reference the movement of water and marine forms.
The luxury development will contain around 280 apartments and 12 waterfront villas with individual yacht berths.
Activity spaces and sports courts will be built on floating platforms.
SOM hopes the development will establish Cunningham Pier as “both a neighbourhood on the water and a destination for Geelong’s residents and visitors”.

“An elevated public promenade forms the organising spine of the proposal,” said SOM. “By positioning new construction alongside the historic pier, the design preserves the existing structure below while creating a pedestrian environment above.”
“Shops, restaurants, and places to gather would line the route, connecting the city to activities and views across Corio Bay.”
According to SOM, the redevelopment will involve creating new marine habitats at the pier to support biodiversity.
“This ecological ambition forms part of a broader approach that considers the waterfront as a place for both public life and marine life,” said the studio.
Other projects recently unveiled by SOM include a tiered skyscraper that rises on a waterfront site in Chicago, and plans to build a 20-storey data centre in Kansas City.

items.title: Delhi air quality worsens ahead of Diwali as firework restrictions enter force
paragraphs: Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality to India's capital.

The city's air quality index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.
Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.
Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.

GRAP is a set of emergency measures that become progressively stricter as pollution levels rise. The latest restrictions include more intensive road cleaning, higher parking charges to discourage private vehicle use and increased public transport services. Delhi Metro has introduced 20 additional weekday train trips, while authorities have been directed to stagger government office timings to ease traffic congestion.
Officials said the measures were introduced after forecasts suggested air quality would remain very poor over the coming days.
Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.
The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.

The annual pollution crisis is driven by a combination of factors, including vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, falling temperatures, low wind speeds and the burning of crop stubble in neighbouring states.
The sharp rise in pollution follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years.
Experts have attributed the sudden deterioration to falling temperatures, slow winds and an increase in crop-residue burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab and Haryana.
A recent storm had brought rain and stronger winds, helping clear the air. But as the weather settled, northwesterly winds returned, carrying smoke from burning fields towards the capital.
India's pollution watchdog classifies AQI readings between 301 and 400 as "very poor", while anything above 400 is considered "severe". On Wednesday morning, Delhi's AQI stood at 377.
The index takes into account eight major pollutants, including PM2.5 - tiny particles about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair that can penetrate deep into the lungs.
With Diwali just days away, there are concerns that fireworks could push pollution levels even higher.
Last year, Delhi woke up to a toxic haze the morning after the festival, despite a court directive to use less-polluting firecrackers.
Authorities have imposed restrictions on firecrackers over the years, including outright bans on their manufacture, sale and use, but enforcing them has proved difficult.
On Monday, India's Supreme Court allowed the manufacture, sale and use of certified green firecrackers in Delhi and neighbouring areas for a limited period.
It said the crackers could be set off only between 06:00 and 07:00 local time (00:30-01:30 GMT) and between 20:00 and 22:00 (14:30-16:30 GMT) on 7 and 8 November, during the Diwali weekend.
The court also banned fireworks within 300m of hospitals, care homes, schools and other designated silence zones.

Green firecrackers use modified chemical formulations designed to produce fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. They must carry QR codes that allow buyers and authorities to verify details of their manufacturer and certification.
But ensuring that only approved firecrackers are sold remains a major challenge.
In its latest order, the Supreme Court acknowledged that conventional firecrackers had continued to be sold as green alternatives, even when a complete ban was in place.
It has directed police to patrol designated sales areas, carry out random QR-code checks and seize illegal firecrackers.
During particularly severe pollution episodes, Delhi authorities have also introduced measures such as hybrid schooling, work-from-home arrangements and restrictions on certain vehicles.

The problem is not confined to the capital. Mumbai, India's financial hub, has also recorded elevated pollution levels over the past month, despite benefiting from coastal winds that typically help disperse pollutants.

On 24 October, Mumbai's AQI had reached 322, placing it in the "very poor" category. The spike was attributed to a combination of low wind speeds, construction dust, garbage burning, firecracker emissions and pollutants carried from neighbouring regions.
The city's air quality has improved in recent days - and it recorded an AQI of 89, classified as "satisfactory", on Wednesday. Neighbouring Navi Mumbai recorded a "moderate" AQI of 118.
The improvement follows nearly two weeks of smoggy conditions, with residents sharing photos and videos of the haze on social media.

items.title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
paragraphs: The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.

The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls show it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.
Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.
Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery.

Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week, has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.

Johannesburg, Ekurhuleni and Tshwane are in Gauteng, South Africa’s most populous and densely populated province and its economic engine. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance is leading the polls in all three metros but has not been polling above 40%.

The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media, mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs with a combination of the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters and the populist Patriotic Alliance and ActionSA across the province’s three metros.

In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to controversial past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town, which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.

The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.

In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma is polling above 40%. The 84-year-old Zuma, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.
The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.

South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.

items.title: Why Kim Kardashian came back to 'the worst TV drama ever'
paragraphs: "We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is they can see what the response is and write accordingly to that."

All's Fair, which was created by American Horror Story and Glee showrunner Ryan Murphy, became the Hulu network's most-watched scripted series debut of the last three years and was immediately renewed.
Following a group of divorce lawyers - played by Kardashian, Close, Paulson, Naomi Watts and Niecy Nash-Betts - the show was panned for bad acting, with Kardashian baring the brunt of criticism.
The Hollywood Reporter called her "wooden", and the Times declared that the show "may be the worst TV drama ever".

But the hallmark of Kardashian's career has been her ability to back herself - whether that's going from years of being snubbed by Met Gala organisers to becoming its most anticipated guest, or overcoming backlash to the launch of her shapewear company to turn it into a $5bn (£3.7bn) brand.
Kardashian says: "What is the alternative, right? What is the other choice that you have when you're getting criticised?
"Do you just fall in and feel that, or keep your head down and try better, try harder and try a different path?"
Having been in the spotlight for more than 20 years, she's "always had a really good sense of my mental health", and says that comes from being able to "brush off" those who seek to bring her down.
"I always do things that are tough because I genuinely want to learn," Kardashian says.

While she was promoting the legal drama last year, Kardashian was waiting to find out if she had passed exams to become a lawyer in real life, after six years of studying for an apprenticeship that negated the need for a university degree.
Shortly after the first series aired, she found out she had failed the exam - but says that won't be the end of her pursuit of the qualification.
"If I don't pass something, if I don't do the best at something, then I'll get there," she says. "I don't worry. I just have to keep going."
But after her admission that she had used AI for legal advice, external, she does say she will change how public she is about her studies.

"I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there," says Kardashian, who has four children with rapper Kanye West and is now in a relationship with British Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton.
"I know there was a lot of talk out there like, 'she's given up', and that's funny to me.
"I like people to think what they want to think and I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," she says.
Audiences have only been given a glimpse of what to expect from the second series of All's Fair so far.

Co-star Watts, who also serves as a producer on the show alongside Kardashian, says they have "doubled down" on "the high fashion, high drama and heightened reality" that audiences enjoyed the first time around.
As for Kardashian's acting, Watts says she's on a "trajectory" that sees her "stepping up in the second season".
"She was improvising, riffing, doing all kind of things that I thought were deeply impressive," Watts adds, to which Kardashian jokes: "I think I'm just naturally so funny."

One of the positives that critics did cite was the show's desire to spotlight the duality of professional women who were both feminine and successful, which Kardashian says she "loves" because it is "a really realistic depiction of a lot of women I know".
"It doesn't mean that just because you're super smart that you can't be fashionable and into glamorous things as well," she adds.

items.title: Graduates are managing AI - but are they learning much else?
paragraphs: Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.
Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing.

She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation.
A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media.
Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others.
"A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood.
AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts, but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's.

Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement.

Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI.
"My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel.
Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company.
CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI.

"We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell.
"We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way."

Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role."

If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier.
Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires.

For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, external, it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building.
Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%.
There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers.
But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?
Underwood says she'd like to still pick up the traditional PR skills her role isn't currently focused on, but is confident of her future in the agency's growing AI team.
"There's certain things that I haven't had the chance to do yet, like directly pitching to the media. I absolutely plan to do this," she says.

Graduates becoming too AI-centric is an issue for Simon Pratt, chief operating officer at Portman Finance Group. He says being able to use AI effectively is important, but the company's two-year graduate programme is fully centred on "learning the trade".
"Our graduates rotate across four areas at six-month intervals, working directly alongside senior relationship managers to learn their trade," Northampton-based Pratt explains.

"They'll learn all of our financial products, how to draft credit papers for submission to lenders, and how to build meaningful relationships with our customers. They'll progress to running transactions from start to finish."
Claire Reed, PwC UK's chief technology and innovation officer, believes graduate roles that are too AI heavy won't necessarily provide graduates long-term career progression.
"There will be no graduate job now that doesn't require a baseline of AI literacy," says Glasgow-based Reed.
"But AI skills on their own are not going to help you in your career. You've got to couple that with that sector knowledge of what that client actually wants."
Back in Coventry, Dillan Patel is confident his AI work will continue to be valuable, and he wants to keep building on it.

"I don't think I'd want to explore different positions within the business. Through my involvement in AI-related projects, I already work closely with different areas of the business and I'm gaining valuable knowledge and experience along the way," he says.

items.title: Constantinople to Istanbul review – you won’t want to leave this lavish celebration of double imperial splendour
paragraphs: Two empires compete to bewitch you in this exhibition that offers a double bubble of beauty. It collides the Byzantine empire, whose capital Constantinople was officially inaugurated on 11 May AD330, with the Ottoman Turks who conquered this great city in 1453 and turned it into Istanbul. The combined glories of two lost worlds – the Ottoman empire was dissolved in 1922 – beget an utterly enrapturing blockbuster. I lost all track of time in this dream city of gold and ivory.

Even the human form is magically transfigured here into mineral and metal. The martyred abbess St Eudokia becomes a Byzantine icon of marble inlaid with coloured glass, wearing a crown of precious stones and an exquisite dress patterned with diamonds and decorated with pearls and emeralds. It is a masterpiece of abstract splendour that looks like a Klimt painting, but this icon can’t have influenced him because it wasn’t excavated until 1929.

Beat that for splendour – but the Ottoman empire could. A 16th-century kaftan, probably worn by Sultan Selim II, irradiates you with light-giving yellow and geometric white designs, part flower, part solar disc: it is made of zerbaft, a fabric said to be “woven from gold”, and looks it.

Staggering. But it’s not all precious metals. There are blue and white glazed tiles from a hamam that conjure images of steaming bathhouse comfort, along with a bath wrap of red silk. Wooden foot supports from a women’s hamam are inlaid with mother of pearl. As a wall text points out, if you have a nice bathroom you are living under the influence of Ottoman Istanbul.

The story all begins with Constantine, the emperor who accepted Christianity. He created New Rome, or Constantinople, at a strategic point between Europe and Asia to deal with the unmanageably vast Roman empire. You can see here sublime relics of this eastern capital including a mosaic from Constantine’s palace of a huge moustached face of weird godlike mystery.

That luxury was seen in public places too. Constantine brought the Roman policy of “bread and circuses” here and adorned the chariot racing hub, the Hippodrome, with artistic masterpieces pillaged from ancient Greece and Egypt. Here you can see the bronze head of a snake that was part of the celebrated Serpent Column and a less scary goose. Ivory reliefs portray consuls at the Hippodrome, holding a mappa, the piece of cloth they let fall to start the games. These men are ancient Romans, with names such as Flavius Taurus Clementinus but by their time, the sixth century AD, the Roman empire in western Europe and north Africa was finished.

Yet it lived on in the east. Byzantine schoolchildren studied Homer and monasteries preserved Plato’s writings. Facing the final Turkish attack in 1453, the last Byzantine emperor urged his people to throw their javelins and spears to let the enemy know they were fighting “the descendants of the Greeks and Romans”. However, the Ottomans had cannon.

By the end, the Byzantine empire was reduced almost entirely to Constantinople with its massive walls and secret weapon, “Greek fire”. The survival of this final fortress of ancient civilisation for so long was such a historical freak that it gets politely passed over in history books as a kind of wondrous but irrelevant exception to the laws of progress: the golden, mystical Byzantium where nothing changed or was invented. This exhibition takes you to the unreal city WB Yeats evokes in his poem Sailing to Byzantium.

Then you cross a gap between galleries that feels like a rupture in time, and find yourself looking at Gentile Bellini’s portrait of Sultan Mehmed II, painted from life in 1480. Mehmed poses in a white turban and fur-lined red robe, and the Venetian artist shows the sensitive profile of this ruler whose Muslim empire terrified European Christians. The Ottomans were culturally curious, as this experiment in importing Renaissance art reveals. Was there in fact an Ottoman Renaissance, to mirror and match the western one?

A wooden chest made to hold a copy of the Qu’ran in the late 16th century may look like yet another luxury but it is also a document of that Istanbul Renaissance, for it takes the shape of a magnificent dome. The conquerors of Constantinople were fascinated by one of its wonders above all others: the church of Hagia Sophia, consecrated in 537 AD, with its colossal, dreamlike cavern of an interior beneath a majestic dome.

The Ottomans made it a mosque but with minimal changes to its fabric. Just as Brunelleschi, Michelangelo and Wren were inspired by antiquity to build domes, Istanbul’s Blue Mosque and Süleymaniye Mosque are inspired by Hagia Sophia. Watercolours by early European visitors show how the mystery of Hagia Sophia became globally known. From 1935 to 2020 it was a museum. Now it is a mosque again by edict of populist president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who described the change as “Hagia Sophia breaking away from its chains of captivity” – a strange way to characterise a building that is 90% ancient Roman and was built as a church.

This is a sumptuous voyage to Byzantium via Istanbul. Linger in the baths, in your tall wooden shoes and silk towel, and enjoy the artifice of eternity. I spent two hours here, but I wanted to do the whole thing again immediately, in reverse.

items.title: Houses of Parliament at risk of ‘Notre Dame-style fire’ as renovation costs rise
paragraphs: The Palace of Westminster will be at risk of a Notre Dame-style fire or a similar catastrophic event if MPs do not tackle the issue of funding refurbishments, a parliamentary committee has said.

Decisions about how and when to begin a full restoration of the building, which is Grade I-listed and a Unesco world heritage site, have been repeatedly delayed amid disagreement over how it should be done and spiralling costs.
The cost of maintaining the estate will soon hit £2m a week, and a recent estimate found the work could cost as much as £40bn and potentially last for six decades.

The cross-party Commons public accounts committee (PAC) said urgent action was needed to avoid the risk of a major fire or similar disaster, and to staunch increasing costs, with every year of inaction adding an estimated £420m to the restoration programme.
There has been a “political allergy” to making decisions, Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the Conservative MP who chairs the PAC, said.
As well as the ever-increasing costs, he said, MPs should also “imagine the blow suffered by the UK’s morale and reputation of some kind of catastrophic failure”.

“Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building’s roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life,” he said.
“These are not notional possibilities, but real and rising risks.”

The Victorian estate has been beset by problems that are barely kept in check by ongoing maintenance, including regular plumbing failures, leaking roofs, crumbling masonry protected by a maze of scaffolding and a persistent risk of fire, mainly from outdated electrics, necessitating 24-hour fire patrols.
This has resulted in a maintenance bill of about £1.5m a week. The PAC report said that without action the figure was expected to reach £2m.

The issue has been seen as a matter for MPs and peers for decide, rather than the government. The PAC stressed that it was not its role to recommend a particular programme, but the report urges action and has made a series of recommendations for making the process work better.

It says that in the next six months the clerks of the Commons and the Lords – who are nominally in charge of the process – should set out a plan to properly engage parliamentarians, something it says has so far been lacking.

Other recommendations include a more robust set of cost estimates and a timetable to help a decision about the main project in 2030, as well as a more urgent approach to finalising temporary accommodation for both chambers while the works take place.

Calling the current governance of the scheme “far too complex”, it says it should be made easier, and a new restoration and renewal select committee formed, allowing MPs to hold senior officials to account.

Four proposals for refurbishment, ranging from a nearly-full exit from the estate during the works to a version in which only the Lords would move, have been narrowed to two, from which MPs must choose.

The first, a “full decant”, would involve staff moving to buildings on the north side of the estate, with the Commons being put in Richmond House, a nearby government building, and the Lords to the QEII conference centre. The project would last up to 24 years and cost about £15.6bn.
A “staged decant” would last anything from 38 to 61 years and involve the Commons moving to the Lords chamber for up to two years. That project would cost about £39.2bn.
The report says there are particular worries about the temporary accommodation in terms of ensuring it is available and the cost.

It states that the estimate to refurbish the QEII centre of £417m, and a bill of about £2bn to set up the northern part of the estate for a decant, feel “very high”, noting that Canada had managed to install a temporary chamber as its parliamentary estate was refurbished for much less.
“We are concerned that the programme is being shaped around the availability of temporary accommodation, rather than temporary accommodation being delivered to meet the programme’s needs,” it said.
A parliament spokesperson said the report “provides welcome scrutiny”.

“The PAC concludes that without action, the Palace of Westminster will, at best, be in a process of managed decline,” they said. “Work is already happening across the parliamentary estate to ensure the ongoing safety of those working here and visiting.”

items.title: Prince William says UK faces terrifying risk of more wildfires due to climate change
paragraphs: There is a "terrifying prospect" of more UK wildfires in future due to climate change and preparation will be "crucial", the Prince of Wales has said.
Visiting Treherbert in Rhondda Cynon Taf, which was threatened by a huge mountain fire in August, Prince William praised a "gargantuan" effort to save homes, land and lives.
"We need to start taking wildfires as seriously as the continent has done," he said, raising issues such as a lack of firefighting aircraft.
He also suggested the community's response to the incident was an example for others to follow, after locals rallied around to support those fighting the flames.
The hillside, just metres away from the community centre where Prince William met fire crews, military personnel and local volunteers is burnt black.
"You looked up [and] the mountain was alight - it was like lava," explained Kath Edwards, managing director of charity Valleys Kids, which runs the building.
"I genuinely thought we were going to lose the centre - but more importantly people were going to lose their homes.
"You never think this is going to come literally to your door and that's what it was - it was just crazy."

items.title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
paragraphs: Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.
Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".

It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.
Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".
In a post on X, external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.
These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts.
Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.
It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images.
The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.

Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.
The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.
Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened.
"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.
The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.
It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.
The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date.
US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.
The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea.
Pyongyang hit back at the claims on Tuesday, denying it was behind the hack.

Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image.
The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.

But on Tuesday, the company wrote in its post on X, external: "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident."

As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident.
It also said that it would seek to stablish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives.

items.title: UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers
paragraphs: Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."
The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.
The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.
Two members saw their fridges begin to defrost, AIMS said, while another saw their cold units rise up to 100C (212F) in temperature.
AIMS spokesman Tony Goodger said the affected devices were empty at the time so no produce was lost - but urged businesses to be vigilant.
The incident "must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets," he said.
On Monday, supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges and freezers being hiked in temperature.
The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.
Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.
Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.
But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date.

"That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments disconnected from the internet.
Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited.
But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries".
"We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said.
"We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected in Monday's cyber incident, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up.
The same method was thought to have been used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
As with that incident, many of the retailers affected on Monday said they had no choice but to throw away spoiled food - some saying this amounted to hundreds of thousands of euro in lost produce.
Mathieu Tilman, who runs a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, told the BBC he found it "truly distressing".
"There's so many people starving, people who don't have enough to eat. How can we end up throwing away so much food?"
"In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
So far, there have been little to no signs of any such impact in the UK.
But the BBC has approached major UK supermarkets for comment and asked what action, if any, they are taking to safeguard against any similar hacks attempts.

"Retailers invest heavily in their cybersecurity and are currently working with the NCSC to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks," said Graham Wynn, assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium.
Asda, Lidl, M&S, Sainsbury's and Tesco are among the retail trade association's members.
Paul Chichester, director of operations at the NCSC, said at the launch of its annual report on Tuesday it was continuing to work with and monitor UK organisations affected.
"At the moment, the impact is minimal," he added.
"We're working with organisations identifying existing vulnerabilities in the UK and trying to get those closed before somebody exploits them."

items.title: Scientists detect signals at the smallest scale ever explored
paragraphs: Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.
Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.
So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.
One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.
The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.
Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.

Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.
"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.
He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.
"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.
Among those early-career researchers is Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper, who is part of the team that made the zeptoverse discovery. She is reconsidering her future in light of the physics cuts.
"I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad because that seems to be where there are more opportunities at the moment," said Richardson-Slipper.
She added that "lots" of her fellow researchers working in fundamental physics had already moved.
The cuts are being made despite an overall record increase in the science budget.
UK research hit by cuts despite record science funding
Prof Brian Cox, TV presenter and particle researcher at the University of Manchester, who is not part of the research team, described the result as "important".
But he condemned the recent decision to cut UK funding for the Cern project.
"It would be extraordinary to walk away from UK scientific leadership at this moment, damaging the future research programme and seriously damaging our hard-won international reputation," Cox said.
The UKRI told BBC News that it remained a fully engaged member of Cern as its second largest funder at around £175m per year.

A UKRI spokesperson said: "We sought independent advice and have taken forward an exciting portfolio of new infrastructure investments, which include projects in clean energy, medical imaging and cultural heritage.
"However, as usual, there were more exciting applications for funding than we were able to support."

items.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
paragraphs: North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations an "absurd rhetoric".

Kim Yo-jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage the country's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack - which has been described as the largest in history.
Pyongyang has also been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks - accusations that it has consistently denied.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.
The incident is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its economy.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.

Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo-jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".
The BBC has contacted Binance for comment. Since the hack, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.
The company said initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
Binance said on Sunday that its customers pulled out more than $3.6bn of assets from its exchange as it reopened after suspending all transactions in the wake of the hack.
The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

items.title: Apple unsure when more foldable iPhones will be available after selling out
paragraphs: The new head of Apple says the company is working to get its new foldable iPhones available to more people after the $1,999 smartphone quickly sold out when it was released just over a week ago.
John Ternus, who in September took over the role as Apple's chief executive from Tim Cook, said on Monday that he was "thrilled" at the early reaction to the iPhone Duo.
While the costly phone, which sells for £1,999 in the UK, immediately sold out, some buyers have seen their screens crack.
The phones are still in high demand and Sabhi Kahn, Apple's new chief operating officer, said the technology giant did not know when more Duos would be available.
"At this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance," Kahn said during a call with financial analysts to discuss Apple's latest financial results.

Apple executives did not mention during the call any issues with the iPhone Duo. But last week, the company said it would replace any phones that were impacted by an issue that caused a "small number" of the new phones to crack along the inside fold.
Nevertheless, Apple said on Monday that over the last year it sold more iPhones globally than it ever has before.
During the three months to 26 September, which did not include sales of the iPhone Duo that went on sale toward the end of October, Apple saw iPhone sales rise 17% to $57bn.

Apple has boasted throughout the year that iPhone sales have been surging, despite the company's warnings that crucial components for the device, along with Mac computers and iPads, were constrained to the point of weighing down sales.
Sales of Mac computers also grew during the quarter by 27%, hitting $10.7bn, another record for Apple.
Overall sales at the company rose by 15% for the year, to $479bn.
However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and Watch fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.
Kahn noted during the call that most Apple devices are still seeing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with "advanced nodes."
Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allows Apple's devices to operate more quickly, most of which Apple has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.

Khan said that such supply constraints are expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.
Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of Apple devices to store data like apps, photos, and text messages.

Much of that memory storage runs through data centres which have seen a huge boom in demand for space as artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots and platforms, including those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, have become popular.
As demand for memory has grown, storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.
Cook had earlier this year referred to the sudden increase in data centre costs that Apple was seeing as a "thousand year flood."
It has led to the company raising prices on essentially all of its hardware products by around 20%.

items.title: Do the Shetland Isles need Cold War-style military protection?
paragraphs: The Shetland Isles previously had many army, naval and RAF personnel stationed across the isles
ByCatherine Lyst and Cameron Angus-MackayBBC Scotland
Calls are being made for the defence of the Shetland Isles to be strengthened after increased sightings of Russian trawlers off the coast of Scotland.

Recent analysis by the Daily Telegraph, external also revealed that there have been more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables linking Britain with Europe and the US.
These cables carry the majority of telecoms data abroad.

The growing importance of undersea infrastructure prompted a parliamentary report, external last year to warn of security vulnerabilities in areas including transport and supply chains, financial services and payment systems.
There are also concerns that the £30m SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland could be a Russian target.
But do the Shetland Isles really need better protection by the military?
A Russian vessel was suspected of damaging an undersea telecoms cable running from Helsinki to Estonia
In recent years there have been a number of incidents in the Baltic Sea where underwater cables have been damaged or completely cut.
In December last year, Finnish police detained a vessel sailing from Russia, which was suspected of damaging an undersea telecoms cable running from Helsinki to Estonia, across the Gulf of Finland.
In 2022, Shetland was cut off from the mainland after a nearby subsea cable was damaged.
And last year there were two cable breaks in Shetland, which disrupted internet services and, in one case, took weeks to repair.

There has been no suggestion that there was any Russian involvement in the Shetland incidents but they demonstrate how fragile the cables are and show the devastating effect on the islanders when they are damaged.
In July, Royal Navy warships and helicopters spent 21 days monitoring Russian activity in UK waters and the North Atlantic - this was a 25% increase on previous time spent monitoring.
The recent Telegraph revelation of more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables has also caused concern.
History teacher and tour guide Jon Sandison said military presence in Shetland reduced in the second half of the 20th Century
Jon Sandison, a high school history teacher and Shetland tour guide, said there were real concerns that Shetland could be attacked after Germany invaded Norway in 1940, during World War Two.
"Shetland could have been a stepping stone towards Orkney and mainland Scotland," he said.
There were many army, naval and RAF personnel stationed across the isles and coastal defences were built to defend Lerwick and the rest of the archipelago.
The SaxaVord Spaceport sits on a former RAF base and RAF Skaw played an important role in efforts to detect enemy aircraft from 1941.
RAF Saxa Vord was later involved in Nato's radar network to monitor Soviet activity during the Cold War.
Scotcast: Is Shetland really in Putin’s sights?
The radar station closed in 2006 but it was revived in 2018 for Arctic surveillance as an automated remote radar head.
Sandison said that while military presence reduced in the second half of the 20th Century, Shetland's geographical position would never change.
"Where we are in the UK is always going to be a pivotal geographical location in relation to the North Sea, the Arctic Circle and wider scope of Britain," he said.
He added that coastal infrastructure was built very quickly during the Second World War.
"Air raid shelters, anti-aircraft defences - it's remarkable how much was built in a short space of time," he added.
"Not much of the infrastructure remains. It's part of our history, and part of our past."
MP Alistair Carmichael has urged the UK government to step up efforts to protect critical infrastructure
First Minister John Swinney has accused the UK government of leaving "Scotland's vast coastline dangerously exposed".
He pointed to waters off Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity.
"I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News.
Liberal Democrat MP Alistair Carmichael, whose constituency covers Shetland, has urged the UK government to step up efforts to protect critical infrastructure.
He told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme: "This is something we do need to be taking seriously.
"We're not expecting an imminent problem here but this is a time where the government is already telling us that we should all be keeping baked beans and a wind-up torch in a cupboard."
Carmichael added that if the world had changed so much, some of the decisions made by the UK government to remove military presence from the northern isles may now need to be looked at again.
He said that over the last 20 years, there had been just one local full-time soldier running a reserved unit in Shetland but they were now managed from the Scottish mainland.
Carmichael said there should be restoration of a full-time presence to support the unit and more reserves should be recruited in the northern isles as numbers were low.

But he added: "If the signal that the government is sending the community is that we don't even think its important enough to send one full-time solider to run these units then you can't expect the community themselves to be particularly enthusiastic about it."
SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport
SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport with several companies interested in using the site to launch small satellites into orbit.
In September, the UK government announced investment of £30m in the project, as part of a new £7.8bn space strategy.
Alistair Carmichael said the spaceport would draw more attention to Shetland as a significant asset.
The German and UK governments plan to use SaxaVord to deepen their co-operation on space.
In October, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor Friedrich Merz met in Berlin and announced plans to work more closely on economic growth, defence and technology.
SaxaVord Spaceport was identified as a focus for immediate work on European launches.
Two German companies are currently in a race to be the first to test a rocket in Shetland.
Chief executive Scott Hammond said: "The space strategy is absolutely critical.
"We're at the heart of the UK government's plans for assured access to space.
"That's also for our economic and Nato partners."
He added that the UK government had joined as one of its majority investors, with a member on the board, but stressed that SaxaVord Spaceport was still a private commercial company.
A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: "We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses.

"Through the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force, we are leading allied activity across the High North, strengthening Nato's northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats.

"This government is also investing in the capabilities needed to meet those threats, with £1.5bn backing Atlantic Bastion to deliver a next-generation Hybrid Navy and a further £330m to strengthen the protection of critical undersea infrastructure."
