items.title: Wild West crypto: Staggering Binance heist exposes sector fragility
paragraphs: A massive cyber heist of crypto exchange Binance is exposing some of the fragilities of the sector and reinforcing perceptions of the industry as a financial Wild West, critics warn.

items.title: Your writing was flagged as AI. What does that actually mean?
paragraphs: Some writers worry that AI detection software could falsely flag their work, potentially ruining reputations or job opportunities before they have a chance to prove the detectors wrong. karetoria/Getty Images hide caption

Ghostwriter Sally McGraw was hoping to land a job developing a book proposal for a prospective client. But after submitting a writing sample, she got an unexpected response: an email telling her that multiple artificial intelligence detection tools had flagged her work as machine-generated.
"I was floored because I had not used AI to generate the text," McGraw said. "I'd written it all myself."
Having spent more than 20 years as a professional nonfiction writer, McGraw said she was angry that her work had been dismissed as AI-written.
"You know where you see a cartoon character going red from their chin all the way up to the crown of their head? I felt my ears starting to burn," she said. "I thought, what is going on?"
McGraw said she assured the client she had written the proposal herself, but decided not to press the issue because she considered the job "minor."
Sally McGraw, a ghostwriter, said she's changed her writing style after a prospective client suggested her work was AI-generated. Sally McGraw hide caption

In an email to NPR, the client confirmed that she had screened McGraw's work for AI. But she said the results were not the determining factor in choosing to hire a different writer, instead citing experience and fit. McGraw says she was paid for her writing samples, but believes the detector results cost her the opportunity to write the full book proposal.

As editors struggle to keep up with a growing influx of AI-generated content, some are turning to detection tools to help sift through the mounting number of submissions. But these tools aren't perfect: They've been known to falsely flag human-written work as AI, which can leave writers with little idea of what triggered the result and how to prove otherwise.
"Everyone knows that these screeners are not 100% accurate," said McGraw.
Neil Clarke, publisher and editor of Clarkesworld, says a flood of AI submissions at the science-fiction magazine has put pressure on the editing staff.

In 2021, the publication received roughly 1,100 submissions a month. By February 2023, after AI agents like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini started to become widely available, that number had doubled, forcing Clarke to temporarily close its submission portal. He estimates his own workload has increased by about 30%.
"It's introduced an element of mistrust into the process," he said.

While AI detectors have gotten more sophisticated in recent years, the companies behind the detectors acknowledge that the tools aren't foolproof. Researchers have found that different AI detection tools can reach dramatically different conclusions about the same piece of writing.

In a study published in June, in the International Journal for Educational Integrity, researchers compared the accuracy of four widely used detectors. They tested 160 academic papers comprising four different categories: entirely human-written, entirely AI-written, a combination of the two, and AI material rewritten by a human.

Among the four detectors, Pangram was the most consistently accurate, correctly identifying the use of AI in 37 of the 40 papers with the combined text and in 37 of the 40 papers where a human rewrote AI-generated text.
Pangram CEO Max Spero, in an emailed statement, said his company's detector can make mistakes, particularly when there is not much writing to evaluate.
Previously published writing can pose an additional problem, says Chris Callison-Burch, a professor of computer and information science at the University of Pennsylvania.

"Many AI detectors work by asking a large language model how predictable a passage is," Callison-Burch said. "The catch is that the language models also tend to find text from their training data unusually predictable."

That could explain what science blogger Janelle Shane encountered in late 2022 when she tested excerpts from her 2019 book about how AI works, You Look Like a Thing and I Love You. One detector reported a 98.7% confidence that a passage was machine-generated.
"This is a clear, glaring, blinking-light false positive," Shane said. "I had written this text myself."
An unpublished draft like McGraw's writing sample wouldn't face that particular problem, Callison-Burch said, but could still be falsely flagged based on patterns in the writing style.

Detectors look for clues in word choice, punctuation and the way sentences are put together. The word "delve," frequent em dashes, and ideas grouped in lists of threes can trigger an AI-positive result, he said. So can opening sentences with adverbs such as "notably" or "crucially," or posing a question immediately followed by answering it.

At the same time, those are familiar habits for human writers. Callison-Burch says detectors weigh patterns across a whole piece, so an em dash or a particular word alone doesn't necessarily mean that a bot was used.

The Authors Guild, an organization that advocates for writers' rights, said in May that the use of AI detectors "creates an environment reminiscent of witch hunts," with writers worried about false accusations and how to defend themselves.

"A false positive can cost an author their publishing contract and reputation, and a false negative, when AI-generated work slips through reputable publishing undetected, can cause readers to lose their trust in authors and the industry," the Guild wrote.

Clarke, the sci-fi magazine publisher, sits somewhere in the middle. He says that while he doesn't personally use AI detectors to screen incoming manuscripts, he thinks certain detection tools could help overwhelmed editors manage the volume, provided they check the detector's findings. But he cautions against turning suspicions into accusations that could damage a writer's reputation.
"Submissions should end in rejection, not an accusation," he said.

McGraw says the fear of another accusation has changed how she writes. She says she now avoids using certain words and sentence constructions, and occasionally leaves out commas she used to include, hoping the inconsistency will help prove that a human wrote the text.
"I miss my em dash. It was something that I learned in journalism school and I've used it for decades," she said.
The ghostwriter also sees the irony. Large language models learn from human prose, yet she says feels the pressure to make hers look less like AI.
"It's like trying to fool a machine into thinking I'm not a machine," McGraw said.
And she worries about facing another accusation when a bigger opportunity is on the line.
"I'm bracing for the time when it's an assignment that I'm really gunning for and the outcome makes or breaks me," she said.

items.title: CENTCOM top commander says no sign of IRGC in the Strait of Hormuz
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

The commander of the U.S. Central Command known as CENTCOM operating in the Middle East says Iran's Revolutionary Guard naval forces which once had a near constant presence in the strategic Strait of Hormuz have disappeared.
Admiral Brad Cooper was speaking on Friday after visiting the region earlier this week where over 10,000 U.S. forces are enforcing naval blockade on Iranian ports and oil terminals.

"When I flew over the strait, I saw dozens of commercial vessels transiting all types, cargo, crude oil, liquid natural gas, or LNG. And I also saw our U.S. assets in the air and on the water," he said in a video published by CENTCOM Friday.
"Here's what I didn't see. I didn't see the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] out there, at all."

He said the U.S.-designated terror force's decades-long control of the waters and its harassment and threats, and seizure of commercial shipping has been decimated by the precision strikes of the U.S. military which sank Iran's navy vessels.
"They were not out there because Iran's navy is all at the bottom of the sea," he said.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard has long insisted it's in control of the strait and warned that any vessel attempting to pass the strait without prior approval from Tehran could be targeted.

On Friday, Iran's navy warned commercial vessels that the southern route close to Oman's coastline is "contaminated with mines," and threatened to hold the vessels’ owners and crews "responsible for using it," according to Iranian state media.
Iran's state news agency on Friday reported its navy destroyed a U.S. navy boat and that two tankers hit sea mines in the eastern side of Hormuz.
CENTCOM on Friday denied IRGC claims that it destroyed a U.S. military sea drone in the Strait of Hormuz.
"This claim is FALSE, just like many other IRGC lies this week," CENTCOM said in a post on X.
"All U.S. military unmanned surface vessels in the Middle East are accounted for, including a squadron of advanced sea drones on patrol in the Strait of Hormuz supporting CENTCOM's defensive layer."

The British maritime organization, UKMTO late Friday reported that a vessel has been hit by an unknown projectile on the port side, resulting fire. The incident occurred 40 nautical miles south of Lavan Island, Iran. Crews are safe and there is no reported environmental impact at this time, UKMTO said.
Cooper said the U.S. military has helped nations in the Persian Gulf export over 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer.
In contrast, he pointed out that due to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, Iran has been unable to export any oil since the U.S. reimposed the blockade in mid-July.

items.title: Oleshky evacuation begins as former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine calls Vladimir Putin an “obstacle” to talks
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

A large evacuation and humanitarian mission is currently under way in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky on the Dnipro River. The temporary ceasefire that made the truce evacuation possible, brokered by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, is a rare example of successful Russia-Ukraine negotiations. Speaking to VOA, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine says this temporary ceasefire is proof progress towards peace can be made.
On Friday morning, a delegation of Russian and Ukrainian human rights officials entered the war-ravaged town, and residents began boarding a convoy of buses to leave.

The convoy of about 25 buses arrived in Oleshky via Russian-occupied Crimea, about 85 km away. Ukraine’s ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the road had to be demined before the buses could travel safely. Two people were killed during the demining according to Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova.

Residents of Oleshky can choose to go to Ukraine or Russia. Residents who choose to go to Ukraine will travel to Russia, then fly to Belarus before crossing into Ukraine. Others are choosing to stay in Russia. About 2 thousand people were living in Oleshky when the evacuation was announced. Over 500 evacuees are choosing to relocate to Ukraine.

William B. Taylor, an expert at the Atlantic Council who served as U.S. Ambassador (2006-2009) and later as Chargé d’Affaires (2019–2020) in Ukraine, spoke to the VOA Russian Service about the prospects for the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky and its potential impact on U.S. President Donald Trump’s planned trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States.

According to Ambassador Taylor, the situation in Oleshky was horrific, and many people around the world, particularly Ukrainians, have been making the case that this horrible humanitarian situation needs to be addressed.
The city has been under constant shelling, and the residents who remain there have been left without drinking water or food. The routes out of the city have been mined.

Eventually, Taylor said, high profile figures such as Pope Leo XIV, the White House and Melania Trump took notice: "They raised it to a higher level of attention, and put some pressure on Putin." On October 23, an agreement on a temporary, localized ceasefire around the city was announced.
While it is impossible to say for sure, he believed it forced Putin to agree to a ceasefire: "It looked so bad for the Russians that they had to act."
The ceasefire was initially scheduled to start on October 29, but it went into effect earlier, on October 27, and is expected to remain in place through November 1.

Regarding U.S. involvement, Taylor described the ceasefire agreement as long overdue: "This should have happened a long time ago. The delay only prolonged the suffering of Ukrainians living in Russian-controlled territories."

According to Taylor, it is yet unknown whether this localized ceasefire could affect the upcoming scheduled trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and U.S., either at the technical level or at the summit level. The experience with prisoner exchanges and the P.O.W. exchanges between Russian and Ukraine demonstrate that progress can be achieved: "It shows that it's possible for the Ukrainians and the Russians to have an agreement, having a talk come to some understanding about how things can work. And that may be a good signal."
Taylor pointed that the Ukrainians have made it very clear that they're willing to talk and have already made some compromises, for example, about freezing the front lines.

"Many people, many Ukrainians want to push the Russians all the way out of their country back to 1991 borders. So, the point is, the Ukrainians have already made compromises. The Ukrainians have already proposed ceasefires. The Ukrainians have agreed with Trump on an energy cease fire."
The single obstacle for a successful trilateral meeting is the president of Russia: "There's one obstacle. There's just one obstacle, and that's Vladimir Putin," said Taylor.

items.title: UN reports sharp increase in opium poppy cultivation and production in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

Opium poppy cultivation in Afghanistan increased by 330 percent and opium production rose by 400 percent in 2026 compared to last year, according to a new survey by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.

The survey released Thursday found that opium poppy cultivation increased from 10,000 hectares in 2025 to 43,000 in 2026, while estimated opium production rose from 300 tons in 2025 to just under 1,500 tons in 2026.
The Taliban’s Ministry of Interior rejected the report, saying that its findings contradict official figures.

Before the Taliban’s takeover in 2021, Afghanistan was one of the world’s largest opiate suppliers. The group, however, outlawed the cultivation of narcotics nationwide in April 2022, which led to a massive decline in opium poppy production.
The UNODC report said that despite the sharp increase in 2026, opium poppy cultivation remained below the pre-ban levels, when more than 200,000 hectares of land were planted with poppy.
The report said the Taliban government reported eradicating about 22,000 hectares of poppy fields in 2026. UNODC, however, said that it could not independently verify the figures.
UNODC said that Afghan farmers have found ways to get around the Taliban’s restrictions.
The report said that opium poppy cultivation expanded from 29 provinces in 2025 to 34 provinces, and that only the southern Zabul province was opium free.
“The farmers are concealing small poppy plots within cereal fields or inside walled compounds or are planting and harvesting at staggered intervals to reduce the risk of detection,” said the report.

UNODC also reported that the prices of opium fell from $570 to $500 per kilogram compared with the previous year. However, prices remained three times higher than the seasonal averages before the Taliban’s ban on poppy cultivation.
A Kabul-based agricultural expert, who requested anonymity, told VOA that the survey paints a grim picture of unemployment in Afghanistan.
“It shows how people are struggling to cope with economic consequences of the Taliban’s rule,” he said.
The expert also said that the report calls into question the Taliban’s claim of having complete control over the country.
“The Taliban, because of that, say that they have reduced poppy cultivation to zero,” he added.
On Tuesday, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi said group's fight against narcotics was one of the its greatest achievements.
The expert, however, said the new report “damages the Taliban’s global image’ on the issue.

items.title: Nearly 2 out of 3 teens and tweens use AI chatbots, new research shows
paragraphs: According to survey data from Common Sense Media, nearly half 9-to-12-year-olds have used an AI chatbot or companion, and by age 13, nearly three-quarters of kids have used chatbots. Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images hide caption
Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Artificial intelligence chatbots are increasingly becoming a regular part of life for American youth. Two new surveys show that nearly two-thirds of tweens and teens use AI chatbots. While most kids use the technology for help with school work, and for companionship and emotional support, certain uses were linked with worse mental health symptoms.

One survey, done by the online safety advocacy group, Common Sense Media, found that AI use starts early – years before kids hit the minimum age of 13 on most popular chatbots. Nearly half 9-to-12-year-olds have used an AI chatbot or companion. By the time kids are 13 years old, nearly three-quarters of them have used chatbots.

The other survey, done by the mental health advocacy group JED Foundation, found that 90% of the 5,500 9-to-17-year-olds in schools across the country have used an AI chatbot. Nearly two-thirds use it both for schoolwork and as companions, or when they are stressed, lonely, anxious or overwhelmed.

The findings are "remarkable" in showing how dramatically AI use by children and teens has changed in a short time, says developmental psychologist Anne Maheux at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, who wasn't involved in the surveys.

"It seems like just a few years ago, no one was using" the technology, she says. "And now it seems like roughly the same number of kids using it for homework are using it to get emotional support or help with coping."

"I use it to make myself practice sample questions – sample test questions that I will answer with my own work," says 15-year-old Arjun Sharda, in Round Rock, Texas. "I use it to understand concepts outside of the classroom."
He uses both OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, he says, although he prefers the latter lately.

In Raynham, Mass., McKenzie Craig, 17, has been using chatbots since she was in eighth grade. "I use it typically if I'm overwhelmed with a bunch of tasks I have," she says. "I'll have it help me prioritize the tasks."

She also uses it for help with assignments. "If I write an essay, I'll run it through either Grammarly or ChatGPT and have it graded, so to speak," says Craig. "It gives me feedback, and then I can edit accordingly."
Sharda says he and his friends also turn to chatbots when they are stressed and anxious.
"With tests, for example," he says, "I was so scared of failing one of my first chemistry tests on conversions and moles that I kept asking ChatGPT 'Will I be OK? Will my GPA still be fine?'"
Researchers at the JED Foundation also surveyed students on symptoms of overall well-being and mental health.

"We were able to look at how young people are using AI and then how that correlates separately with indicators of well-being, history of suicidal ideation and attempts, and poor mental health," says psychologist Kayla Anderson, vice president of research and evaluation at the JED Foundation.

"When young people are using AI, when they're in emotional distress," she adds, "they're more likely to report poor mental health and well-being outcomes." They also report a greater history of suicidal thoughts and attempts.
But the data don't suggest a causal link, cautions Anderson.

"It's unclear, based on these data, whether AI use is contributing to poor mental health and well-being, or whether students who are already in distress in certain ways are more likely to turn to AI," she explains.
But preliminary data collected by other researchers suggests that the link between chatbots and poorer mental health symptoms in young people might go both ways, says Maheux.
"So kids who do have worse mental health are seeking out AI to help them," she says. "But that AI use may be exacerbating those mental health challenges instead of helping."
In a soon-to-be-published study of middle schoolers in one state, Maheux and her colleagues at UNC found that students who use chatbots for companionship grew lonelier over time.

They found similar results in another study of young adults. "We see that people who are using AI more for companionship or feeling like they're overreliant on AI to solve various emotional or cognitive problems, are developing worse mental health over time."

One potential explanation for this effect, she says, is that AI is easing people's emotional distress — loneliness, anxiety, stress — in the immediate moment, but that reliance on the technology is preventing young people from developing the skills to tolerate and navigate normal daily stresses.
That, she explains, "can lead to worse mental health."

items.title: Websites pretending to be local news are boosting Democratic candidates
paragraphs: 📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App

Ahead of the midterms, some voters are turning to ChatGPT to help them decide who to vote for. When asked for information about candidates in some highly competitive races, NPR found that OpenAI's AI chatbot cited a set of websites that are thinly veiled political ads made to look like reporting from local news outlets.

Less than two weeks before Election Day, when asked "Which House candidates in [Michigan's 4th Congressional District] care about affordability?," the chatbot said Democrat Sean McCann had the "Most detailed published affordability plan" at the very top of its answer. The stakes in this race are high – it's one of the competitive U.S. House races that could determine control of the chamber.
ChatGPT's response when NPR asked "Which House candidates in [Michigan's 4th Congressional District] care about affordability?" hide caption

As a citation, ChatGPT linked to a website called the Kalamazoo Beacon. The Beacon labels its articles as "news articles" in the website's source code. The outlet also describes itself in the site's source code as "Reporting on Kalamazoo, southwest Michigan, and the issues shaping lakeshore communities."
But the Kalamazoo Beacon has only published 16 stories, all about McCann, his policy positions and his record as a state legislator, NPR's review shows.

The Beacon is one of 10 "local news" websites that promote one Democrat apiece in competitive U.S. House races. The 10 sites are part of a larger group of 37 websites identified by the digital security firm VisionHeight that promote many more candidates, mostly Democrats, for a slew of federal, state and local offices, as well as some nonpartisan posts like judges.

ChatGPT's citation of these websites highlights how AI-generated answers can become yet another avenue for stealthy political advertising as more voters consult chatbots before they head to the polls.

While it makes sense that political campaigns and their allies would try to optimize their message for pickup by AI chatbots, pretending to operate as news outlets crosses a line into deception, said Renée DiResta, an associate research professor at Georgetown University who studies online influence campaigns.
When users ask AI chatbots questions, less-credible websites can make an appearance when the chatbots search the internet and summarize the content of links in the search results.

"Disclosing funding … would be obviously the ethical thing to do here, or at least indicating that this is a linked effort," DiResta said. At the same time, she said, opposition research entities are trying to make sure that bad information about candidates is found. "So there really is this competition for curation, and it's going to have interesting ramifications as the frontier companies themselves try to figure out how to get better at not falling for it."

It's unclear who operates the websites. NPR was unable to find or reach the site operators. One of the Democrats promoted by the network, JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona, said she wasn't behind the websites and doesn't know who is. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the campaign arm of the House Democrats, denied involvement in a phone call with NPR. Other candidates the websites promoted, including McCann, as well as other Democratic super PACs that support the candidates, including American Bridge 21st Century, Tomorrow Together and House Majority PAC, did not respond to NPR's requests for comment.

The set of 37 websites presents candidates in different, overlapping groups. Each of the 10 Democrats covered by a site purporting to cover local news is also the sole subject of a site that offers opinion articles about why voters should support them. The various candidates, who are running in different states, also show up in roundup-style articles on five more websites that have names such as "Public Safety Democrats" and "Democratic Women in the House."
The volume of websites and articles may also help the network's operator boost their preferred narratives, DiResta said.

Another 12 websites, each focusing on a state, covered the House candidates in those states as well as other state and local candidates running for office. The state and national websites also boosted an 11th House candidate that did not have her own dedicated site purporting to be local news.

While most of the sites are openly partisan, the articles published by the network link out to sources for the claims they make, such as congressional voting records, mainstream news articles and partisan news sources, such as the pro-Democrat Courier network.

Opposing candidates mostly made infrequent and brief appearances in articles published by the network that VisionHeight found, NPR's review shows. The articles that did bring up opposing candidates substantively included candidate profiles, as well as writeups that focused on their records on issues that could be possible political liabilities, like support for data centers, not stopping the Iran war, rolling back Medicaid and supporting tariffs.

Multiple indicators suggest that all 37 websites share a common operator. All the websites were set up on September 15 – all but one were registered within an 8-minute period – according to registry and digital certificate data gathered by VisionHeight and Andreas Sjöstedt, a co-founder of Erebus, a hybrid threat forensics firm. Sjöstedt was not involved in VisionHeight's research.

Hundreds of articles appeared on the websites in batches in September and October. The large volume of articles in a concentrated amount of time suggests that the operator may have used AI to fill out the material, VisionHeight's report said.

After the websites went online, their operator continued to polish them. Earlier in October, the 10 websites that posed as local news outlets, including the Kalamazoo Beacon that had promoted Sean McCann, shared the same description: "Straight local news - reports on the race and (once a content-sourcing workflow exists) community storylines, in neutral third-person news style." Since then, those descriptions have become more tailored to the areas the outlets purported to cover.

The websites transparently welcome AI chatbots: All the websites explicitly allow a long list of AI crawlers made by major AI companies to scrape information off of them. Many articles are formatted as questions and answers, which chatbots tend to prefer to cite. Many news organizations prevent such crawlers from going through their websites because the crawlers take content without bringing in revenue.

Every website in the network also contained a file called llms.txt, which lists articles on the site in plain text. This is surprising because most websites don't have these files, said Alisha Ukani, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Washington's Center for an Informed Public, who noticed these files while reviewing the sites at NPR's request. Ukani focuses on how AI is changing the internet. In an email, she noted that the websites that do have llms.txt files tend to be "biased towards technology and business-related websites."

To gauge the group's success in getting picked up by AI chatbots, NPR drafted 37 questions and used them on ChatGPT and Gemini, the two most popular AI chatbots, as well as Google search, which sometimes provides AI-generated answers in its results. For each of the 10 congressional races, NPR asked more general questions, such as which candidates care about issues such as public safety. NPR also asked the chatbots questions more specific to individual candidates, such as their priorities.

In 19 responses, or about half the time, ChatGPT cited at least one article from the network of websites, often citing them alongside other sources such as Ballotpedia, a website that tracks races and candidates, or the candidates' own campaign websites. In 17 of those 19 times, the chatbot cited one of the outlets that pretended to be a local news site. In the other two instances, ChatGPT cited websites from the network that purport to cover politics in a state.

The group's output may have been even more successful in being picked up when users ask about down ballot candidates. NPR identified five city council candidates in Michigan that a website in the group called the Wolverine State Report covered. When NPR asked ChatGPT about the positions of each of the candidates, ChatGPT cited the website every time.

Unlike traditional search engines, submitting the same question multiple times to a chatbot can give users significantly different responses. NPR submitted each query only once, so future or parallel experiments may yield different results. However, preliminary research has shown that chatbots tend to cite questionable sources more often when there are very few sources of credible reporting, such as downballot races where there is often less news coverage. The phenomenon is called a "data void."

Google's products behaved very differently. Gemini did not cite any links from the group of websites in all the responses. In seven instances, the chatbot also declined to respond to the questions at all and pointed NPR to external sources. Google search also did not surface any links from the group in its first page search results, and its AI Overview did not mention the websites either.

VisionHeight's report showed that in early October, at least one site did show up on Google's first page result, ranking higher than Ballotpedia. The company did not systematically measure how the sites showed up for different candidates, VisionHeight's CTO Nitsan Daniel told NPR.
Google spokesperson Davis Thompson said that the company detected a policy violation in this instance and took "swift action."
"Our generative AI features are built on Search ranking systems, which are designed to show high quality content and block spam and abuse," Thompson said.

OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans said, "ChatGPT's search tools cite from a range of sources so people can explore and make their own judgements." He added that, "When issues are brought to our attention, we take action to improve our model responses."

It's unclear what OpenAI has changed since NPR flagged the sites to it. The Kalamazoo Beacon was still cited as a source every time after NPR received OpenAI's response and ran a query five times. In some instances, McCann no longer gets the distinction as having the "most detailed affordability plan," but in other instances, he still does.

Thinly veiled advertising that purports to be a news source has a long history, said Patrick Warren, a professor at Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub. People used to get ad flyers that look like newspapers, or glance at ads mixed in with legitimate news in traditional online search, Warren said, and reading AI chatbot answers without evaluating the underlying sources is just the latest version of the experience. "There's nothing new under the sun."

To better understand the content of the websites and how they changed, NPR downloaded every website homepage and article page twice, on October 19 and October 24, which enabled NPR to see how they evolved. These records were also used to verify VisionHeight's observations. NPR manually reviewed all the "local news" and "local opinion" sites and used AI to analyze every article posted on the sites focused on state and national races.

For every candidate mentioned in the articles, AI was used to extract the names, party affiliation and offices in contention. NPR then conducted keyword searches and manually reviewed articles to examine how opposing candidates were portrayed and confirm findings.
To test whether ChatGPT, Gemini and Google search cited the websites, NPR entered the following prompts:

NPR substituted [district] and [candidate] with the 10 candidates and districts the websites focused on. In some races there was either no female candidate or the woman wasn't one who was being promoted by the network.

NPR ran the queries manually on October 22 and 23, using a VPN to change the IP address to the corresponding state or a nearby state. NPR also used individual private browsing sessions for each tool and prompt.

items.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
paragraphs: Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.
South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.
Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.
The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.
The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.
However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.
“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.
“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

items.title: Inter and Milan unveil plans for new shared stadium to replace San Siro
paragraphs: Internazionale and Milan have unveiled plans for their new Generali Stadium, which will replace the shared San Siro venue from the 2031-32 season.

The stadium, sponsored by Generali – Italy’s largest insurance company – will have a capacity of 71,500 seats and is expected to cost the two clubs €1.2 billion (£1bn). The plans were revealed at a gala event at Milan’s Castello Sforzesco on Thursday – but some fans in attendance voiced their opposition to San Siro being demolished.

Shortly before the briefing began, a group of Inter fans walked into the courtyard of the castle and unfurled a banner reading “you will never extinguish the lights at San Siro,” and chanting “hands off San Siro.” Work on the new stadium is set to begin in 2028, on the site of the existing 75,000-capacity venue.

The Generali Stadium will be shaped “low in the body, and rises up at either end” behind the goals, architect Norman Foster said. David Manica, a stadium specialist who collaborated with Foster on the project, added that the steep-sided design aims to bring fans as close to the pitch as possible.

“The most important thing that we realised when we designed this project is that San Siro is a feeling,” Manica said. “It’s more than a building, it’s a feeling … we brought all the seats as close as possible to the field. They could not be any closer, it’ll actually feel as though you’re sitting on the grass.”

The stadium will also be capable of hosting NFL international games, rugby matches and concerts. Milan and Inter paid €197 million (£165m) to acquire the current San Siro stadium and its adjacent parking arenas. The current ground will be largely demolished once construction work nears completion.

Also known as the Giuseppe Meazza Stadium, San Siro opened in 1926 and is the largest sports stadium in Italy. It is considered to be one of European football’s most iconic venues, but requires extensive modernisation despite undergoing a number of renovations during its lifespan.

The Generali Stadium could be used as a venue for Euro 2032, which is being jointly hosted by Italy and Turkey. Foster and Manica previously worked together on the new Wembley Stadium, while the architect’s Foster + Partners firm also designed the plans for Manchester United’s proposed new 100,000-capacity home.
Additional reporting from Associated Press

items.title: Skulls, bulls and someone peeing in her own eye: four great exhibitions to see for free
paragraphs: Andy Warhol’s skull leers at Francisco de Zurbarán’s trussed-up little lamb from across the length of the gallery. Separated by hundreds of years – Warhol’s painting from the 1970s, Zurbarán’s from the 1630s – it’s an intergenerational conversation about still life’s staying power, and the inevitability of death.

This brilliant little show brings together still life paintings from way back in the past right up to the present day. There’s a gorgeous 1610-19 Dutch flower painting by Osaias Beert the Elder, and a vast vision of meats and cheeses with a pair of animal lungs hung grossly on a hook behind by Giovanni Battista Recco from the 1650s. There are piles of 19th-century French apples, vases of undulating 18th-century flowers. And then that little Zurbarán lamb – one of six he painted – glassy-eyed and morose, so laden with religious symbolism.

When we hit the modern era, there’s a lovely Pierre Bonnard painting of grapes and apples in sickly yellow and orange, a genuinely amazing Nicolas de Staël composition of stark, blocky bottles, lumps of pink rock by Philip Guston that look like cheese. Ignore the crap Picasso and the lumpen Juan Gris, and you get to come face to face with Warhol’s grim, grinning neon orange skull.

The whole show reinforces the idea that still life painting is terribly named. Because it’s not about life at all, it’s about death. Every fruit and vegetable in these works is about to rot, every flower is wilting, every animal carcass is about to go fetid. These are paintings of life’s fragility and precariousness. This is about how time is fleeting, how life is temporary. Mortality is written into every brush stroke.

Is this the greatest still life show ever put on? Does it have a tight curatorial concept? Does it tell an important story about the history and evolution of the genre? No, no and no. It’s just a bunch of really good, historic paintings. See, still life isn’t all just flowers and fruit. And even when it is, it’s pretty good.

Panting, his grey tongue hanging out, blood streaming down his back, the bull is on the verge of death. Paul Pfeiffer’s newest film captures the moment a matador plunges a sword into that bull’s back, but with no fanfare, no drama, no judgment. This is a film about ritual and spectacle, not about animal cruelty or cultural violence.

This isn’t Pfeiffer at his most attractive or impressive. Instead, this long, awkward, often ugly piece of art cinema zooms in on the faces of the crowd at a corrida, the hands of the saxophone players in the band, the colours of the walls, the patterns on the matadors’ clothing. It’s all the tiny details of this spectacle, the intricacies that make it tick.

It is, essentially, a film about how humanity creates spectacles to lose ourselves in, and how we repeat actions, sounds and movements to create some kind of meaning. The film is outwardly about bullfighting, but more widely about all rituals, religious or cultural. Is the corrida any different from going to church or a concert or a football match? In the end, we’re all just trying to find meaning by taking part, by belonging, by coming together and cheering as one. Throughout the film, people cheer, drink and eat, the band plays, a bull dies. That’s life, I guess. Joy and sorrow with some snacks in between.
Thomas Dane Gallery, London, until 19 December
Ebecho Muslimova has gone through the looking-glass, and what she has found on the other side is more worrying and uncomfortable than any kind of horror fantasy land. She’s found reality.

In every painting and installation here, Muslimova’s cartoon alter ego Fatebe is navigating a world turned upside down, spun on its head and inverted. Fatebe is a lewd, rude, nude comic book character, her naked body able to twist and contort, her face always plastered with a grin and her orifices always on display. One painting finds multiple Fatebes bent over, gleefully scrubbing parquet floors (a nod to a Gustave Caillebotte painting, this show is drowning in art history references) while another Fatebe makes a paper chain out of fabric she’s yoinking out of her nethers. Yet another work sees hundreds of Fatebes filing up the stairs of the gallery itself, but the plaster is crumbling and the print is peeling.

Fatebe is trapped under a glass like a spider, or she’s turned herself into the legs of a table. In one drawing she has grown two heads, one peeing into the other’s eye, the other defecating back in return.

All this gross-out weirdness and art historical density isn’t about fantasy and escape though. I think it’s about feeling pulled in endless directions, it’s about being stuck between the place you came from and the place you’re in now, it’s about discomfort and alienation. Or it’s about being able to wee in your own eye. Who knows, really. Either way, it works.

Back in 2013, a Palestinian fisherman found an ancient Greek statue of Apollo poking out of the sand. Thinking it was gold, they cut off a finger, but it was just beautiful, mottled green bronze. They tried to sell it on eBay, posting pictures of the sculpture laid carefully on Smurf bedsheets, but the authorities stepped in and confiscated the sculpture. No one knows where it is now, but Rosalind Nashashibi has painted it here, preserving its strange, almost magical history in hazy visions of green limbs on cartoon-covered sheets.

Not all the works are good, and the images of nudes and landscapes feel either like a distraction or filler. But the Apollo images are great. They’re like paintings of an autopsy, stark and unsettling. They’re filled with narratives – a clash of ancient art and modern cartoon, a beleaguered people finding hope of salvation in a gift from the gods, an act of care as those people gently try to preserve this sculpture on their softest bedsheets. Hope and despair, history and the present, all colliding in some often beautiful, washed-out painting.

items.title: LS Lowry review – matchstick men, or the broken denizens of a smog-filled hellscape?
paragraphs: While people queue at the British Museum to see the Battle of Hastings, this excellent survey of LS Lowry at the MK Gallery in Milton Keynes takes you back to another, maybe more decisive part of our past – the age when Britain was the most industrialised society on Earth. Laurence Lowry was born in 1887 and worked for 41 years as a rent collector, a job that took him all over his native Greater Manchester observing its people and places. He had the city’s grime and grind in his soul. The MK wants to show him as a fully rounded artist, to uncover the Lowry with a song in his heart, but it’s the misery of his urban hell that holds and harrows you.

In his 1930 painting Coming from the Mill it’s the end of the shift and scores of people emerge from a factory’s bleak yellow gatehouse as if leaving prison. Their daily captivity has left them broken and exhausted and the little abstracted figures hunch forwards as they walk without pausing to laugh or chat, going to their separate homes, each one withdrawn, wretched. They are not the painting’s protagonists – they are passive victims. The architecture of industry dominates the picture as it rules their lives. How can any of these little people, dwarfed by the mill that eats their time and energy, attain individuality? No wonder they all look the same except for minor variations in their drab clothes. They’ve been reduced by the Industrial Revolution to matchstick people.

Lowry is the Franz Kafka of industrial Britain. He is not a naive artist who painted crudely because that’s the best he could do. Nor is he a patient social realist laying bare the injustices of capitalism – although Friedrich Engels would surely have recognised his Manchester. He is a modern expressionist who finds his inner melancholy reflected in the industrial sublime. He drinks in its despair, feasts on its poetry of alienation. As you journey through Lowry’s North, you sink ever further into his personal slough of despond.

Slough of Despond would make a good alternative title for his 1924 drawing The River Irwell at the Adelphi. Heaps of mud and ash choke the slow-moving river that runs through Salford, its shores lined with decaying sheds and slums against a smoggy, chimney-lined sky. It’s Lowry at his purest as he depicts the stunning, crushing presence of the city itself. He draws and paints the black, gnarled spires of urban churches with as much relish as those monstrous mills. In the second world war he was a fire-watcher with a privileged view of the blitz: a drawing of freshly bombed buildings in Piccadilly, Manchester shows husks of charred brick still wreathed in smoke.

This show digs out other, less well known dimensions to his talent. But his paintings of the Lake District are even more chilling than his cities. Lake Landscape, painted in 1950, is a vista of low curving hills divided by silvery still water, receding in abstract, musical pulses of sadness. No people or animals inhabit this eerie world. When he paints people close up it’s even more disturbing: a young man with staring eyes, a father and sons who all seem equally desperate. He lightens up to paint his ideal woman with a simplified doll-like face apparently intended as his tribute to Pre-Raphaelite red-lipped beauties but the result is weirdly robotic. Her face is on the exhibition merchandise, perhaps because Halloween is coming.

The most bizarre painting, however, is his 1963 work In a Park. At first glance it’s another city crowd scene until you realise everyone in this fenced enclosure has something different about them. A one-eyed face screams while people walk around the white-earthed, empty space with spinal deformities, facial palsies, amputated limbs. The catalogue gets itself in knots – is Lowry mocking the disabled or questioning how we define disability?
But this painting is not about disability in a political sense at all. It uses it as an image of humanity in general: all people are broken and alone, misshapen in Lowry’s hopeless universe.

Lowry is a tricky customer. If it is pure snobbery to look down on him for being popular it is also patronising to see this troubled artist as a warmly sentimental nostalgist of the north. He is a painter of modern life in the age when that meant huge crowds staggering home in the shadow of smoking chimneys in cities blackened by carbon. At his best, Lowry is a great modern artist. His 1919 painting Pit Tragedy shows working-class people waiting for the worst news. They are statuesque, tragically posed in the grey dusty light. A woman turns towards us, her head veiled. Her pain is lost in the past but lives on here, observed and recorded by Lowry, visionary of the industrial age.
LS Lowry: The Theatre of Life is at MK Gallery, Milton Keynes until 28 February

items.title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?
paragraphs: In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream.

“Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes.

A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss.

Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee.

In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare.

The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently, France, India and Argentina are among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee.

Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recent global survey found greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows the same pattern, with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.”

Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.”

Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, he replied: “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?”

Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways.

“The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said.

Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychological benefits. While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College.

“Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.”

In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project.

Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products.

If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement.

In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE.

Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise.

The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods.

Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.”

items.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new features
paragraphs: As the Ultra enters its fourth year as Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch it gets the best kind of spec upgrade – longer battery life – while waiting for something potentially more transformative.

That’s because several of the key features announced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026 have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically the same as last year’s model.
The Ultra 4’s body, screen, colours and design are identical to the previous versions. It weighs about 1g more, but the bigger changes are on the back and inside.

Upgraded sensors on the back of the watch take heart rate (HR) readings every five seconds during the day, up from every five minutes on previous generation Apple Watches. They also enable the measurement of your heart rate variability (HRV) during the day, not only at night, which feeds into some new recovery metrics.

The Ultra 4 is the first Apple Watch in several generations to get a meaningfully faster chip with the new S11. The battery life for general use in my testing now stretches to 79 hours, too, meaning the watch lasted well into its third day between charges. Most will be able to charge it every third morning, or less if you use the low power modes, although that is far behind the week-plus stamina of top adventure watch rivals.
The new watch charges at 10W with its little magnetic puck, up from 5W of previous generations, and reached 82% in under an hour and 100% in less than 90 minutes.
Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, wifi 4, 5G RedCap/4G, UWB
Sensors: HR, ECG, spO2, temp, depth, dual-band GPS, compass, altimeter

The Apple Watch features some of the most comprehensive health tracking available on your wrist, which on the Ultra includes extremely accurate dual-band GPS tracking for exercise. The more frequent HR and HRV measurements enable a few new features for the Ultra 4. The Vitals app, which monitors your stats overnight, now works during the day giving you an assessment of your general health. It can let you know when your HR and HRV are outside your usual baseline, indicating strain or sickness that might be on the way.

The new readiness app adds a popular feature from sports watches, which looks at your activity, vitals and sleep and works out whether you have properly recovered from strenuous exercise or stressful days. It gives you a score out of 10 and some advice on how ready you are for exercise, which can be a useful tool for training for a race or goal.

The Ultra 4 runs watchOS 27, just like Apple Watches back to the Series 9 and Ultra 2, which includes Apple’s new Siri and improved AI tools, some of which are available now, while other exclusive features are awaiting updates planned for later this year.

The upgraded Siri is available to talk to and behaves very similarly to that on a modern iPhone, including the Siri app for reviewing previous interactions. The new Siri Modular watch face features the top timely widget, which has been surprisingly useful. It shows simple things such as the timer when you have one running, or the weather when it starts raining. It also puts your vitals front and centre in the morning, or your calendar if you have an upcoming event, replacing the need for multiple complications.

Shazam music recognition is now significantly faster, while the sound recognition accessibility feature, which listens out for certain sounds, such as a fire alarm, doorbell, car horn or baby crying, and sends an alert to your wrist could be very useful.

But the marquee “audio intelligence” features that could be transformative and controversial are not yet enabled, being expected in “late 2026”. Siri Recap promises to transcribe conversations all day before delivering them as an AI summary. It doesn’t record audio or keep full transcripts, just the text summaries, but the Live Rewind feature can show you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation so you can see what you missed.
Apple says the battery should last more than 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £95. Damage repairs cost £539.
The watch contains more than 45% recycled material, which is broken down in its environmental impact report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling for devices.
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in a choice of two colours and multiple bands costing from £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349).
For comparison, the Apple Watch Series 12 costs from £369, the Watch SE 3 costs £219 and the Garmin Fenix 9 costs from £860.

The Ultra 4 is the best smartwatch Apple makes. It has a great screen, rugged looks and all the trappings of other Apple Watches, including Apple Pay, comprehensive health tracking and full integration with an iPhone.

The faster charging and longer battery life are welcome, lasting about six hours more for general use than previous versions in testing. The more frequent heart rate readings and daytime heart rate variability monitoring are additive rather than revolutionary. The readiness and recovery monitoring add to the existing suite of training tools to close the gap to top-tier sports watches from Garmin and others.
Upgraded Siri is more useful on your wrist, and the new Siri Modular watch face was a surprisingly good addition. But the new audio intelligence features are not here yet.
That makes the Ultra 4 a great Apple Watch, just not a significant upgrade on those that came before.

Pros: great screen, rugged yet sophisticated design, hands-free gestures, three-plus-day battery life, 4G/5G and satellite SOS/messaging, comprehensive health tracking, great activity tracking with dual-band GPS, recovery/readiness tracking, better Siri, extra action button, 100-metre water resistance and 40-metre dive-ready, long software support.
Cons: no big upgrade on previous model, very expensive, only works with an iPhone, no third-party watch faces, shorter battery life than adventure watch rivals, marquee AI features not yet available.

items.title: Why has a crumbling bottle plant been rebuilt in Paris? The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shaped
paragraphs: Ibrahim Mahama has dug through the ruins of post-colonial Ghana, sorted through the ashes of its ancient history, picked through the industrial detritus, the corporate waste, the piles of rubbish, and found something pretty unique: hope.

Sit on one of the Asante stools in his circular Parliament of Ghosts and you can almost feel a new future being worked out right in front of you. It’s the first installation in this huge exhibition at the Fondation Cartier in Paris, and it sums Mahama up pretty neatly. He’s looking at the collapse of the Ghanaian government in 1966, the way the hope of the post-colonial project was crushed in a military coup, and he’s looking at ancient Ghanaian history, at the empires that fell centuries ago and the way colonialism tore them to shreds. But he’s not lamenting any of them. He’s not mourning. Instead, he’s reclaiming them, asking how things can be rebuilt, how we can move forwards by learning from the past.

And he does it over and over. In 2024 he bought an old bottle factory – a symbol of industry and its collapse. He’s rebuilt it here, in the centre of Paris. Its steel roof beams, rusted and crumbling, reach up to the ceiling, its walls are lined with thousands of green bottles in Coca-Cola, Schweppes, Kool and Club Minerals crates. It’s a whole history of manufacturing, of commerce in West Africa post-independence. Not left to rot, but rebuilt and reconfigured into something new.
Nearby, he’s taken some of those bottles and piled them around a collection of local pottery. The industrial meets the artisanal, two lost arts creating a new one.

But this huge show isn’t really about Mahama, it’s about the people around him. Most of the work here is by nine other artists and collectives. Mahama runs three art centres near Tamale in Ghana, giving time, space and opportunities to local artists. Their work is given priority here, alongside art by his mentors and collaborators. He’s taken this massive exhibition opportunity and used it as a chance to celebrate his community. It’s almost as if he’s trying to make the rest of us feel bad.

Way up on the top floor, a long scroll of jute and bark by Dorothy Akpene Amenuke undulates across the floor. If it looks like Mahama’s work, it should: she was his art teacher back in 2013. Knowledge, and the past, gets reconfigured and reshaped once again.

Nearby, the wall of a farmhouse has been built by artist and architect Courage Dzidula Kpodo out of red earth clay, a material lost as modernism brought in concrete. Now, historic methods become a kind of resistance, a symbol of tradition’s ability to endure.

Those core ideas get repeated through pretty much every presentation here. Influential 97-year-old photographer James Barnor captures the communities around Mahama in large format, grainy Polaroids. Gideon Appah’s hazy, dream-like paintings imagine fictional Ghanaian youths staring out to sea, congregating on beaches in utopian, idealised visions of the country’s past. Some of the works are absolutely stunning, like Peter Doig and Noah Davis transported to Accra.

The best work, appropriately enough, isn’t by one artist but a collective. On the top floor, a bunch of lumpy, surreal sculptures of birds, bodies and men wrestling bulls is by the Congolese Plantation Workers Art League (CATPC). Each one is made of chocolate, sculpted in the DRC but poured into moulds in Amsterdam. Everything they make from selling the art goes towards buying back land confiscated in the early 20th century by the Lever Brothers, who we now know as Unilever. The work is a whole conversation about global trade taking place in sculptural form, an act of resistance and reclamation through chocolate.

This exhibition is essentially an ambitious, ultra-idealistic group show of West African art. It is art exhibition as political utopianism. Which is great, even if not everything in it is good. And the real draw is Mahama, with his archival approach to monumental installation art, and it’s a shame to not get a load more of it.

Mahama has sacrificed himself for the greater good, basically. But this collaborative approach is the point: he’s saying collective action, community, togetherness, that’s how we’ll build a future. It might sound a bit cloying and earnest, but then you see the results, you see the art and the ideas, you see the community and the hope and the idealism and you eventually say: “Get me a one-way ticket to Accra. I’m in.”
